en: In the beginning, the great one stood upright before the dawns; emerging from the darkness, he came with light.
Agni, the fair-limbed, with his radiant luster, having been born, has filled all dwellings.
Born as the embryo of heaven and earth, O Agni, you are lovely, distributed among the plants;
a wondrous infant, you have gone forth from your mothers, crying aloud beyond the darkness and the nights.
Viṣṇu, thus knowing his highest [abode], great when born, protects the third [step]. When they have offered him the milk from his mouth, those who are of one mind sing praises here.
Therefore, the mothers who bear the nourishment approach you, the increaser of food, with offerings of food.
You go toward them again; you are the Hotṛ among the human clans, assuming various forms.

The Hotṛ-priest of the sacrifice, with his brilliant chariot, the radiant banner of every rite—Agni, by virtue of his greatness, is the counterpart of every god through his splendor; he is the guest of men.
Wearing well-fashioned garments, Agni, born at the navel of the earth, ruddy in his station at the place of Iḷā, the royal domestic priest— do thou worship the gods here.

For you, O Agni, have always extended across both Heaven and Earth, as a son extends over his two mothers. Come forth toward those who long for you, O youngest one; then, O powerful one, bring the gods here.
Satisfy the longing gods, O youngest one; knowing the seasons, O Lord of Seasons, sacrifice here.
With those who are the divine officiants, O Agni, you are the most excellent sacrificer among all invokers.
You perform the office of the *hotṛ* and the *potṛ* for the people; you are the wise thinker (*mandhātṛ*), the giver of wealth, and the observer of Truth (*ṛtāvā*).
With the cry of *svāhā*, let us prepare the oblations; may Agni, the worthy god, worship the gods.
We have come to the path of the gods so that we may follow and accomplish what we are able to do.
Agni, the knower, shall sacrifice; he is the Hotṛ-priest; he shall arrange the sacrifices and the seasons.
O gods, if we, being more ignorant, violate the vows of you who are wise,
may Agni, the knower, fulfill all that through those seasons by which he ordains the gods.
When mortals, with simple minds and feeble skill, do not comprehend the sacrifice,
then Agni— the Hotṛ who knows the rite, the discerning one, the best of sacrificers— shall worship the gods according to the seasons.
For the progenitor begot you as the face of all sacrifices, a wondrous banner.
So, perform your worship according to the man-filled lands; [grant] desirable foods, abundant in cattle and beneficial to all people.
O Agni, you whom Heaven and Earth, you whom the Waters, and you whom Tvaṣṭṛ of noble birth have generated—
you, knowing well the path traveled by the fathers, shine forth brilliantly as you are kindled.
O King, the kindler, the impetuous one, well-enkindled for skill, has been seen;
he shines forth, conscious, with lofty luster, driving away the black night and approaching the radiant dawn.
When he, generating the dark, speckled maiden— the daughter of the great father— overcame her with his form, he, the messenger of heaven,
shines forth with his riches, supporting the upward-rising beam of the sun.
The auspicious one has come, accompanied by the auspicious; the lover follows after his sister.
Spreading abroad with days of excellent luster, Agni has overcome the darkness with his radiant colors.
The paths of this great Agni, kindled like the voices of his friend, the auspicious one—
of the adorable, mighty bull, the fair-faced ones and the splendors have shone forth like nights upon his course.
Whose brilliant rays flow forth like sounds, as he shines brightly, lofty, and fair of aspect;
he who reaches the sky with his most excellent, most piercing, playful, and most exalted beams of light.
The breaths of this one, whose fellies are visible as he speeds along with his teams, resound loudly;
he who, the most divine messenger, shines far and wide with his ancient, radiant, and resonant flames.
May he bring us great wealth and may he sit as the messenger between the two youthful ones, Heaven and Earth.
Agni, swift with his swift horses, impetuous with his impetuous steeds, may he come hither.
I sacrifice to you; I send forth this thought to you, so that you may become worthy of praise in our invocations.
O Agni, ancient King, you are like a watering-place in the desert for the Pūru who desires to worship.
O youngest one, you whom the people approach from all sides as cattle seek their warm stall— you are the messenger of both gods and mortals; great, you move between them with your radiant light.
Like a noble infant, thy mother, cherishing thee, bears thee while seeking thy favor;
from the dry land thou rushest down the slope, longing for it, like a beast let loose to win the prize.
O wise one, we are fools; you alone, O Agni, truly know your own greatness.
As the Lord of the People, he lies down, he moves about in his covering, and as he eats with his tongue, he repeatedly licks the youthful maiden.
Nowhere is he born; though ancient, he is ever new. He stands in the wood, gray-haired, smoke-bannered.
Without bathing in the waters, like a bull, he goes forth—he whom mortals of one mind lead forward.
Like two thieves who risk their lives, seeking forest game, they have bound [the victim] with ten cords.
O Agni, this is a newer hymn for you; yoke your chariot as it were with your radiant limbs.
O Jātavedas, may this prayer and this song of homage be ever-increasing for you.
O Agni, protect our children and our progeny; guard our bodies as well, never being heedless.
The one ocean, the supporter of riches, born of many origins, gazes from our heart;
he attends to the udder in the lap of the two secret ones; the bird’s foot is placed in the midst of the spring.
Occupying a common nest, the bulls have united with the mares;
the sages guard the station of the Eternal Law (Ṛta) and have established supreme names in secret.
The two faithful ones, possessing creative power, have brought him together; having measured him out, they have given birth to the infant, nourishing him.
They move toward the navel of all that is firm, as they follow with their mind the thread of the Sage.
For the paths of Truth, from of old, attend upon the well-born one for food and for strength;
the two worlds, clothed in their upper garment, have grown strong with the offerings of clarified butter and the foods of honey.
Longing for them, the wise one has brought forth the seven ruddy sisters from the honeyed [substance] so that they may be seen;
born of old, he has entered into the intermediate space and, seeking it, found the covering of Pūṣan.
The seers have fashioned seven boundaries; the one who is in distress has stepped beyond only one of them.
The pillar of Āyu stands in the dwelling of the highest, at the release of paths, upon the foundations.
The non-existent and the existent in the highest heaven, at the birth of Dakṣa in the lap of Aditi—
Agni is indeed our first-born of Ṛta, the bull and the cow in the earliest age.
This is he, under whose protection and through whose assistance the singer prospers in his desire; he who, radiant and encompassed by the highest beams of the kindled fires, moves all around.
Agni, who shines resplendent with his rays, radiant and eternal, the observer of *ṛta* among the gods;
he who has extended his friendship to his friends, unassailable like a swift steed.
He who rules over every divine feast, who rules over all life at the dawning of the dawn— he, O Agni, whose chariot is unharmed, in whom the mind establishes the oblations with its strengths.
Increasing through invigorating hymns and enjoying the songs of praise, he hastens toward the gods with rapid flight;
the joyous Hotṛ, the most skilled sacrificer, Agni, being closely united, sprinkles the gods with his ladle.
Bring hither with songs and prostrations that Agni who trembles like Indra at dawn—
the Jātavedas whom the inspired poets praise with their hymns as the one who carries the oblations of the conquerors.
In whom all treasures have gathered together, like horses with their riders in a race toward the prize—
O Agni, bring hither those aids of yours, most desired by Indra, directed toward us.

For then, O Agni, having sat down by your greatness, as soon as you were born, you became worthy of oblations. The gods followed that intention of yours; then the first protectors increased in strength.

O Agni, bestow upon us well-being from heaven and from earth for the sake of sacrifice, O God; may we be united with your insights, O Wondrous One, and protect us, O God, with your far-reaching blessings.
O Agni, these prayers born for you celebrate your bounty with cattle and horses; when a mortal has attained enjoyment from you, O Vasu, well-born one, he bestows gifts through his hymns.
I deem Agni to be my father, Agni my kinsman, Agni my brother, and ever my friend.
I worship the face of the lofty Agni, the bright and holy radiance of Sūrya in heaven.
O Agni, our prayers are successful and winning, for you, the eternal priest, protect us in our home.
May he who is true to the *ṛta*, the possessor of ruddy horses and abundant food, grant us desirable wealth through days and nights.

Like a friend established by days, like a long-standing ritual application, the men have generated Agni with their two arms— the ancient priest, the lover of the sacrifice— and they have seated him as the Hotṛ among the people.
O God, sacrifice yourself to the gods in heaven; what can a simpleton, lacking in wisdom, do for you?
O God, just as you have sacrificed to the gods according to the seasons, so now, O well-born one, sacrifice to your own self.
Be our protector and guardian, O Agni; be the maker of our strength and the bestower of vitality upon us.
Grant us, O most mighty one, the gift of oblations, and protect our bodies with unceasing care.
Agni advances with his lofty banner; the bull bellows forth to the two worlds.
He has reached even the furthest ends of heaven; the buffalo has grown great in the lap of the waters.
The bull, the humped embryo, has rejoiced; the vigorous calf, never-wearying, has bellowed. Making the divine powers rise up, he goes forth first among his own dwellings.
He who has grasped the head of his parents; they have established him, like the wave of the sun, at the sacrifice.
At his flight, the ruddy ones, whose base is the horse, have delighted their bodies in the womb of *ṛta*.
For at every dawn, O Vasu, you go to the forefront; you have become the radiant one between the two Yamas.
For the sake of cosmic order (*ṛta*), you have established the seven steps, generating Mitra for your own body.
You have become the eye of the great Order, the guardian; you have become Varuṇa when you go for the sake of Truth.
You have become the Son of the Waters, O Jātavedas; you have become the messenger of him whose oblation you have accepted.
You are the leader of the sacrifice and of the mid-world, where you accompany [us] with your auspicious teams of horses;
you place your head in heaven, winning the light, and you have made your tongue, O Agni, the bearer of the oblation.
By the will of this [Agni], Trita, seeking the inspired thought of the supreme Father according to his ways, dwells within the cave;
being attended in the lap of the two parents, calling the weapons kin, he goes forth.
Knowing the weapons of his fathers, the Aptya, urged on by Indra, went forth to battle;
having slain the three-headed, seven-rayed one, Trita released the cattle of Tvaṣṭṛ's son.
O Indra, Lord of the Good, you struck down with force the one who was striving for great power and considering himself secure;
seizing the cattle of Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, you tore off his three heads and cast them away.
O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss;
grant us strength for great joy and for the sight [of the divine].
O Waters, may you grant us a share here of that most auspicious sap of yours,
like longing mothers.
To him for whose dwelling you quicken us, to him let us go gladly;
O Waters, give us life.
May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking;
may they flow toward us with peace and well-being.
Rulers of precious things, dwelling among the people—
I beg the waters for medicine.
Soma has told me that within the waters are all healing remedies,
and Agni, who brings well-being to all.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body,
so that I may long behold the sun.
O Waters, carry away this whatever evil is in me—
whether it be that I have committed an offense against others, or that I have sworn falsely, or even spoken untruth.
Today I have entered the waters; we have united with their essence.
O Agni, come hither full of milk; endow me with splendor.
Perhaps I may win back my friend through friendship, having traveled across even the vast ocean.
May the wise one, contemplating further on the earth, take up the grandson of his father.
Your friend does not desire this friendship, that she who shares the same mark should become of different form.
The sons of the great Asura, the heroes, the upholders of heaven, look out widely around.
The immortals indeed desire this: even the abandonment of the sole mortal.
May your mind be fixed upon our mind; as a husband, may you enter the body of your wife.
What we have never done before, how could we now speak untruth while proclaiming the Truth?
The Gandharva in the waters and the watery maiden—she is our kinship; that is our supreme bond of consanguinity.
In the womb, the progenitor, the god Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller who takes all forms, made us two, husband and wife.
No one violates his ordinances; both Earth and Heaven know this of us.
Who knows of this first day? Who has seen it? Who here can declare it?
Great is the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa; what, O speaker, will you say to men with your speech?
Yama’s desire for me, his twin, has come, that we may lie together in the same womb.
Like a wife yielding her body to her husband, let me cast it off as a charioteer casts off his wheels.
These spies of the gods who move here do not stand still, nor do they close their eyes.
O you who provoke me, go quickly by another way; tear him away from me like the two wheels of a chariot.
May she honor him with nights and days; may she repeatedly measure out the eye of the sun.
Day and earth are a pair of kindred kin; Yamī might commit the incestuous act of Yama.
Surely those later generations will come when kinsmen shall commit what is unbecoming between siblings. Press thy arm close to the bull; O fortunate one, seek another husband than me.
What is a brother when one becomes protectorless? Or what is a sister when Destruction (Nirṛti) overtakes her? Driven by desire, I utter this much lamentation; unite my body with thy body.
"Indeed, I would not have my body joined with your body; they call it an evil thing when one approaches his own sister.
Arrange your pleasures with another than me; O fortunate one, your brother does not desire this."
Alas, you are truly lost, O Yama! We have found neither your mind nor your heart.
Surely another shall embrace you, as a girth-belt clasps a harnessed horse, or as a creeper clings to a tree.
O Yami, one shall surely embrace another, and another shall embrace you, as a creeper clings to a tree.
Do you desire his heart, or let him desire yours; then indeed, establish a most auspicious bond of union.
The bull has yielded for the bull the milks of heaven by his milking; the mighty one, the undeceivable son of Aditi, knows all through his wisdom.
May he, the worthy of sacrifice, perform the sacrifices according to the seasons.
May the Gandharva woman and the water-nymph protect my mind within the roar of the river. May Aditi place us in the midst of what is desired; may our eldest brother speak forth first for us.
Truly, that auspicious, wealthy, and glorious Dawn has shone forth for mankind with her light,
since they have brought forth Agni as the Hotṛ-priest for the sacrifice, according to the will of those who desire him.
Then the Falcon, dispatched to the sacrifice, brought down that far-reaching, all-seeing drop;
when the Aryan tribes chose Agni, the wonder-worker, as their Hotṛ-priest, then indeed was the sage born.
O Agni, you are always delightful to the man who performs the sacrifice well with his oblations, like a pasture for one who thrives;
or when, having won the prize of the inspired singer who exerts himself in the recitation of hymns, you approach with your many [attendants].
Raise up the two parents like a lover; the beloved one desires fortune and sends it forth from his heart.
The bearer speaks, the sacrificer performs his work well; the Asura exerts his power and trembles with inspired thought.
O Agni, son of strength, that mortal who attains your favor becomes renowned far and wide;
bestowing nourishment and borne by his horses, he, radiant and powerful, adorns the days.
O Agni, worthy of worship, when this divine assembly takes place among the gods, O holy one;
and when you, O self-dependent lord, distribute treasures, grant us here our share of wealth.
Hear us, O Agni, in this common dwelling; yoke your swift chariot of immortality.
Bring hither to us the two worlds, the parents of the gods; let none of the gods be absent, but remain here with us.
Heaven and Earth, first by the Eternal Law, become attentive with their true speech,
when the god, making mortals ready for sacrifice, sits down as the Hotṛ-priest, turning toward his own vital breath.
The god who encompasses the gods by the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), carry our oblation, you who are foremost and wise;
smoke-bannered, with kindled fuel, radiant in luster, the joyous and eternal Hotṛ-priest, most skilled in sacrifice through speech.
The cow’s own turn is the immortal nectar of the god; born from that, they have sustained the two wide worlds.
All the gods followed that sacred formula of yours, whereby the dappled cow milks forth the celestial ghee and water.
I praise you both for our prosperity, O waters that drip with clarity; O Heaven and Earth, you two worlds, hear me!
Since the days have gone toward the lack of guidance, may our two Parents here sharpen us with sweetness.
What has the King seized from us? When have we transgressed his decree? Who knows?
For even Mitra himself may lead the gods astray; there is even strength in them like the cry of those who go forth.
The name of immortality is difficult to perceive here, when she who shares a common origin becomes manifold in form.
O lofty Agni, protect without ceasing that man who meditates upon the thought of Yama with a well-disposed mind.
In which sacrificial assembly the gods rejoice, and in the seat of Vivasvat they maintain their station;
they placed light in the sun and established the nights within the month, while the two exhaustless ones move around the radiant orb.
In that secret counsel wherein the gods move together, we do not know it. May Mitra, Aditi, and the divine Savitṛ proclaim us sinless to Varuṇa in this matter.
Hear us, O Agni, in our common dwelling and place; yoke your chariot that speeds through the immortal realm.
Bring hither to us the two worlds, the parents of the gods; let none of the gods be absent; may you be present here.
I yoke for you both an ancient prayer with prostrations; let the hymn go forth like a path to the patron.
May all the sons of immortality hear it, they who have taken up their stations in the celestial realms.
When you two came like two Yamas striving together, the god-seeking men brought you forward.
Sit down in your own place, you who know it; be well-seated for our Soma juice.
I have ascended after the five steps of Rūpā; I follow the four-footed one with my vow.
By means of the syllable, I measure this out; I purify it upon the navel of Ṛta.
For the sake of the gods he chose death; for the sake of progeny he did not choose immortality.
They made Bṛhaspati the seer their sacrifice; Yama left his own dear body behind.
Seven flow for the infant accompanied by the Maruts; the sons have established the cosmic order (*ṛta*) for their father.
Both worlds indeed belong to him; he rules over both, both strive for him, and both nourish him.
Honor with an oblation Yama, the king, the son of Vivasvat, the assembler of people, who has departed along the great downward slopes and has spied out the path for many.
Yama was the first to find the path for us; this pasture-land is not to be taken away, where our ancient fathers have departed, having been born according to their own paths.
Mātali is magnified by the Kavyas, Yama by the Aṅgirases, and Bṛhaspati by the Ṛkvans;
those whom the gods have magnified and those who have magnified the gods—some rejoice with the cry of Svāhā, others with the cry of Svadhā.
O Yama, sit down upon this sacrificial grass, in harmony with the Aṅgiras fathers;
let the mantras recited by the seers bring you here, O King, and rejoice in this oblation.
Come hither with the Angirases who are worthy of sacrifice; O Yama, rejoice here with the Vairūpas.
I invoke Vivasvat, who is your father, that he may sit down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice.
The Aṅgirases are our fathers, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of Soma; may we abide in the good-will of those worthy of sacrifice, and in their auspicious benevolence.
Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths whereon our former fathers have departed;
there you shall see both kings rejoicing in the funeral offering—Yama and the god Varuṇa.

Unite with the fathers, unite with Yama, and with the merit of your sacrifices and good deeds in the highest heaven. Leaving behind all that is blameworthy, return once more to your home; unite with a body, full of luster.
Depart, go away, and creep away from here; the fathers have prepared this world for him.
Yama gives him a dwelling clearly revealed by days, waters, and nights, along with his own protection.
Run past the two dogs, the sons of Saramā, the four-eyed brindled ones, by the righteous path;
then approach the benevolent fathers who rejoice in the banquet together with Yama.
O Yama, those two dogs of yours who are the guardians, four-eyed, protectors of the path, and watchers over men—to them entrust him, O King; bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease.
The two broad-nosed, honey-colored messengers of Yama, who delight in the life-force of men, wander among the people.
May they today grant us here once more the auspicious breath of life, so that we may behold the sun.
Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama. To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its messenger, well-prepared.
Offer to Yama an oblation rich in ghee and step forward;
may he lead us among the gods to a long life, that we may live on.
Offer to King Yama this most honey-sweet oblation;
here is homage to the seers of old, the ancient makers of the path.
With the three *trikadruka* cups it flies; six are the wide ones, and the one is the Great One. The *triṣṭubh*, the *gāyatrī*, and all the meters—these are placed within Yama.
May the lower, the higher, and the middle Soma-loving Fathers rise up—those who have gone to the life-span, who are harmless and knowers of the *ṛta*; may those Fathers protect us in our invocations.
Let this homage be offered today to the fathers— those who went before and those who followed after,
those who have settled in the earthly realm, or those who are now among the well-fortified clans.

I have found the benevolent Fathers, and the descendant, and the wide stride of Viṣṇu. Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass and partake of the pressed food with the Svadhā-call—may they be most ready to come here.
O Fathers who sit upon the sacred grass, come hither with your aid; we have prepared these oblations for you, so please accept them.
Come to us with most auspicious protection, and then bestow upon us well-being, health, and freedom from harm.
The Soma-loving ancestors have been invited to their dear offerings placed upon the sacrificial grass;
may they come hither, may they hear us here, may they speak for us, and may they protect us.
Bending your knees and sitting down to the south, may you all favor this sacrifice.
O Fathers, do not harm us for anything, whatever offense we may have committed against you through our human nature.
Sitting in the lap of the ruddy dawns, bestow wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations.
O Fathers, grant that wealth to his sons; bestow strength upon them here.
Our ancient fathers, worthy of Soma, the Vasiṣṭhas who have followed after the drinking of Soma—
may Yama, rejoicing with them, desiring [the offerings], eat the oblations according to his desire along with those who desire them.
Those who have thirsted among the gods, panting, knowing the priestly office, fashioning hymns with their chants—
O Agni, come hither with those well-known, true Kavyas, the fathers who sit at the *gharma* vessel.

O Agni, come with the thousand true ones who eat the oblation, who drink the oblation, who share the same chariot with Indra and the gods— the ancient and later Fathers who sit at the *gharma* vessel and praise the gods.

O Fathers consumed by Agni, come hither; sit each upon his own seat, O excellent leaders. Eat the oblations presented upon the sacred grass, and then bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
O Agni Jātavedas, you, being invoked, have carried the oblations after making them fragrant;
you have given them to the fathers, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Eat, O God, these presented offerings.

Those ancestors who are here and those who are not here, those whom we know and those whom we do not know—you know how many they are, O Jātavedas; accept this well-prepared sacrifice with the *svadhā* offerings.

Those who have been consumed by fire and those who have not been consumed by fire, who rejoice in the midst of heaven through their own inherent power (*svadhā*),— with them, O Sovereign Lord, fashion this body for the journey to the sun according to your will.
Do not burn him up, O Agni; do not consume him with heat; do not scorch his skin nor his body.
When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers.
O Jātavedas, when you have cooked him, then deliver him over to the Fathers;
when he goes to this world of the departed spirits, then let him become one who obeys the will of the gods.
Let your eye go to the sun, your breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to the cosmic law.
Or go to the waters if it is beneficial for you there; take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts.
The goat is your portion; heat it with heat. Let your flame heat it, let your radiance heat it. O Jātavedas, with those forms of yours that are auspicious, carry him to the world of the righteous.

Release him again, O Agni, to the Fathers—he who, offered by you, moves with his own funeral offerings (*svadhā*). Clothed in life, let him approach his kin; O Jātavedas, let him be united with a body.
Whatever the black bird has pecked at you, or the ant, the serpent, or even the wild beast—
may Agni make all that free from disease, and Soma, who has entered into the Brahmins.

Envelop yourself with the cow-hides as a shield against Agni; cover yourself completely with fat and marrow, so that the bold one, exulting in his heat and seeking to seize you, may not, intent on burning, encircle you.
O Agni, do not overturn this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those who offer Soma.
This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it the immortal gods rejoice.
I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of Yama, carrying off the impurities. Let this other Jātavedas remain right here, knowing well how to carry the oblation to the gods.
The flesh-eating Agni who has entered your house, beholding this other Jātavedas—him I bring away for the sacrifice to the Fathers; may that god promote the Gharma in the highest dwelling-place.
May Agni, the carrier of raw flesh, worship the Fathers who increase the cosmic order;
may he announce the oblations to the gods and to the Fathers.
Desiring you, we set you down; desiring you, we kindle you. Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation.
O Agni, that which you have completely consumed, extinguish that once again;
let the *kiyāmbu* grow here, along with the *pākadūrvā* and the *vyalkaśā*.
O cool one, O you who possess coolness! O refreshing one, O you who possess refreshment! Come together well with the female frog and gladden this Agni.
"Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the bridal procession for his daughter"—at this thought the entire world assembles.
The mother of Yama, being led away, the wife of the great Vivasvat, has vanished.
They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar appearance, they gave her to Vivasvat.
And she brought forth the two Aśvins when that happened; Saraṇyū abandoned the two pairs.
May Pūṣan, the guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, lead you forth from here, he who knows the way.
May he entrust you to these ancestors, and may Agni deliver you to the gods who are easy to find.
May Viśvāyu protect your life; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead.
Where the doers of good deeds dwell, where they have gone—there may the god Savitṛ place you.
May Pūṣan know all these regions; may he lead us by the path most free from fear.
Bestowing well-being, glowing, with all his heroes, may he go before us, watchful and knowing.
Pūṣan was born upon the far path of paths, upon the far path of heaven, and upon the far path of earth;
knowing the way, he moves to and fro toward both most beloved dwelling places.

Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī; they invoke Sarasvatī while the sacrifice is being performed. The doers of good have called upon Sarasvatī; may Sarasvatī grant what is desirable to the donor.
O Sarasvatī, you who have come on the same chariot with the Fathers, O Goddess, rejoicing in your own powers;
having seated yourself upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), be exhilarated and bestow upon us food free from disease.
Sarasvatī, whom the ancestors invoke as they approach the sacrifice from the south—
O Iḷā, bestow here a portion worth a thousand, and grant abundance of wealth upon the sacrificers.
May the Waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who cleanse with ghee purify us with ghee. For the goddesses carry away every defilement; rising from them, I go forth bright and purified.
The drop has fallen following the first days, into this womb and that which was before;
I offer the drop as it moves along toward the common womb, according to the seven priestly offices.
Whatever drop of yours spills out, whatever stalk of yours falls from the arms,
from the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā* vessel, or from the hand of the *adhvaryu*, or from the filter— that I offer to you with my mind, consecrated by the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.
That drop of yours which was spilled, that stalk of yours which fell, whether near or far from the ladle—
may this god Bṛhaspati pour it together for our prosperity.
The plants are full of milk; full of milk is my speech. The milk of the waters is indeed full of milk; with that, purify me together.
Go away, O Death, along the other path, which is yours and distinct from the path of the gods.
To you who have eyes and hear, I speak: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes.
Avoiding the path of death as you have come, gaining a longer and more extended life,
may you swell with offspring and wealth— become pure, purified, and worthy of sacrifice.
These living ones have turned away from the dead; today our invocation of the gods has become auspicious.
We have gone forward for dancing and laughter, gaining a further extension of a longer life.
I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other among them may now go to this goal.
May they live a hundred abundant autumns; let them place death beyond by means of this mountain.
Just as days follow one another in succession, and just as seasons proceed duly with the seasons, so,
O Ordainer, arrange their lifespans such that the later does not abandon the earlier.
Ascend [to life], choosing old age, striving one after another as you go.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, the skillful creator of offspring, being well-disposed, grant you long life here that you may live.
May these women, not widows and having noble husbands, enter together with ointment and clarified butter.
Free from tears, free from disease, and possessing fine jewels, let the wives ascend first to the place of birth.
Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living; come to this one whose life has departed; lie down beside him.
You have entered into this state of wifehood for your husband, who took your hand and wooed you.
Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased for our sovereignty, for splendor, and for strength—
right here you remain, and we here, possessing excellent heroes, shall conquer all rivals and adversaries.
Approach this mother earth, the wide-extending, the very gracious Pṛthivī;
may she, the youthful maiden soft as wool for the possessor of sacrificial gifts, protect you from the lap of Destruction.
Open wide, O Earth; do not press down upon him. Be easy of access to him and easy for him to traverse. As a mother covers her son with the hem of her garment, so do you, O Earth, cover him.
May the earth, swelling wide, stand firm; may a thousand pillars be fixed upon it.
May these dwellings drip with clarified butter, and may they be a refuge for him here at all times.
I prop up the earth for you; placing this dwelling around you, may I not come to harm. May the Fathers hold up this pillar for you; here Yama shall establish your seat.
The days have placed me face to face, like a leaf upon a tree; I have grasped the speech directed toward me, as one holds a horse with a rein.
Turn back, do not go further; follow us, O wealthy ones.
Agni and Soma, you who bring back wealth, bestow riches upon us.
Bring them back again; bring them back once more.
May Indra restrain them; may Agni drive them hither.
Let these cows return again; let them thrive under this master of cattle.
O Agni, hold them fast right here; let whatever wealth there is remain right here.
The path by which one goes forth, the path by which one returns, that which is the point of meeting, and that which is the final goal;
the turning away, the turning back, and even the guardian—I call upon him as well.
May the Guardian who has reached the departure, who has reached the final goal,
and who knows the turning back and the returning, bring us back again.
O Indra, bring them back, turn them back; give us our cows again. May we enjoy them while they are still living.
I bestow upon you from every side strength, with clarified butter and milk.
May those gods who are worthy of sacrifice endow us with wealth.
O Bringer-back, bring them back; O Returner, cause them to return.
From the four quarters of the earth, from those directions, bring them back to us.
May you inspire our minds toward what is auspicious.
I praise Agni, the youngest of those who enjoy, the friend who is difficult to resist by command;
he under whose law the bright ones serve the udder of the mother in the light.
Him whom they strengthen with their mouths— the one whose dwelling is the pit, whose banner is light—
he shines forth, his teeth in a row.
The noble one goes forth as the path for the clans when he has reached the ends of heaven;
the seer, shining brightly, [pierces] the cloud.
May he enjoy the oblations of man; standing erect and skillful at the sacrifice, he goes before us, establishing his dwelling.
For he is security, the oblation, and the sacrifice; his path goes forth with readiness.
To Agni, the gods [approach] him who wields the axe.
I have performed worship for the sake of food, seeking Agni who conquers through sacrifice; they call him the life-sustaining son of the mountain, the bringer of ancient bliss.
Whatever men there may be who are ours, let them all partake of your favor,
increasing Agni with oblations.
Black, white, ruddy is his path; tawny, dappled, and crimson is he, the glorious one. The progenitor begot him of golden form.

Thus, O Agni, son of strength, Vimada, being in harmony with the immortals, has brought his inspired thought and songs to you; seeking your favor, he has obtained food, vigor, a secure dwelling, and all things.

We choose you as the Hotṛ priest with our own well-fashioned hymns, like Agni, for the sacrifice upon which the sacred grass is strewn—O you of purifying luster, you who are sharp; in your exhilaration, you are waxing great.
The self-sustaining ones, who bestow horses as wealth, adorn you;
the ladle that pours forth seeks you. O Agni, in this exhilaration of yours, the straight-flying oblation is offered; you are waxing great.
In you the cosmic laws abide, as if pouring forth with ladles.
Black forms and white—during your exhilaration—you assume all splendors; you swell with power.

O immortal Agni, whatever wealth you deem fit, O powerful one—bring that to us for the winning of booty at our sacrifices; bring it, the wondrous thing, in the exhilaration of the Soma-pressing. You are waxing great.
Agni, born by Atharvan, has discovered all poetic wisdom;
he became the messenger of Vivasvat. At your exhilaration, he—dear to Yama and desirable—is celebrated.
O Agni, they invoke you at the sacrifices when the ritual has begun;
you bestow all desirable treasures upon the donor—thus you proclaim it in the exhilaration of the Soma.

In the sacrifices, men have established you, O Agni, as the lovely officiating priest; with eyes brightened by exhilaration from the Soma, you shine forth—bright, most observant, with your face anointed with ghee. In the exhilaration of the Soma, you speak out with your eyes.
O Agni, with your bright flame you spread yourself out widely and loftily;
bellowing, you act like a bull. In your exhilaration, you bestow the embryo upon your sisters; you desire to speak aloud.
Where is Indra heard of? Among which people today is he renowned like Mitra? Is he celebrated with song in the abode of the seers, or in secret?
Hearken here, O Indra; today he is praised among us, the wielder of the thunderbolt, worthy of hymns.
Like Mitra among the people, he has established his matchless glory.
He who is the lord of great and incomparable power, the impeller of mighty manliness,
the bearer of the bold thunderbolt, like a father cherishing his beloved son.
Harnessing the two roaring horses of the wind, O god, wielder of the thunderbolt,
you who hasten along the radiant path, having set them loose, you shall praise the ways.
You yourself have come as the two bay horses of Vāta, to carry you by your own power—
those for whom no driver is to be found, whether god or mortal.
Then Uśanas asked you two as you were coming: "For what purpose have you come to our house from afar, from heaven and earth, to this mortal man?"
O Indra, take note of our nourishment; our prayer has been raised up.
We entreat you for that protection, so that we may slay Śuṣṇa, the non-human.
The Dasyu is without ritual action, mindless toward us, following alien laws, and non-human. O slayer of enemies, strike down the weapon of that Dāsa.
O Indra, you are a hero among our heroes; and we, protected by you, are mighty in our strength.
Your bounties have resounded in many places, like the voices of the people.
O Hero, wielder of the thunderbolt, you urged those men on in the slaying of Vṛtra and in the drawing of the sword,
when you were hidden among the seers and the clans of star-like power.
Swiftly, O Indra, doer of great deeds, you are the one who bestows gifts; O hero, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you crushed all the offspring of Śuṣṇa with your companions.
O Indra, O Hero, let not our excellent aids be directed elsewhere; may they be with us.
O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, may we, each one of us, abide in the favor of these [aids].
O Indra, may those touches of yours be true for us—
those harmless ones that we may enjoy, O wielder of the thunderbolt, like the yield of milch-cows.
When the handless and footless one grew strong through the powers of the knowable things, you,
moving from left to right, struck down Śuṣṇa for every living being.
Drink, drink the soma, O heroic Indra! Do not fail, you who possess wealth and are a benefactor. And protect the singers and the patrons; make us rich with great and abundant riches.
Let us worship Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his right hand, the charioteer of the bay steeds that move in various directions.
Shaking his beard upward, he stands forth, distributing [gifts] with his armies and with his bounty.
His two bay steeds indeed find wealth in the wood; Indra, the bounteous slayer of Vṛtra, has become great through his riches.
As Ṛbhu, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣan, he rules over power; I even erase the very name of the Dāsa.
When he takes up his golden thunderbolt and his chariot which his two bay horses draw, Maghavan, renowned from of old, mounts it together with the patrons—
Indra, the lord of long-famed strength.
He indeed, Indra, the lord of the herd, together with his own rain, sprinkles his golden beard;
he seeks the well-housed dwelling when the mead is pressed, and he shakes it like the wind shaking a forest.

He who with his voice struck down many thousands of ill-omened, discordant, and foolish speakers— that very manly deed of his we celebrate, he who, like a father, has increased his power and his might.
The Vimadas have generated for you, O Indra, a hymn of praise—unprecedented and most abundant—for you, the giver of good gifts;
for we know the enjoyment of this mighty one, when we make it our own, as a herdsman makes his cattle.
May our friendship never be severed—yours, O Indra, and that of the seer Vimada;
for we know your providence, O God, like that of a kinsman. May your auspicious friendships be with us.
O Indra, drink this honeyed Soma pressed in the ladle; bestow wealth upon us. In the exhilaration of the draught, O Lord of many riches, you shall proclaim thousandfold bounty.
We approach you with sacrifices, with hymns, and with oblations;
O Lord of powers, among all powers, bestow upon us the most excellent treasure in your exhilaration—this you proclaim.
You who are the lord of desirable things, the impeller of the weak, O Indra, the protector of those who praise you—protect us from hatred and from distress in your exhilaration; you wax great.
O powerful ones, masters of magic, you two churned forth the two joined worlds together,
when, implored by Vimada, O Nāsatyas, you churned them out.
All the gods lamented as the two [worlds] were closing together and falling apart; the gods said to the Nāsatyas, "Bring them back again!"
Sweet be my departure, sweet my return;
O Gods, by your divine power, make both of these sweet for us.
Send us a gracious mind, and skill, and mental power.
Then, in your friendship with the soma-juice, may we rejoice in your exhilaration like cattle in a pasture; you are waxing great.
O Soma, they all dwell touching the heart within all your abodes.
And now, these desires of mine, seeking wealth, spread out among you in your exhilaration; you are waxing great.
Moreover, O Soma, through my simplicity I violate your sacred laws;
therefore, as a father toward his son, be gracious to us in your exhilaration, even from the blow of death—you are waxing great.

Our prayers go forth together like streams from springs; O Soma, for our life, maintain our mental power—O you who are exhilarated by the libations, you are being poured out like the cups. You are waxing great.
Through your powers, O Soma, these eager ones have opened wide the stall rich in cattle and horses; the wise, through you, the skillful and strong—into your exhilaration we proclaim this aloud.
O Soma, you guard our cattle and the moving world spread out in many places; you bring them together so that they may live. In your exhilaration, surveying all beings, you desire to speak forth.
O Soma, be our invincible protector on every side.
O King, drive away our adversaries; let not the malevolent prevail over us—at your exhilarating outpouring, you speak forth.
O Soma, you who possess excellent wisdom, remain watchful for us so that we may gain vital strength.
As one who knows the field better than man, protect us from malice and from distress in your exhilaration; you are waxing great.
O Indu, you are our most excellent slayer of Vṛtra and the auspicious friend of Indra.
When they call upon you in the clash of battle, O you who are exhilarated by the soma-juice, you are invoked by those fighting for the sake of their offspring; thus you are celebrated.
This indeed is that potent, beloved exhilaration which increases Indra’s strength.
This [Soma], at your great exhilaration, increased the inspired thought of the mighty Kakṣīvat; you, O Soma, desire to speak.
This one sends forth strengths rich in cattle for the inspired singer who offers oblations;
this one, the best among the seven, shall further the blind and the lame for you—at your exhilaration—O you who speak with power!
For the desirable teams of horses advance toward him with inspired hymns;
may the wondrous Pūṣan, whose chariot is drawn by teams of horses, the majestic one, come to our aid.
The greatness of this man, his capacity for friendship, which this people possesses—may the inspired singer win it through his prayers; he has discerned it through his well-spoken hymns.
He knows the beautiful hymns of praise; like the drop, like Pūṣan, he is the bull.
He sprinkles nourishment upon us; he sprinkles it upon our stall like a cow.
May we honor you, O divine Pūṣan, as our own—
our accomplisher of thoughts and our protector of the wise.
He is the counterpart of sacrifices, the steed that urges on chariots; he is the seer established by Manu, the friend who protects the inspired singer.
The lord of her who longs for a husband, and of both the sorrowing woman and the sorrowing man—
he, the wind of the garments, has thoroughly cleansed the woolen robes.
Lord of spoils, lord of nourishments, friend of prosperity— he,
the irresistible one, the beloved, has vigorously shaken his beard at will.
O Pūṣan, may the goats turn the pole of your chariot;
you are the friend of every seeker, born of old, and unshakable.
May the majestic Pūṣan protect our chariot with nourishment;
may he be the increaser of our strengths and hear this our invocation.

O singer, my impetuous force is truly great when I bestow aid upon the one who presses the juice and performs the sacrifice. I am the slayer of him who offers no blessing, the one who acts with falsehood, the crooked, and the arrogant.

If indeed I were to lead forth for battle those godless ones who swell themselves with their own bodies, then at home I would cook for you a powerful bull; I would pour out the sharp pressed juice, the fifteenfold draught.
I do not know him who says "I am he" after having slain the godless in battle;
when he has declared the fierce encounter, then indeed they proclaim my two bulls.
When I was among unknown tribes, all the wealthy patrons were mine;
whether I conquer one who is at ease or one who is powerful, I strike him down on the mountain, seizing him by the foot.
Neither do men restrain me in the assembly, nor do the mountains, whenever I resolve my mind.
From my roar, the one with quick ears shall be afraid; indeed, day after day, the dust shall rise up.
Behold here those who drink the boiled [milk], devoid of Indra, who dwell in their arms and fall before the arrow;
or those who have reviled their own bold friend—may the rims of the wheels now roll over them!
You have become great; you have increased and extended our life-span. The former has indeed pierced [the darkness], and the latter shall pierce it too.
Two filters do not encompass him who has penetrated to the further shore of this world-space.

The cows of the nobleman, let loose, have eaten the barley; I saw them wandering together with their herdsman. The calls of the nobleman gathered around them from all sides; how much of these will the master enjoy?

When we, who eat the fodder of men, and I, the eater of barley within the wide field, are joined together here, he who is harnessed seeks one to unharness him; thus, having won, he yokes the one who was unyoked.
In this matter, you shall consider my words spoken as truth: I shall unite those who are biped and quadruped.
Whoever here should attack the bull with women, his wealth I shall divide without a fight.
Whose daughter was ever without eyes—who, knowing her to be blind, would desire her?
Which of the two would release his resentment against her: he who carries her away, or he who would woo her?
How great is the bride, the wife of a mortal, when she is completely gladdened by excellent and desirable wealth?
A bride becomes auspicious when she is well-adorned; she herself wins a friend even among the common folk.

The one who has arrived has swallowed him; he eats him as he faces him. With his own head, he has set his head in place as a protection. Sitting in his lap, he destroys the upright one; turning downward, he follows the outstretched earth.
Great, shadowless, and leafless, the courser stands; the mother is released, and the embryo devours him.
Licking the calf of another, she has lowed; in what world has the cow laid down her udder?
Seven heroes rose up from below; eight came together from above.
Nine came from behind, possessing firmness; ten from the front traverse the mountain ridge of the stone.
Of ten, they urge on that one who is tawny and common for the sake of the final rite;
the mother bears the well-placed embryo within her womb, nourishing him as he gazes upward.
The heroes cooked a fat ram; the dice were cast and followed the game. Two [of them] move within the vast waters, possessing filters, purifying themselves.
Crying out, they have gone in all directions; one half shall cook, for the other half will not cook.
This god Savitṛ has told me this: "He who has wood for food shall win it, as shall he who has ghee for food."
I saw a village being carried away from afar, moving by its own inherent power without wheels.
The noble one follows the generations of men, instantly destroying the phalluses as he, ever new, advances.
These two oxen of Pramara are yoked for me; do not drive them away, but rather let them delight me again and again.
Even the waters fail to achieve their purpose against him; the sun and the demon have both become his subordinates.

This very thunderbolt which has been hurled in many ways from below the vast mass of the sun—fame indeed is one thing, and beyond it there is another; through that, they overcome old age without distress.
Bound to every tree, the cow lowed; from there the man-eating birds flew forth.
Then this entire world was struck with fear; let it offer libations for Indra and provide for the seer.
In the dwelling-place of the gods, the first ones stood firm; from their cutting away, the later ones rose up. Three heat the earth with moisture; two carry the *bṛbūka* as their watery soil.
This is your life; know that of him as well. Do not hide such a thing from me in the assembly.
He makes the light manifest and hides the chaff; he is exposed, and his raiment does not escape him.
Every other kinsman has indeed arrived; alas, my father-in-law alone has not come.
May he eat the parched grain and drink the Soma, and being well-fed, may he return home again.
Roaring like a bull with sharpened horns, he stands upon the height and the expanse of the earth. "I protect him in all his struggles—he who, having pressed the Soma, fills both my flanks."
With the stone they press out for you, O Indra, the exhilarating Soma juices quickly; you drink of them.
They cook bulls for you; you eat of them when you are invoked, O Maghavan, with nourishing food.
O singer, understand this well for me: the rivers carry their curse against the current. The fox has devoured the lion as he faced him; the jackal has driven the boar out from the thicket.
How shall I, a simple mortal, comprehend this thought of yours, the wise and powerful one?
As one who knows, declare to us in due season that half of yours which, O Maghavan, is the secure chariot-pole.
For thus they strengthen me, the powerful one; even from high heaven my yoke-pole is higher still.
I sharpen many thousands all at once, for my progenitor begot me without a foe.
For thus have the gods known me, Indra, as powerful, fierce, and a bull in every deed.
Exulting, I slew Vṛtra with the thunderbolt; by my greatness, I opened the enclosure for the donor.
The gods came, bearing axes; felling the forests, they approached with their tribes. Placing Sudrva among the trees, they burn him up wherever there is dry wood.
The hare has swallowed the razor facing him; from afar I have split the mountain with a clod of earth.
I shall subject even the great to the small; the calf, growing strong, shall overcome the bull.
The eagle has thus struck his claw, hemmed in like a lion in an enclosure;
though the thirsty buffalo is trapped, the leather thong drags him helplessly along.
The iguana shall drag away by the neck those who, with their food, seek to treat the sacred word with contempt;
they devour the bulls that have been let loose, while they themselves crush the strength of their own bodies.
These have become well-performing through their labors, who have impelled their bodies with Soma and hymns.
Speaking like a man, bestow wealth upon us; you have established your name as a hero in heaven.
Like one who has been placed in the wood, he has shone; O you two swift ones, the pure hymn has awakened you.
He whose Hotar-priest is Indra on many days—he who is the manly, most heroic protector of men, the lord of the night.
May we be yours at the dancing of this dawn and of the future one, O most heroic of heroes among men. May the victorious chariot, which won with Kutsa, bring hither a hundred men along with Triśoka.
What exhilaration of yours, O Indra, has been delightful? O fierce one, let your doors and songs open wide for you.
Or rather, what thought shall bring you hither toward me? May I be able to provide you with the highest gift through offerings of food.
When indeed will the glory of one like you, O Indra, [favor] men? With what intention will you act?
Why have you not come to us—O wide-striding one, true as Mitra—for our sustenance, so that the inspired thoughts of everyone may find food?
O Hero, drive forward those who have come to fulfill his desire like those seeking the further shore;
O Indra, born of many powers, those men who with their offerings strive to win back your many songs of praise.
O Indra, for you indeed the two well-measured worlds were created of old: the heavens by your might and the earth by your wisdom.
For your choice, let the pressed juices be rich in ghee; let the sweet draughts be delicious for your drinking.
They have poured out the vessel full of honeyed mead for this Indra, for he is truly bountiful;
he has grown great across the expanse of the earth, preeminent through his wisdom and manly deeds.
Indra, self-strong, has shattered the hostile armies; many seek him for friendship.
Mount his chariot in battles like a warrior, whom you shall urge on with auspicious favor.
May the path toward the gods proceed for the sacred prayer, as if toward the waters by the impulse of the mind.
I offer this well-fashioned hymn to the vast-moving one, the great sustenance of Mitra and Varuṇa.
O Adhvaryus, be possessed of the oblation; desiring them, come hither toward the longing waters.
Those which the ruddy, fair-winged one gazes down upon—those waves, seize today with your skillful hands!
O Adhvaryus, go forth to the waters, to the ocean; worship the Son of the Waters with an oblation. May he grant you today a well-purified wave; for him, press the honeyed Soma.
He who shines unkindled within the waters, whom the sages invoke at the sacrifices—
O Son of the Waters, grant us the honey-sweet waters, by which Indra was strengthened for heroic power.
With those [waters] by which Soma rejoices and exults, like a young man with beautiful maidens—go toward those waters, O Adhvaryu; when you pour them out, purify him with the plants.
Even so do the young maidens bow down to the youth when he, desiring them, goes toward them who desire him;
they are of one mind and have agreed together—the Adhvaryus, the Dhiṣaṇās, and the divine Waters.
O Waters, send forth for that Indra a wave rich in sweetness, which gladdens the gods— a wave that made room for you when you were hemmed in, and which released you from great cursing.

Send forth for him a honeyed wave, O rivers, which is your embryo and a spring of sweetness—[the wave] whose back is sprinkled with ghee, worthy of praise at the sacrifices. O wealthy Waters, hear my call!
O rivers, send forth that exhilarating wave for Indra’s drinking, which sets both worlds in motion—
that intoxicating, offspring of the uśanas-plant, born of the cloud, the three-threaded fountain that flows everywhere.
Turning hitherward in two streams, like those who fight for cattle wandering toward their stalls—
O Seer, pay homage to the Waters, the mothers and mistresses of the world, who increase us and share a common origin.
Further our sacrifice with the worship of the gods; further our prayer for the winning of riches.
Unbind your udder for the joining of the *ṛta*; O Waters, be gracious hearers unto us.
O wealthy Waters, for you indeed rule over riches; you bear auspicious wisdom and immortality.
You are the mistresses of wealth consisting of noble offspring; may Sarasvatī grant that vitality to the one who praises her.
When the waters were seen approaching, bearing ghee, milk, and honey,
they agreed in spirit with the *adhvaryu* priests, bringing well-pressed soma for Indra.
These wealthy ones, bringing wealth to the living, have come; O friends, Adhvaryus, set them down!
Place them upon the sacrificial grass, O Soma-offerers, in harmony with Apām Napāt.
The longing waters have come to this sacred grass; seeking the gods, they have settled at the sacrifice.
O Adhvaryus, press the Soma for Indra! Your worship of the gods has now become easy to perform.
May the praiseworthy invocation of the gods come to us for protection with all their swift ones;
through them may we be well-favored friends, and crossing over all difficulties, may we remain secure.
A mortal should surely consider wealth as his own; let him seek to win it through the path of Truth with reverence.
Let him also consult with his own wisdom and grasp a more excellent skill with his mind.
The prayer has been established; the portions have been poured out. Like friends at a watering-place, they approach the wondrous one.
We have attained the strength of prosperity; we have become acquainted with the immortals.
May the eternal lord of the house, the domestic friend, be pleased with him, he whom the god Savitṛ has brought forth;
may Bhaga or Aryaman adorn him with cattle, and may he appear beautiful and pleasing to him.
May this [praise] become like the dwelling place of the Dawns, when those possessing food have come together with power. Seeking the singer's praise of him, may strengthening gains come to us.
This benevolent thought of his has spread wide, the ancient one, like a cow in her fullness;
they who dwell together in the womb of this Asura, being supported in their common nourishment.
What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned forth heaven and earth? Standing together, undecaying, and providing aid, they have caused many days and many dawns to age.
There is nothing else beyond this; he is the bull who supports heaven and earth.
Self-dependent, he makes his skin a purifier when the bay steeds carry him like the sun.
Like a chariot he traverses the broad earth; like the wind he blows through the mist upon the ground, where Mitra and Varuṇa, being anointed, have released their splendor like Agni in the forest.

When the barren cow, being suddenly anointed with oil, brought forth her calf, she who was distressed became free from distress, having found her own protector. When the son was born before his parents, the cow swallowed the sacrificial pin (śamyā), as if she were asked about it.
And they say that Kaṇva was the son of Nṛṣad; moreover, the swift steed won the prize.
For Kṛṣṇa, the bright udder swelled; there, no one else caused the Truth to flow for him.
May the two who come forth, the strengtheners of him who meditates, sit down well with their choice gifts toward our choice offerings.
May Indra enjoy both of us, when he takes notice of the Soma juice.
O Indra, much-praised one, you traverse the celestial luminaries and the earthly realms through the mid-air;
may those who repeatedly bring you to the sacrifices overcome the boastful words of the stingy.
That indeed is more beautiful than beauty itself, which the son recites from his parents;
the wife leads her husband with her voice, for the auspicious bridal procession of a man is well-adorned.
I have meditated upon that lovely place of assembly where the cows lowed like milch-cows for their calf;
where the ancient mother of the herd, the sevenfold source of the song, and the people gathered together.
Your footprint has surpassed [all others] as you seek the gods; alone, he goes among the Rudras, victorious.
Among those immortals through whom there is praise for the granting of gifts, pour forth the honey for your protectors.
"Being deposited and hidden within the waters, the guardian of the laws of the gods spoke to me:
'Indra, the knower, has indeed perceived you. Thus instructed by him, O Agni, have I come."
One who does not know the field has indeed spoken to one who knows the field; instructed by the knower of the field, he goes forth.
This is truly the blessing of instruction: one finds the direct path.

Today he breathed forth and these [beings] rejoiced; though unswollen, they sucked at the mother’s udder. Old age has come upon him, yet he remains young; free from anger, the benevolent one has become well-disposed.
O Kalaśa, O Kuruśravaṇa, may we perform these auspicious deeds while bestowing gifts.
O bounteous ones, let this be your gift, and let this Soma which I carry in my heart be yours as well.
The impulses of men have harnessed me; I carry Pūṣan along the middle way.
Then all the gods protected me; there was a cry that "the evil-intentioned one has arrived."
The ribs pain me on all sides like rival wives;
the thought of nakedness oppresses me; I am exhausted like a bird, and my mind trembles.
Like rats gnawing at their own tails, they devour me, your praiser, O Śatakratu.
O Maghavan Indra, be gracious to us once for all; then, be like a father to us.
I, the seer, have chosen King Kuruśravaṇa, the son of Trasadasyu,
the most bountiful among the sacrificers.
He whose three bay horses carry me straightway on his chariot— him, at the sacrifice where a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā is given, I shall praise.
Whose songs, like those of Upamaśravas’s father, have tasted of his favor— songs as delightful as a field to one who has won it.
O Upamaśravas, go to the grandson of Mitrātithi;
I am the one who honors your father.
If I were the lord of the immortals or even of mortals,
then my bountiful patron would surely live.
No one, even though possessed of a hundred lives, lives beyond the decree of the gods; thus has my companion been separated from me.
The dangling fruits of the great tree exhilarate me, growing in the windy place and rolling upon the gaming board.
Like a draught of Soma from Mount Mujavat, the wakeful Vibhīdaka nut has pleased me.
She did not scold me, nor was she angry; she was kind toward my friends and toward me. For the sake of a single throw of the die, I have driven away my devoted wife.
My mother-in-law hates me, my wife holds me back; though I am in distress, I find no one to comfort me. Like the worn-out hide of a horse for sale, I find no use for this gambler.
Others caress the wife of him whose wealth the swift die has coveted.
Father, mother, and brothers say of him: "We do not know him; lead him away bound."
When I thought, "I shall not play with these," I was left behind by my departing friends.
And when the brown dice were cast down, they raised their voices; I go to their appointed place like a mistress to her lover.
The gambler goes to the assembly hall, asking himself, "Shall I win?", his body trembling with excitement.
The dice thwart his desire, bestowing upon his opponent the very stakes he has won.
The dice indeed are like goads, pricking and piercing; they are deceivers, burning and causing torment.
Bestowing gifts upon children, they strike again the victor; mingled with honey, they are the ruin of the gambler.
Their troop of fifty-three plays about like the god Savitṛ, whose laws are true. Even before the wrath of the fierce one they bow down; even a king pays homage to them with a salutation.
They move downward yet leap upward; though handless, they overcome the one who has hands.
Like divine coals cast upon the parched ground, though cold themselves, they utterly consume the heart.
The gambler’s wife is left desolate and suffers; his mother grieves for her son, wondering where he may be wandering.
Indebted and trembling, seeking wealth, he goes to the houses of others by night.
Seeing a woman, the gambler was tormented by the wife of another and her well-made dwelling;
for he had yoked his brown horses in the forenoon, yet that low-born man fell down at the edge of the fire.
To him who was the commander of your great host, the king who became the first of the troop—to him I pay homage;
I do not withhold wealth for ten days. Facing eastward, I speak this truth.
Do not play with dice; practice agriculture instead, and take delight in your wealth, regarding it as abundant.
There are cows there, O gambler, and there is a wife; this the noble Savitṛ has revealed to me.
Make friends with us; indeed, have mercy on us. Do not act with violence against us through your terrible power.
Let your wrath and hostility now depart; let another fall into the snare of the brown serpents.

The fires, accompanied by Indra, have awakened; bearing light at the dawning of the mornings, may the great Heaven and Earth take notice of our work. Today we choose for ourselves the protection of the gods.
We choose for ourselves protection from heaven and earth, from the mother rivers and the mountains of Śaryaṇāvat.
We pray to Sūrya and Uṣas for sinlessness; may the well-pressed Soma bring us auspiciousness today.
May Heaven and Earth, the two great Mothers, protect us today from sin for our well-being;
may the dawning Uṣas drive away evil. We pray for well-being to the kindled Agni.
May this first Dawn, rich in wealth, shine forth with auspicious favor for us who seek riches.
May we keep far away the wrath of the malevolent; we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
The Dawns, which stream forth with the rays of the sun, bringing light at their breakings—may they shine upon us today auspiciously for our renown. We pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
May the healing Dawns approach us; may the fires rise up with lofty light.
May the Aśvins yoke their swift chariot; we pray for well-being to the kindled Agni.
O Savitṛ, impel for us today a most excellent and desirable portion, for you are the bestower of treasures.
I address Dhiṣaṇā, the mother of wealth; we pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled with fuel.
May that proclamation of the *ṛta* carry me across—that which we mortals have meditated upon among the gods.
The sun rises, beholding all the dawns. We pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled with fuel.
Free from hatred today, as we spread the sacred grass (*barhis*) and employ the pressing-stones, we pray for the success of our thought.
Abiding in the protection of the Ādityas, you move restlessly; we pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled.
Upon our great sacrificial grass at the joint feast, I invoke the gods in heaven; I seat the seven priests.
For the sake of gain, we seek Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Bhaga; for well-being, we pray to the kindled Agni.
O Ādityas, come hither for our complete well-being; with one accord, protect our sacrifice for our prosperity. We pray to Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, Bhaga, and the kindled Agni for our welfare.
O Gods, Ādityas, grant us that well-praised shelter which is easy to maintain and protects our men;
for our cattle, our children, our progeny, and for life itself, we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.
May all the Maruts come today with every aid; may all the fires be well-kindled.
May all the gods come to us with their protection; may all wealth and strength be ours.
O gods, whomsoever you favor in the winning of booty, whomsoever you protect and deliver from distress—
he who knows no fear under your guardianship— may we be such as these for the feast of the gods, O swift ones.
Dawn and Night, the lofty and well-adorned; Heaven and Earth, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—I invoke Indra, the Maruts, the mountains, the waters, the Ādityas, Heaven and Earth, the waters, and the sun.
May Heaven and Earth, the wise ones who follow the Eternal Order (*ṛta*), protect us from distress and from harm.
Let not destructive Nirṛti hold power over us. Today we choose that protection of the gods.
May Aditi protect us from all distress—the mother of Mitra and of wealthy Varuṇa.
May we attain the light of heaven, free from predators; today we choose that favor of the gods.
May the sounding pressing-stone drive away the demons, bad dreams, destruction, and every devouring fiend.
May we obtain the protection of the Ādityas and the Maruts; today we choose that favor of the gods.
May Indra sit upon the sacred grass; may the sacrificial food swell; may Bṛhaspati, the singer, chant with the Sāman hymns.
Let us fashion a well-awakened prayer for life; we choose today that protection of the gods.
O Aśvins, make our sacrifice touch the heavens and quicken the rite for the sake of seeking favor;
we choose today that protection of the gods which is offered with ghee and has its reins directed eastward.
I invoke the well-invoked host of Maruts, the purifying and lofty ones, who bring prosperity for our friendship.
May we obtain an increase of wealth for the sake of high renown; today we choose that protection of the gods.
We bring forth the filler of the waters, the source of life, the one who aids the gods, the easy to invoke, the glory of the sacrifice;
we have restrained the Soma of Indra with its bright rays—today we choose that protection of the gods.
May we, living with our sons living, being sinless, win that through easy victories by means of our gains.
May those who hate sacred prayer bear the guilt away in every direction; today we choose the protection of the gods.
O you who are worthy of sacrifice among men, listen! O gods, grant us that which we implore you for:
a victorious resolve, wealth, and glory consisting of heroes. Today we choose this protection of the gods.
Today we choose for ourselves the great protection of the great gods, the lofty and the unassailable;
so that we may obtain wealth born of heroes, we choose today that protection of the gods.
In the protection of the great kindled Agni, being sinless before Mitra and Varuṇa for our well-being, may we abide in the most excellent impulsion of Savitṛ; that favor of the gods we choose today.
O all you gods who are in the ordinance of Savitṛ of true impulse, of Mitra, and of Varuṇa—
bestow upon us prosperity consisting of heroes and cattle, and wonderful wealth.
Savitar from behind, Savitar from the front, Savitar from above, Savitar from below—may Savitar impel all well-being for us; may Savitar grant us long life.
Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa! Offer this sacred rite (*ṛta*) to the great god.
Praise Sūrya, the far-seeing, the banner born of the gods, the son of Heaven.
May that word of truth protect me on every side, as far as heaven and earth extend their days;
everything else that moves goes to rest, yet the waters flow forever and the sun goes forth for all time.
No godless man from of old can stay thee back when thou dost drive upon thy chariot with thy winged coursers.
One [path] follows the eastern region; with the other light, O Sūrya, thou goest forth.

O Sūrya, with that light by which you drive away the darkness and with which you rise up over the entire world with your radiance— with that, drive away from us all lack of nourishment, lack of offerings, disease, and evil dreams.
For, sent forth, you guard the sacred law of the universe; rising up without anger, you proceed according to your own nature.
O Sūrya, whatever resolve we declare to you today, may the gods favor that intention of ours.
May Heaven and Earth, may the Waters, Indra, and the Maruts hear this our invocation and this word.
May we not be deprived of the sight of the sun; living auspiciously, may we reach old age.
May we, with benevolent minds and clear vision, possessing offspring, free from disease and sin,
behold you day after day as you rise, O Sūrya of Mitra-like luster— may we long live to see you.
O far-seeing Sūrya, may we, while still living, behold you as you ascend from the vast expanse of light— you who bear great radiance, who shine with splendor, and who bring delight to every eye.
O Sūrya, you by whose signal all beings move forth and by whose rays they return to rest,
O golden-haired one, come to us day after day with greater and ever-greater sinlessness and prosperity.
Be auspicious to us with your eye, auspicious to us by day, auspicious with your light, auspicious with the cold, and auspicious with the heat!
O Sūrya, bestow upon us that wonderful wealth so that there may be well-being on our journey and well-being in our home.
O Gods, grant protection to both our classes of beings—our bipeds and our quadrupeds.
Grant us that which is eaten, drunk, and strengthening; bestow upon us peace, well-being, and freedom from harm.

O gods, whatever grave offense we have committed against you through our tongue or through a lapse of mind that provokes the wrath of the gods— if anyone who is hostile toward us seeks to bring misfortune upon us, O Vasus, lay that sin upon him.
O Indra, protect us in this glorious and powerful battle-cry for the sake of victory,
where in the struggle for cattle among the bold and armored warriors, the missiles fly in all directions in the conquest of men.
O Indra, unclose for us at our dwelling wealth accompanied by food, a flood of cattle, and glory.
O Śakra, may we be the allies of you as you conquer; O Vasu, do as we desire.
O Indra, much-praised by many, whoever—whether a Dāsa or an Ārya—plots against us for battle, may those enemies be easy for us to overcome; with you, may we conquer them in the encounter.
He who is to be invoked by the few and by the many, he who in close combat provides wide space in the struggle for men—
that famous hero, the winner in the contest, Indra, we shall today bring hither for our protection.
For I have heard of you, O Indra, as one who follows his own will, the bull who drives on the weak;
release yourself from Kutsa and come here! How can one like you remain bound by the testicles?

O Aśvins, that all-pervading, well-rolling chariot of yours which is to be invoked at evening and at dawn by the offerer of oblations— that very chariot of yours, ever-present, we now invoke as one whose name is easy to call, like that of a father.
Impel our truthful hymns, nourish our thoughts, and send forth our inspired prayers; that is what we desire.
O Aśvins, make for us a glorious portion, and make us as dear to the patrons as Soma is.
Even for the aged, you two become a source of fortune; even for the blind, you are protectors;
even for the destitute, O Nāsatyas, and even for the emaciated, they call upon you two as physicians for his healing.
You two fashioned Cyavāna, who was worn out like an old chariot, into a youth again for the sake of movement;
you carried Niṣṭaugrya out from the waters—all these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at the libations.
I shall proclaim your ancient heroic deeds among the people; thus you have been physicians, bringers of joy.
As such, we now make you new for our protection, O Nāsatyas, so that this pious man may place his trust in you.
I have called upon you both; hear me, O Aśvins! Bestow your favor upon me as parents do for their son.
I am friendless, unknown, and without kin, lacking wisdom; rescue me before that curse reaches me.
On your chariot you brought Śundhyū down for Vimada, the maiden of Purumitra;
you came to the call of Vadhrimatī and you brought forth good offspring for Purandhi.
You restored the vigor of the sage Kali, who had reached old age, back to youth once more;
you raised Vandana up from the pit, and you instantly enabled Viśpalā to walk again.
O Ashvins, you two, O bulls, raised up Rebha who was hidden in a cave and nearly dead;
you made the heated cauldron a source of protection for Atri, the son of Saptavadhri.
O Aśvins, you gave to Pedu a white horse, powerful with ninety-nine steeds;
a horse worthy of praise, who speeds his friend along, like Bhaga to be invoked by men, the source of joy.

Neither from any side, O two Kings, O Aditi, does distress, misfortune, nor any fear reach him whom you, O Aśvins— easily invoked, whose path is like that of Rudra— make the leader with his chariot together with his wife.
Come hither with that chariot swifter than thought, which the R̥bhus fashioned for you, O Aśvins—
the chariot at the harnessing of which the Daughter of Heaven is born, and both the fair days of Vivasvat arise.

O Aśvins, you two went on your circuit and, with victory, caused the mountain to open; O Aśvins, you made the cow swell for Śayu. Even the quail that had been swallowed within the mouth of a wolf, you released by your mighty deeds.
O Aśvins, we have fashioned this hymn for you, as the Bhṛgus fashion a chariot;
we have polished it like a maiden for a suitor, cherishing it as one would a constant son or offspring.
Where is the chariot going, and who, O heroes, awaits your radiant one for our well-being?
It travels at dawn, far-reaching, bringing sustenance to every clan, day after day, through prayer and ritual labor.
Where indeed are you at night, O Aśvins, and where by day? Where do you go toward us, and where have you stayed?
Who brings you to your dwelling, as a widow brings her brother-in-law, or as a young woman brings her husband?

At dawn you two awaken like two aged women out of longing; day after day, O worshipful ones, you go to the house. Whose [house] do you, the destroyers, frequent? Or for whom, O heroes, do you go to the libations like two princes?
Like two wild elephants pursued by hunters, we invoke you both with oblations at evening and at dawn.
To the man who offers the sacrifice at the appointed time, O Lords of Splendor, you bring nourishment.
O Aśvins, Ghōṣā, the daughter of the king, as she was going along, said to you: "I ask you, O heroes:
be present for me by day and be present for the night; help the one who possesses horses and a chariot, and assist the steed."
O Aśvins, you two are sages; like Kutsa, you bring your chariot to the people, and you reach the singer as if to a home.
O Aśvins, the bee brings honey from you both with its mouth, like a maiden bringing a prepared gift.
O Aśvins, you indeed brought Bhujyu, you brought Vaśa, and you rescued Śiñjāra and Uśanas.
The liberal donor sits around your friendship; through your protection, I long for your favor.
