O Aśvins, you indeed protect Kṛśa, you protect Śayu, and you protect the widow who serves you;
O Aśvins, for the sake of those seeking gain, you open the thundering stall with its seven mouths.
The maiden was born; the young man flew forth; the plants sprouted according to his wondrous deeds. For him the rivers flow like valleys; for this day, that state of being a husband comes to pass.
They weep for the living and part at the sacrifice; the men have fixed their thoughts upon a long-lasting lineage.
They who have prepared this [offering] for the fathers have brought forth what is desirable: a joy for the husbands and wives for their embrace.
We do not know that; speak it forth clearly—how it is that the youth dwells within the wombs of the young maidens.
O Aśvins, we desire to go to the home of the beloved bull, the possessor of seed and of ruddy cows.

Your benevolence has come to us, O lords of ample wealth; O Aśvins, desires have been directed toward our hearts. You have become our protectors, a pair of lords of splendor; may we attain the dear dwellings of Aryaman.

Rejoicing in the dwelling of man, O Lords of Splendor, bestow upon the eloquent singer wealth together with heroic sons. Create a ford with good watering-places; strike down the obstacle standing in the path and the evil-minded one.

Where indeed today, in which people's dwellings, do the two Aśvins, the wonder-workers and lords of splendor, rejoice? Who has detained them? To whose house have they gone—that of a sage or of a sacrificer?

We invoke with well-fashioned hymns that same much-invoked, praiseworthy three-wheeled chariot which comes to the libations; it travels all around, worthy of the assembly, as we call upon it at the breaking of dawn.
O Nāsatyas, you mount at dawn the chariot that is yoked at early morning, which travels at dawn and carries honey;
by means of which, O Heroes, you go to the people who perform sacrifice, even to the sacrifice of the poor man accompanied by a Hotṛ-priest, O Aśvins.
Whether you go to the *adhvaryu* with honeyed hands and skillful fingers, or to the *agnīdh* who is firm in resolve and domestic,
or to the libations of the inspired singer— come from there, O Aśvins, to drink the honeyed draught.
Like an archer aiming at a well-marked target, bring forth this hymn for him as if adorning it.
O sages, cross over the speech of the enemy with your own voice; O singer, cause Indra to settle his mind upon the Soma.
Win over the cow with milking; O singer, awaken your friend Indra as a lover. Like a full vessel overflowing with wealth, cause the hero to pour forth for the granting of riches.
Why indeed, O Maghavan, do they call you a liberal giver? Sharpen me; I hear that you are one who sharpens.
O Śakra, let my inspired thought be fruitful; O Indra, bring us Bhaga, the finder of wealth.
O Indra, people standing together in the heat of battle call upon you in their desire for possessions.
In this conflict, the hero makes him who offers oblations his ally; he does not seek friendship with one who presses no Soma.
Like abundant, flowing wealth, he who, providing the sacrificial food, presses out strong Soma juices for him—
for that man he slays the Vṛtra at dawn, making his enemies swift to flee and easy to subdue.
In that Indra we place our hope, he who, the bounteous Maghavan, has directed his desire toward us—let his enemy, even though far away, tremble before him; let all human glories bow down before him.
Drive the enemy far away with that fierce *śamba* weapon, O you who are invoked by many!
Bestow upon us wealth consisting of barley and cattle, O Indra; grant the singer a prayer rich in booty.
Into whom the strong-pressing, sharp Somas with abundant ends have entered Indra—Maghavan does not withhold his gift; he brings much wealth to the one who presses the juice.
Moreover, he shall win the prize by casting the die beyond the limit, when the gambler gathers his winnings at the proper time;
the self-reliant one unites with wealth that man who desires the gods and does not withhold his riches.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over all evil-minded poverty with cattle, and over all hunger with barley;
may we, as the foremost, win riches through the kings and by our own vigorous band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below against the malevolent one;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as our friend.
Toward me, Indra, our thoughts—seeking the light of heaven, all united and longing—have cried out.
They embrace him as wives embrace a husband, as they would a handsome youth, for the sake of the bounteous one’s protection.

My mind indeed does not turn away from you; in you alone, O Much-invoked One, have I placed my desire. Sit down like a king, O Wondrous One, upon this sacred grass; let there be a place for you to drink at this fine Soma.

Indra is the one who overcomes both want and hunger; he alone, the bounteous Maghavan, rules over wealth and treasure. These seven rivers flow down his slope, increasing the vital strength of that impetuous bull.
Like birds upon a tree with fair foliage, the exhilarating Soma drops have settled in the vessels for Indra.
Their vanguard, flashing with power, has found the light of heaven, the Aryan light, for mankind.
As a gambler gathers his winnings at play, so Maghavan won the sun as his total prize;
no other, O Maghavan, neither one of old nor one of recent times, has been able to equal that heroic deed of yours.
Maghavan has taken his place around every clan; the Bull gazes upon the lowing of the people.
He at whose libations Śakra takes delight overcomes his assailants with potent Soma-draughts.
When the Soma juices flow together toward Indra like waters toward the ocean or rivulets toward a lake,
the inspired singers increase his greatness at the place of sacrifice, just as rain increases the barley with its divine bounty.
Like a bull enraged, he rushed through the mid-air, he who made these waters the wives of the noble one;
that Maghavan found light for the man who presses the juice, for the swift-giving one who offers oblations.
Let the axe be born anew together with light; let there be, as of old, a cow that yields the milk of Truth.
Let the ruddy one shine forth with his pure radiance; like the bright sky, let the Lord of the True be resplendent.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over ill-will with cattle, and all hunger with barley;
may we, as the foremost, win riches through the kings and by our own heroic band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, from the one who intends evil;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as our friend.
May Indra, the lord of himself, come for exhilaration— he who, powerful and impetuous according to his nature,
has surpassed all strengths with his boundless and great virility.
Well-seated is your chariot, well-governed are your two bay steeds; O Lord of Men, the thunderbolt is firmly grasped in your hand.
Come hither quickly, O King, by fair paths; we shall increase your manly powers once you have drunk.
May the fierce and powerful ones, borne by Indra, bring hither to us this king who wields the thunderbolt, the formidable one;
may they, the swift and vigorous, bring this bull of true strength to our communal feast.
Thus you seek as a husband one who dwells in the vat, who is mindful, the pillar of strength, and the support;
exert your power, gather it within yourself, so that you may be the lord for the increase of those who drink from the wooden vessels.
May he come to us with riches, for I have praised him; come to the bearer of the well-prayed prayer who possesses the Soma!
You are the lord; sit down upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), for by your law your vessels are inviolable.

The first invocations of the gods went forth separately; they performed deeds for glory that were difficult to surpass. Those who were unable to board the sacrificial ship settled down like hairless, creeping things.

Let those of evil intent go away; let those whose ill-yoked horses have been harnessed depart. Truly, those who are here below for the sake of giving, where there are many provisions and means of enjoyment—[to them let the others go].
He has supported the mountains and the plains as they tremble; heaven has roared and shaken the mid-air regions.
He props apart the two converging bowls of the world; having drunk of the bull’s [Soma], he proclaims hymns in his exhilaration.
I carry this well-fashioned goad for you, O Maghavan, with which you shall break those who strike with their hooves.
May it find its home in this libation of yours; O Maghavan, be present at the pressed juice and the sacrifice as a sharer.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over ill-will with cattle, and all hunger with barley;
may we, as the foremost, win riches through the kings and by our own heroic band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, against the malicious one;
may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as a friend.
Agni was first born from heaven; for a second time, Jātavedas was born from us.
A third time he was born in the waters, he whose mind is set on man. The pious man, kindling him, praises this eternal one.
We know your three forms, O Agni, in three ways; we know your stations distributed in many places. We know your supreme name which is hidden in secret; we know that fountain from which you have come.
In the ocean, within the waters, you who are mindful of men and watchful over men, O Agni, I have kindled you in the udder of heaven;
you who stood in the third region, in the lap of the waters, the mighty ones increased you.
Agni roared like the thundering sky, licking the earth and anointing the plants;
as soon as he was born, being kindled, he looked abroad, and with his radiance he shines between the two worlds.
The noble upholder of glories, the supporter of riches, the inspirer of thoughts, and the guardian of Soma;
the Son of Strength, the Vasu, the King, kindled at the forefront of the dawns, shines forth within the waters.
The banner of all, the germ of the world, he filled the two worlds at his birth;
he split even the firm rock as he went forth, when the five peoples sacrificed to Agni.
The eager, purifying, wise messenger, Agni the immortal, has been established among mortals.
Bearing aloft his ruddy smoke, he rises upward, striving to reach the sky with his bright radiance.

Visible like a golden ornament, he has shone far and wide, radiant for the sake of glory with a life-span difficult to surpass. Agni became immortal through his vital powers when the prolific Dyaus brought him forth.
O Agni of auspicious luster, O God, whoever today prepares for you a cake mixed with ghee,
lead him further toward greater wealth, toward the favor bestowed by the gods, O youngest one.
O Agni, grant him a share in glorious deeds; at every hymn being recited, grant him a share.
May he be dear to Sūrya, dear to Agni; may he prevail with what has been born and with what is yet to be born.
O Agni, day after day, the sacrificers have placed all desirable treasures within you;
seeking wealth through you, the yearning ones have opened the cow-filled stall.
Agni has been praised by the seers, the most gracious Vaiśvānara, the guardian of Soma.
We invoke the non-hostile Heaven and Earth; O gods, bestow upon us wealth with heroic sons.
Born as the great Hotṛ-priest, pervading the firmament, he who sits among men has taken his seat in the lap of the waters;
he who was established as the sustainer bestows vital strengths upon you, the protector of the body, bestowing riches upon the worshiper.
Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters, they followed his tracks like one seeking a lost animal;
the wise Bhr̥gus, longing with homages for him who was moving in secret, found him as they sought him.
Trita, the son of Vibhūvasu, seeking him, found him here at the head of the cow.
Born as one who increases prosperity within the dwellings, he, the youth, becomes the central navel of the radiant realm.
With prostrations, the yearning ones have established the delightful Hotṛ-priest— the leader of sacrifices, who guides the ritual forward—
as the steward of the people, the purifier, and the bearer of oblations among mankind.

The foolish brought forward the wise one—the mighty conqueror, the great sustainer of thought, the shatterer of forts—carrying him like the embryo of the woods; they placed their devotion upon him who has golden beard, like a steed that wins the prize.
Trita, supporting himself within the dwellings, sat enveloped in the womb;
from there, the friend of the people, having gathered [the waters], moves among men by means of his ordinances and restraints.
His are the ageless fires, the rudders of the dwellings, with glowing smoke, the purifiers;
white-shining, strengthening, restless, seated in the woods like winds, they are like Soma-draughts.
Agni bears forth his inspired song with his tongue; through his wisdom, he proclaims the ordinances of the earth.
Men have established him as the purifying, radiant, and delightful Hotṛ-priest, the most skilled in sacrifice.
The Heaven and Earth brought forth that Agni, as did the Waters, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the Bhṛgus with their powers;
Mātariśvan and the gods fashioned him, the first one worthy of praise and worship for mankind.

You, whom the gods have established as the bearer of oblations, whom men of many desires worship as the holy one—O Agni, bestow strength upon the singer during his journey; for he who seeks the gods becomes glorious through many ancient [deeds].
We have grasped your right hand, O Indra, seeking wealth, O Lord of treasures.
For we know you, O Hero, as the master of cattle; grant us wonderful, bull-like riches.
O you who possess excellent weapons, excellent power, and excellent guidance, the support of riches from the four oceans— bestow upon us that wonderful,
rain-bestowing wealth which is worthy of praise, worthy of recitation, and possesses abundant boons.
O Indra, grant us wonderful, bull-like wealth— rich in sacred prayer, accompanied by the gods, vast, deep, broad-based, renowned as a seer, fierce, and the subduer of adversaries.

O Indra, grant us wealth that wins the prize, with inspired heroes as its champions, a conqueror, a seeker of riches, ever-increasing, highly skillful, a slayer of Dasyus, a breaker of forts, true, wonderful, and virile.
O Indra, grant us wealth consisting of horses, chariots, and heroes—hundreds and thousands of booty;
grant us a brilliant, bull-like fortune, accompanied by auspicious hosts and wise men, which wins the light of heaven.
My thought goes forth toward Bṛhaspati, the seven-steeded, whose mind is fixed on the Truth, the highly wise;
he who, as an Aṅgiras, is to be approached with homage—may he grant us wondrous, manly wealth.
Seeking you like a lover, my messengers—the hymns of praise—go forth to Indra, imploring his favor;
touching the heart and uttered by the mind, O Bull, grant us wondrous wealth.
O Indra, grant us that which I ask of you: a vast dwelling, unequaled among men. May Heaven and Earth approve of that; bestow upon us wonderful, bull-like wealth.
I have been the ancient lord of wealth; I win all riches forever. Living beings call upon me as they would a father; I distribute food to the one who offers oblations.
I am Indra; I was the dam for Atharvan. For Trita, I brought forth the cows from the serpent. From the Dasyus, I took away their manly strength, bestowing the cow-pens upon Dadhyanc and Mātariśvan.

For me Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the iron thunderbolt; in me the gods have placed their will. My host is difficult to overcome like that of the sun; they honor me for what has been done and for what is yet to be done.

With my arrow I have struck down this cattle-rich, horse-rich, and golden beast, full of abundance, for the sake of the donor—when the Soma juices, accompanied by hymns, have exhilarated me. I destroy many thousands for the one who gives, since the pressed Somas have gladdened me.
I am Indra; I have never been defeated in battle for wealth, nor have I ever yielded to death at any time.
Pressing the Soma, do you entreat me for riches; O Pūrus, you shall suffer no harm in my friendship.

I struck down with my blow those who were panting in pairs against Indra, who had turned their thunderbolt toward battle; calling out to me, I struck them with my weapon, speaking harshly to those who offered homage while I remained unyielding.
I am one, and yet I overcome this one; I overcome two—what then can three do? Like a threshing-floor, I strike down the vast multitude; why do these enemies, who lack Indra, revile me?
I made Ātithigva superior to the Guṅgus; like nourishing food, I established him among the people as a conqueror of Vṛtra.
When Parṇaya was slain, or when Karañja was struck down, I won renown in the great battle for the slaying of Vṛtra.
Namī Sāpya has come forward for my nourishment and enjoyment; in the search for cattle, he has established friendship with me once again.
When I bestowed upon him a missile in the battles, I then made him worthy of praise and fit for hymns.
Soma is seen within one of these two; he makes the other manifest as a protector. Desiring to fight the sharp-horned bull, the Deceiver stood bound within the vast expanse.
I do not violate the station of the Ādityas, the Vasus, or the sons of Rudra—the god among gods. They have fashioned me for auspicious power: unconquered, unassailable, and invincible.
I have granted ancient wealth to the singer; I have made the sacred word (*brahman*) my own means of increase.
I have become the instigator for the sacrificer; in every battle, I am the witness against the non-sacrificer.
The creatures of heaven, earth, and the waters have placed me in the position of the deity named Indra.
I [have yoked] the two swift, vigorous, and differently directed bay steeds; I have boldly taken up the thunderbolt for the sake of power.

I struck down Atka for the sake of the seer with my blows; I protected Kutsa with these aids. I am the smiter of Śuṣṇa with my weapon, he who did not yield the Āryan name to the Dasyu, as one yields it to Yama.
Like a father, I subdued the Vetasus for the sake of Tugra’s aid, and I delivered Smadibha to Kutsa.
I became the sovereign of the sacrificer when I brought forth [the wealth] for Tuji, so that he might not be overcome by his enemies.
I subdued Mṛgayu for Śrutarvan when he did not follow my instructions even in succession.
I made Veśa bow down for Āyu; I delivered Paḍgṛbhi as a slave to Savya.
I am he who, like the slayer of Vṛtra, crushed the Dāsa Navavāstva Bṛhadratha;
when he was growing and spreading out in due order, I fashioned the luminous realms on the far shore of the mid-region.
I travel around the sun with my swift steeds, borne along by power with the *praitaśa* horses. When the human presser calls me to the bright garment, I utterly subdue the Dāsa Kṛtvya with my blows.

I, the slayer of the seven, more *nahuṣ* than *nahuṣ*, have by my might made Turvaśa and Yadu renowned; I, by force, have subdued another who possessed the power of force, and I have caused ninety-nine of the mighty to grow.
I, the bull, sustain the seven flowing rivers that run in haste upon the earth; I, the wise one, spread out the floods through my power, and by battle I found a path for Manu to seek his goal.
I have placed within these that bright [milk] which not even the god Tvaṣṭṛ himself had placed there—
desirable in the udders of the cows, in their wombs, the honeyed sweetness, the invigorating Soma mixed with milk.
Thus Indra has distinguished himself among the gods and men, the bounteous Maghavan whose gifts are true, by his mighty deed.
All these, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, O Lord of Might, do the swift ones praise as your own glorious power.

Sing forth for the great one who rejoices in the soma-juice, for Viśvānara who is all-pervading— he, Indra, whose battle-winning power is mighty, whose fame is great, and whose manly vigor both heaven and earth revere.
He indeed, the heroic Indra, when praised, is to be celebrated as a friend by a man like me;
O Lord of the Good, you take delight in all burdens, in deeds for the sake of booty, in the slaying of Vṛtra, and in the waters, O Hero.
Who are those men of yours, O Indra, who strive for your refreshment, who strive for your bliss that brings wealth?
Who have urged you on toward heroic power, toward the divine strength, toward the waters, and toward manly valor in the fertile fields?
O Indra, you have become great through the sacred prayer; you have become worthy of sacrifice at all libations.
You have become the shaker of men in every battle; O Lord of all people, you are the most excellent counsel.
Now indeed, you who are greater, favor those who delight in sacrifice; the people know your great protection.
Now indeed, as the ageless one, may you grow; you have made all these libations effective.
All these libations you have made effective for yourself, O Son of Strength, which you have established.
For your choice and for your law, there is the vessel, the sacrifice, the mantra, the sacred formulation, and the uplifted word.
O Sage, those [songs] of yours which were composed as sacred prayers (*brahman*) at the pressing, for the bestowing of riches and treasures—
may they come forth by way of the path of your benevolence through the mind, in the exhilaration of the pressed Soma juice.
Great was that womb, firm was it, enveloped by which you entered the waters;
O Agni Jātavedas, the one god beheld all your many forms, O deity.
Who has seen me? Which god was it that beheld my bodies in their many forms? O Mitra and Varuṇa, where do they abide, and what are all the fire-sticks of Agni that lead to the gods?
O Jātavedas, we sought you in many places, O Agni, as you had entered into the waters and the plants.
Yama perceived you, O you of brilliant luster, shining forth from within the ten intermediate spaces.
O Varuṇa, I fled from the office of the Hotṛ priest out of fear, lest the gods should appoint me to that task here;
my bodies have entered into many places, yet I, Agni, did not perceive this purpose.

Come, O Agni; Manu, seeking the gods and desiring sacrifice, has prepared the rite for you. You shall dwell in the darkness; therefore, make the paths leading to the gods easy to traverse, and, being well-disposed, carry the oblations.
Agni’s elder brothers pursued this goal as a charioteer follows a path;
out of fear of that, O Varuṇa, I went far away, like a wild ox fleeing from the archer’s bowstring.
We grant you an ageless lifespan, O Agni, so that once harnessed, O Jātavedas, you shall not come to harm;
then, being well-disposed, O noble-born one, you shall carry the portion of the oblation to the gods.

O Gods, grant me the fore-offerings and the after-offerings exclusively, and a strengthening portion of the oblation; grant me the fatness of the waters and the essence of the plants, and may there be long life for Agni.
May the fore-offerings and after-offerings be yours alone; may the portions of the oblation be full of vigor.
O Agni, let this entire sacrifice be yours; let the four quarters bow down before you.
O All-Gods, instruct me how, having been chosen as the Hotṛ and having sat down here, I may think;
tell me my portion, how [it is], and by which path I shall bring the oblation to you.
I have sat down as the Hotṛ, the most skilled in sacrifice; all the gods and the Maruts impel me.
Day after day, O Aśvins, the office of Adhvaryu belongs to you; the Brahman is the kindling wood, and he becomes your oblation.
Who indeed is this one who is the Hotṛ of Yama? Whom do the gods intend when they anoint him?
Day after day he is born, month after month; therefore the gods have established him as the bearer of oblations.

The gods have established me as the bearer of oblations, moving through many hardships without faltering. May Agni, the wise one, arrange for us the sacrifice—five-pathed, threefold, and seven-threaded.
I shall worship you for immortality and heroic strength, so that, O Gods, I may create wide space for you.
May I place the thunderbolt in Indra’s arms, and then he shall conquer all these hostile armies.
Three thousand, three hundred, and thirty-nine gods have honored Agni;
they have sprinkled him with clarified butter, spread the sacrificial grass for him, and then seated him as the Hotṛ priest.

He whom we sought with our mind has arrived—he who knows the joint of the sacrifice and is wise. May he, the most excellent sacrificer, worship us in the assembly of the gods; for may he sit down as our intimate and foremost guest.
The Hotṛ, the most excellent sacrificer, has been successful through his sitting down; for he has looked upon the well-placed offerings.
Let us sacrifice to the gods worthy of sacrifice; come, let us honor with clarified butter those who are worthy of praise.
He has made our feast for the gods successful today; we have found the secret tongue of the sacrifice.
He has come, fragrant and clothed in life; he has made our invocation of the gods auspicious today.
May I today perceive that first word of speech by which we gods may overcome the Asuras.
O eaters of strength, worthy of sacrifice, you five peoples, graciously accept my oblation!
May the five peoples enjoy my oblation—both those born of the cow and those who are worthy of sacrifice.
May the earth protect us from earthly distress; may the atmosphere protect us from celestial distress.
Spinning out the thread, follow the radiance of the mid-region; guard the luminous paths prepared by wisdom.
Weave the web without flaw for those who urge you on; become Manu and bring forth the divine race.
O you who are worthy of Soma, fasten the axle-pins; prepare the reins and fashion them.
Bring from both sides the chariot with its eight-seated seat, by which the gods led [Indra] toward what is dear.
The stony river flows; hold fast to one another, arise, and cross over, O friends!
Here we leave behind those who were unkind; may we cross over toward auspicious strengths.

Tvaṣṭṛ, the most skillful of workers, knows the creative powers; bearing the most auspicious vessels for the drinking of the gods, he now sharpens his axe of good steel, with which Etaśa, the Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), shall cut away.
O sages, now truly sharpen your axes with which you fashion the existent for the sake of immortality.
Knowing the secret places, perform the work by which the gods attained immortality.
They placed the maiden in the womb and the calf in the mouth, with a secret mind and a tongue;
he, being well-disposed toward all things, seeking to win through his efforts, wins the prize of victory for the singer.
O Maghavan, that fame of yours is truly great through your majesty, since the two worlds, terrified, called upon you.
You protected the gods and overcame the Dāsa’s might, O Indra, when you exerted yourself for the sake of this progeny.
When you went forth, increasing in body and proclaiming your powers among the people, O Indra—that was but a trick of yours;
for those battles of which they speak, you have found no enemy today, nor indeed in the past.
Who indeed among the seers of old have reached the limit of your entire greatness—
[the limit] of you who brought forth both mother and father together from your own body?
Four are your divine names, unassailable, belonging to you, the Mighty One. You indeed know all of them, O Maghavan, by which you performed your deeds.
You possess all treasures exclusively—those that are manifest and those that are hidden.
O Maghavan, do not frustrate my desire; you are the knower, O Indra, you are the giver.
He who placed light within light, who created honeyed things with honey— therefore,
this dear and powerful hymn has been spoken by the maker of prayer for Indra, from Bṛhaduktha.
Far away is that secret name, directed toward the beyond, which the two terrified ones called upon you, O giver of vital strength.
You propped up the earth and the sky in their encounter, O Maghavan, shining fiercely against your brother's sons.
Great is that secret name, touching many, by which you brought forth what has been and what is to be;
the ancient light that was born, which is his beloved—into it the five beloved tribes have entered together.
He filled the two worlds and the intermediate space, and the five classes of gods, seven by seven, according to their seasons.
With his manifold light, which is uniform yet diverse in its movement, he looks out in thirty-four directions.

When you, O Dawn, shone forth as the first of the luminaries, by which you brought forth the nourishment of nourishment; that kinship of yours which is nearer than the further, and that great, unique sovereignty of yours, O Great One.
The gray-haired one has swallowed the moon, who was running in the assembly of many, though he himself was young.
Behold the sage-like power of the god through his greatness: he who was alive yesterday has died today.

By his own power, the powerful one, the ruddy bird, who is great, heroic, and from of old without a nest—whatever he has willed is indeed true and not in vain; he is the winner and giver of desirable wealth.
With these [powers] the wielder of the thunderbolt took up manly strengths and virilities, by which he grew for the slaying of Vṛtra;
those gods who, through the greatness of the deed being performed, arose even before the act was completed.
Performing deeds with his companion, possessing all vigor, slaying the revilers, all-seeing,
and swift-conquering— having drunk of the Soma and grown strong from heaven, the hero blew away the Dasyus from the battle.
This is one [form] of yours, and another is beyond; unite with the third light.
Be gracious to our body in its rest, beloved among the gods in the highest birthplace.
O Steed, may your body, leading your own body [to the sacrifice], bestow what is desirable upon us and protection upon you.
Unharmed, for the support of the great gods, may you measure out your own light like a light in heaven.
You are a prize-winner; with your prize-winning power, go to the well-guided ones, to the hymn of praise, and to heaven—well-guided!
Go according to the first true laws—well-guided! Go to the gods—well-guided! Follow the path—well-guided!
Even their fathers could not master their greatness; the gods placed wisdom within the gods themselves. They encompassed all that they kindled, and it entered back into their very bodies.
With their powers, they have traversed the entire space, measuring out the immeasurable ancient abodes.
They have established all beings within their own bodies and have spread forth progeny in many directions.

In two ways the sons established the Asura, the finder of heaven, by means of the third act. The fathers placed their own offspring and the paternal heritage together among the later generations, like a stretched-out thread.
Like a boat across the waters, through the regions of the earth, may he carry us by blessings past all difficulties.
By his greatness, Bṛhaduktha has established his own offspring among both the lower and the higher ones.
May we not stray from the path, O Indra, nor from the sacrifice, we who possess the Soma;
may no enemies stand against us.
May we attain that which is the fulfiller of the sacrifice, the thread stretched out among the gods, when it has been offered with oblations.
We now invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa Soma and with the hymns of the Fathers.
May your mind return to you for the sake of will, for skill, and for life, so that you may long behold the sun.
May the divine folk, our fathers, grant us back our mind; may we be united with the company of the living.
O Soma, may we, maintaining our minds within your law and within our bodies, abide together with offspring.
O Yama, son of Vivasvat, that mind of yours which has gone far away— to that we cause you to turn back here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Mind, that which of yours has gone far away to heaven or to earth— that we cause to return to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Mind, that which of yours has gone far away to the four-cornered earth— we bring that back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
If your mind has gone far away to the four quarters of space, we bring it back to you here, that you may dwell and live.
O you whose mind has gone far away to the surging ocean, we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
If your mind has gone far away to the rays of light or to the heights, we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Mind, that which has gone far away to the waters or to the plants, we bring that back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O Sūrya, that mind of yours which has gone far away to the sun or to the dawn— we cause it to return to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
O you whose mind has gone far away to the great mountains, we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
This entire world that has gone far away from your mind— we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
Your mind that has gone far away to distant realms beyond— we cause it to return to you here, so that you may dwell and live.
Your mind, O Lord, which has gone far away— to that which was past and that which is yet to be—
we cause it to return here for you, so that you may dwell and live.
May life be further extended, renewed, as by two skillful charioteers of a chariot;
then Cyavāna has achieved his purpose through power—may Nirṛti depart far away.
Now for wealth, let us prepare a treasure-store; now let us create food and manifold glories.
May our singer rejoice in all these things; may Nirṛti depart far away.
May we overcome our enemies with manly deeds, as the sky overcomes the earth, or as mountains overtake the plains.
Our singer has perceived all these things; may Nirṛti depart far away.
O Soma, do not deliver us over to death; may we yet behold the sun rising.
May our old age be set for us by the days; may Nirṛti depart far away.
O Asunīti, maintain the mind within us; prolong our life-span for the sake of living.
Grant us delight in the sight of the sun; do you strengthen our bodies with clarified butter.
O Asunīti, restore sight to us, restore breath, and grant us enjoyment here.
May we long behold the rising sun; O Anumati, be gracious to us for our well-being.
May the Earth give back our breath; may the Goddess Heaven, and the Mid-region, give it back. May Soma give back our body; may Pūṣan give back the path that is well-being.
May Heaven and Earth, the two young mothers of Eternal Order, bring well-being to Subandhu;
may they carry away whatever blemish there is. O Heaven and Earth, let no harm whatsoever afflict you.
Down from the sky come the medicines in twos and threes;
one moves upon the earth. May they both carry away whatever blemish there is. O Heaven and Earth, may no harm whatsoever touch you.
Indra, yoke the ox that drew the wagon of the daughter of Uśīnara.
May Heaven and Earth carry away whatever blemish there is; let no part of you suffer any injury whatsoever.
Bearing our homage, we have come to the people of brilliant aspect, who are praised among the great ones.
The peerless, subduing, brilliant, and ever-advancing chariot—
[we invoke] the true lord of Bhajeratha.
He who, like a buffalo, has stood over the people—
both he who is armed with the spear and he who is without the spear in battle.
He under whose protection Ikṣvāku prospers, wealthy and free from disease,
like the five tribes in heaven.
O Indra, uphold our sovereign power among those who are peerless, like chariot-seats;
make us visible like the sun in the sky.
O Agastya, you have yoked the two ruddy steeds from the rivers;
O King, you have stepped down upon all the Paṇis who offer no gifts.
This is the mother, this is the father; this life-giver has arrived.
This is your place of crawling, Subandhu; come, go forth!
Just as they bind the yoke with a leather thong for the sake of support,
even so have I sustained your mind for life and not for death, but for safety.
Just as this great earth supports these lords of the forest,
so do I support your mind for life, not for death, but for safety and well-being.
From Yama, the son of Vivasvat, I have brought back the spirit of Subandhu,
that he may live and not die, but for his safety and well-being.
Downward blows the wind; downward the sun shines;
downward the cow yields her milk; let your ailment go downward.
This hand of mine is blessed; this hand of mine is more blessed. This hand of mine possesses all healing remedies; this hand is a propitious touch.
This indeed is the formidable prayer of the one of praised speech, fashioned with wisdom and power within the contest;
when his two parents, most eager for the distribution of gifts, performed their work, he carried across the seven Hotṛ-priests at the cooking of the oblation.
Seeking to win for the sake of a deceptive gift, Cyavāna prepared the altar with the Sūdas.
Tūrvayāṇa, whose word is most praised, poured forth the seed like a flood, seeking protection from this world.
In whose invocations you two, like swift thoughts, win the sharp inspired hymns with your power;
he who, possessing great manly vigor, has filled his hand with arrows according to his aim.
When the dark one sits among the ruddy cows, I invoke you two, O Aśvins, sons of Heaven.
Accept my sacrifice; come to my food, you who have won the prize, you whose resolve is unfailing.
He whose heroic deed was extended, who struck down the manly [foe] when it was performed;
he, the unassailable one, draws back again that which was carried away from the maiden’s daughter.
When there was a task to be done in the midst of the encounter, as the father made his desire for the young woman, they both,
departing, left behind their mindful seed poured upon the ridge in the womb of the well-fashioned work.
When the Father, uniting with her, spilled his seed upon his own daughter upon the earth,
the gods, well-disposed, generated the sacred word (*brahman*) and fashioned Vāstoṣpati, the guardian of vows, from it.
Like a bull, he cast forth foam in the battle; with steady mind, he advanced, not failing.
He moved like a gift-bestowing foot, turning away from them; yet those dappled mares did not seize me.
Swiftly like a bearer, the one who makes the people hear sits near Agni as if naked at the udder;
he wins the fuel and wins the prize; he was born as the sustainer, overcoming with might.
Swiftly did the Navagvas come to the maiden’s friendship, speaking the Truth and joined with the Truth;
those of double strength who approached the Guardian, though offering no sacrificial fee, desired to milk the immovable [cow].
Swiftly [I seek] a newer friendship with the maiden; like a gift, I hasten toward the seed, the truth itself—that pure heritage which they offered as the milk of the ever-yielding, ruddy cow.

When he says, "Awakened by the cattle, they have been separated behind," the singer speaks as one who bestows gifts; through his power over wealth, the tireless poet fashions all riches and nourishment.
Then indeed his followers came, many sitting around, seeking to break through the seat of Nārṣada.
The unassailable one found what was hidden in the cave of Śuṣṇa, who had many offspring, though it was intricately entwined.
Thy name is Bharga, O God, and those gods who have sat down in the threefold station like the sun;
thy name is Agni and Jātavedas. Hear us, O Hotṛ; as the guileless Hotṛ of the Ṛta, listen to us.
And may those two Raudras, the radiant Nāsatyas, O Indra, be worshipped for my praise;
being joyful, bestowing gifts upon the man who has trimmed the sacrificial grass like Manu, they are to be honored among the people with well-prepared offerings.
This king, praised and lauded as a wise ordainer, the inspired singer crosses the waters by his own bridge;
he makes Kakṣīvat tremble and he makes Agni shake, like the swift-running wheel of a steed shakes its rim.
He, the doubly kinsman Vaitaraṇa, the sacrificer, shall milk the cow Sabardhu who yields no horse;
when he encompasses Mitra and Varuṇa with hymns and Aryaman with the most excellent protections.
A sage of kin to him, a bestower of devotion in heaven, Nābhānediṣṭha, longing for you, utters his cry.
This is our highest kinship with him; or indeed, was I perhaps even later than that? How many [generations] have passed since then?
This is my navel; here is my dwelling place; these are my gods; here I am in my entirety. I am indeed the twice-born, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta); at my birth, the Cow milked this [world].
Then he, the delightful, radiant, two-pathed one who dwells in the woods, has shone forth;
when, like a line of children rising up, the mother quickly brought forth the firm, joy-increasing infant.
Then the cows followed the example of the maiden, [going] after the breathless one, whoever he may be.
O you who possess beautiful wealth, hear us; come to us! You have grown strong through the truthful words of Āśvaghnī.
Now, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, knower of men, take note of us for great wealth;
protect our patrons, O Maghavan, and guard the wise singers, for they are blameless under your protection, O Lord of the Bay Steeds.

And when the two Kings hasten in the quest for cattle—the swift one and the one who speeds to the singer—then he becomes their most beloved inspired priest; he shall carry them forward and indeed ferry them across.
Now indeed, for the prosperity of this noble one, we approach you with spontaneous hymns; let us pray for that very thing.
His son is the swift steed, and you are the inspired singer, O Sage, in the winning of glory.
If, for the sake of your friendship with us, you have accepted this hymn for the host with reverence—
[the hymn] in which all songs are gathered together— he shall everywhere give way for the sake of prosperity, like an ancient path.

Being praised with waters, accompanied by the gods, and well-kin through homage and hymns, may he grow strong through our recitations and words; for now indeed the path is opened by the milk of the ruddy cow.
O worshipful gods, may you indeed be great and of one accord for our protection—
ye who, moving apart, have brought us strengthening foods, and who stand as wise and infallible observers.

Those who, consecrated by sacrifice and the sacrificial fee, attained the friendship of Indra and immortality—to them, O Aṅgirases, may there be prosperity; O wise ones, accept me, the descendant of Manu.
O Fathers, you who drove forth the wealth of cattle and by the Eternal Law burst Vala open after a full year—may long life be yours, O Aṅgirases; accept me, O wise ones, as a man of human descent.
They who by the *ṛta* caused the sun to ascend to heaven and spread out the mother earth;
O wise Aṅgirases, may you possess noble offspring; accept me, the son of Manu.
This one speaks sweetly for you from the center of the house; O sons of the gods, O seers, listen to that!
May there be excellent Brahman-hood for you, O Aṅgirases; accept Mānava, O wise ones!
These indeed were the seers of diverse forms, they whose inspiration was profound;
they were the sons of Aṅgiras, and they were born from Agni.
Those who were born from Agni, diverse in form, from heaven—
Navagva, Daśagva, the best of the Aṅgirases— he bestows gifts together with the gods.
With Indra as their ally, the worshippers have opened wide the stall rich in cattle and horses;
giving me a thousand [cows] with ears marked by eight [spots], they have established glory among the gods.
May this man now be born; may he grow like a young sprout— he who immediately bestows for a gift a thousand [cattle] and a hundred horses.
No one can reach him, as if trying to grasp the ridge of heaven;
the sacrificial fee of Sāvarṇya has spread out like a river.
And the two Dāsas, Smaddiṣṭi and Goparīṇasa, served him;
Yadu and Turvaśa also made offerings to him.
May the leader, the giver of thousands, not fail; may Manu’s sacrificial fee, striving in unison with the sun, come hither.
May the gods prolong the life of Sāvarṇi, in whom we, unwearied, have won the prize.
May those gods who, from afar, desire kinship, who, pleased by Manu, [guard] the generations of Vivasvat,
and who sit upon the sacrificial grass of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa— may they speak in our favor.
For all your names, O gods, are worthy of homage and praise, and they are worthy of sacrifice. You who are born from Aditi, from the waters, and from the earth—listen here to my call!
For those whom Mother Aditi—of mountain-like strength—causes to swell with honeyed milk and the first-born nectar;
for those Ādityas who are impelled by hymns, who bear the bull, and whose dreams are auspicious—rejoice after them for our well-being!
Beholding men, unwinking, and worthy of worship, the gods have attained the lofty state of immortality.
With chariots of light, possessing the power of serpents and free from sin, they clothe themselves in the height of heaven for our well-being.
Those sovereign lords who, increasing our prosperity, have come to the sacrifice and established their dwelling in heaven unassailed—
invite them hither with reverence and well-fashioned hymns, the great Ādityas and Aditi, for our well-being.
O All-Gods, who among men offers you a hymn that you may enjoy, as many of you as there are?
O you of mighty birth, who shall prepare for you a sacrifice sufficient for your well-being, so that he may carry us across distress?

To whom Manu first offered the oblation with kindled fire and with his mind through the seven Hotṛ-priests—O Ādityas, grant us protection free from fear; make our paths easy to traverse and fair for our well-being.
Those who rule over the world, the wise ones, the thinkers of all that is stationary and moving—
O gods, protect us today from committed and uncommitted sin for our well-being.

In battles we invoke Indra, who is easy to call upon, the deliverer from distress, the well-doing divine host; we invoke Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga for our gain, and Heaven and Earth and the Maruts for our well-being.
May we ascend for our well-being upon the divine ship— well-oared, sinless, and leakless— the good protector Earth, the faultless Heaven, Aditi who provides excellent refuge and excellent guidance.
O all you worshipful ones, speak in our favor for our protection; save us from the malice of the evil-minded.
With a true invocation of the gods, we call upon you, O hearing gods, for your aid and for our well-being.

Drive away disease, drive away every lack of sacrifice, and keep far from us the malice of the malevolent and the treacherous foe. O Gods, remove our hatred; grant us broad protection for our well-being.
Unharmed, that mortal prospers in every way; he is born again through his offspring according to the cosmic law (dharman).
O Ādityas, whom you lead with your excellent guidance across all difficulties for our well-being.
O Gods, that chariot which you protect in the struggle for booty, which you, O Maruts, protect in the battle of heroes when wealth is at stake—
that early-advancing, victorious, and unassailable chariot, O Indra, may we mount for our well-being.
May there be well-being for us on our paths and in the desert wastes; may there be well-being in the waters and in the sunlit assembly.
May there be well-being for us in the wombs that bring forth sons; O Maruts, grant us well-being for the sake of wealth.

Welfare indeed is the best on the distant path, that which brings wealth and approaches what is desirable. May she protect us at home and in the wilderness; may she be well-disposed toward us, having the gods as our guardians.
Thus has the wise son of Plate increased you, O Ādityas and Aditi;
the ruling heroes have been praised by the immortal Gaya, the celestial host.
On which god’s path, among those who hear our names well, shall we meditate? Who will be gracious? Which one will grant us joy? Which one will turn toward us with his aid?
The powers of will act as wills; thoughts long within the hearts; the seekers seek; they fly toward the quarters of space.
No other comforter is found besides them; my desires have been directed toward the gods.
O men, with my song I praise Narāśaṃsa, Pūṣan, Agni—who is not to be hidden—and him kindled by the gods;
Sūrya and Māsa, the two moons, Yama in heaven, Trita, Vāta, Uṣas, Night, and the Aśvins.
How does the poet, the one who roars loudly, [succeed]? With what song is Bṛhaspati magnified by well-fashioned hymns?
May Aja Ekapād and Ahi Budhnya hear our invocation with their well-invoked singers at this call.
At the birth of Dakṣa, in the rite of Aditi, you seek to win over the two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa;
Aryaman, whose paths are unassailable and who possesses many chariots, acts as the sevenfold priest among diverse generations.
May all those coursers, who hear our invocation and run their measured course, hear our call;
they who, like winners at the sacrifice, have by themselves won great wealth in battles, winning thousands.
With hymns of praise, bring forth Vāyu, who yokes his chariot, and Purandhi, and Pūṣan, for friendship.
For they, being of one mind and one purpose, follow the will of the god Savitṛ in his impelling power.
We invoke for our protection the thrice-seven flowing rivers, the great waters, the forest trees, the mountains, and Agni;
we call upon Kṛśānu, the archers, Tiṣya, and Rudra—the lordly one among the Rudras—to their common dwelling place.
May Sarasvatī, Sarayu, and Sindhu with their waves come with great protection, they who are mighty and carry us forward.
O divine Waters, mothers, makers of sweetness, purify for us the milk that is rich in ghee and honey; sing our praise!
May Mother Bṛhaddivā hear our word, and may Tvaṣṭar, the father, together with the gods and their wives;
may R̥bhukṣan, Vāja, Rathaspati, and Bhaga—the delightful praise—protect us who labor in worship.
Delightful to behold like a dwelling-place rich in food, auspicious is the praise of the Rudras, the Maruts.
May we be glorious among the people through our cattle; O Gods, may we ever be united with nourishment.
O Maruts, O Indra, O Gods, O Varuṇa and Mitra, that prayer which you have granted to me—cause it to swell like a cow with milk; will you not carry my songs upon your chariot?
O Maruts, will you indeed take notice of us, as we are your kinsmen?
May Aditi establish our kinship at that navel where we first come together.
For those two great divine Mothers, Heaven and Earth, worthy of sacrifice by virtue of their birth, have come from here to the gods;
both sustain both [worlds] with their supports, and together with the Fathers, they pour down abundant seeds.

May this invocation reach every desirable thing; Bṛhaspati is the most praiseworthy devotion. Where the stone that presses the honeyed juice is raised loudly, there the wise have caused [him] to resound with their hymns.
Thus the sage, loud-voiced, knower of the *ṛta*, seeking wealth and desiring riches,
has here— through hymns and prayers— the inspired poet Gaya caused the celestial generations to swell.
Thus has the wise son of Plate increased you all, O Ādityas and Aditi;
the ruling heroes have been praised by the immortal Gaya, as has the divine folk.
Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, Vāyu, Pūṣan, and Sarasvatī, acting in harmony;
the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, the lofty heaven, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, and Brahmaṇaspati.

Indra and Agni, lords of the good, who in the slayings of Vṛtra impel one another with their bodies, dwelling together in the same abode, have filled the vast mid-air with their might; Soma, adorned with clarity, stirs up his own greatness.

For them, the great and unassailable ones who increase the *ṛta*, I, knowing the *ṛta*, send forth hymns of praise. May they, who possess wonderful wealth and whose power is like the surging ocean, grant us gifts for our glorification, being well-disposed as friends.
With their might, they have propped up the sun, the mid-regions, the luminous spheres, heaven and earth, and the broad ground.
Like nourishing powers, these gods—liberal givers and wise patrons—exalt themselves and are praised by men.

Give gifts to Mitra and Varuṇa, who bestow upon the donor; they are the two sovereign kings who do not neglect the mind. Whose great abode shines by its own law, and whom both heaven and earth encompass as their protection.
The cow who goes around the path to the appointed place, yielding milk, fulfilling her vows from below— she,
announcing herself to Varuṇa the donor, shall serve the gods with oblation for Vivasvat.
Dwelling in heaven, with Agni as their tongue, increasers of Truth, they sit pondering the womb of Truth.
Having propped up the sky, they have brought the waters by their might; having generated the sacrifice, they have measured out its bodies.
The two parents dwelling around, born of old, abide together in the womb of Cosmic Order (Ṛta) in one common home;
Heaven and Earth, acting in harmony with Varuṇa, swell with ghee-rich milk for the mighty Bull.
Parjanya and Vāta, the bulls, the givers of moisture; Indra and Vāyu, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman;
we invoke the Āditya gods and Aditi—those who are on earth, those who are in heaven, and those who are in the waters.

We invoke Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, and the Ṛbhus who are honored; the two divine Hotṛ-priests, and Uṣas for our well-being; Bṛhaspati, the wise devourer of Vṛtra, Indriya, and Soma—we seek them as winners of wealth.
They generated the sacred word, the cow, the horse, the plants, the forest trees, the earth, the mountains, and the waters;
raising the sun in heaven, O bounteous ones, they released the Aryan ordinances over the earth.
O Aśvins, you delivered Bhujyu from distress; you restored Śyāva, the son of Vadhrimatī.
You gave Kamadyū to Vimada; you released Viṣṇāpū for Viśvaka.

The daughter of the thunderbolt, the single-footed one, the goat; the upholder of heaven, the Sindhu, and the waters of the ocean—may all the gods hear my words, along with Sarasvatī, together with our prayers and inspired wisdom.

May all the gods, together with their insights, with Purandhi, the worshipful, immortal ones who know the cosmic order (*ṛta*), those who bestow gifts, those who protect, and those who have found the light— may they take pleasure in our songs, our prayer, and our hymn of praise.
Vasiṣṭha has paid homage to the immortal gods who have extended themselves over all worlds. May they grant us wide space today; and may you [gods] protect us always with your blessings.
I invoke for our well-being the gods of lofty renown, the makers of light, the wise ones of the sacrifice;
those all-knowing ones who have grown ever stronger, with Indra as their chief—immortal, increasers of the Eternal Law.

Impelled by Indra and directed by Varuṇa, those who have attained a share of the light of the sun—within the host of Maruts, in the assembly, we fix our thought; in the bountiful one, the wise have generated the sacrifice.
May Indra with the Vasus protect our household; may Aditi with the Ādityas grant us shelter.
May the god Rudra with the Rudras be gracious to us; may Tvaṣṭṛ with the divine wives (gnās) quicken us toward prosperity.
Aditi, Heaven and Earth, the great *ṛta*, Indra and Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and the lofty sky—these gods, the Ādityas, we invoke for protection: the Vasus, the Rudras, and Savitṛ of wondrous deeds.
May Sarasvat with his prayers, Varuṇa whose laws are firm, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, greatness itself, Vāyu, and the Aśvins—
the immortal creators of sacred knowledge who possess all wealth— grant us a triple-layered protection from distress.
The sacrifice is a bull; may the worthy of worship be bulls; the gods are bulls, and the preparers of the oblation are bulls.
Bullish are Heaven and Earth, the observers of cosmic order; Parjanya is a bull, and the singers of praise are bulls.

O Agni and Soma, you bulls, for the winning of booty, I address you, the highly praised bulls. You whom the bull-like sacrificers have worshipped with the sacrifice to the gods—grant us a triple-layered protection.
The Kṣatriyas of firm vows, who perfect the sacrifice, who dwell in the high heaven, the glory of the rites;
the Agni-priests, seekers of Truth, free from guile—they released the waters in the conquest of Vṛtra.
Generating heaven and earth according to their sacred laws, [the gods] filled the waters, the plants, and the holy trees;
they pervaded the mid-air and the light for our protection, and the gods fashioned their bodies according to their will.

The upholders of heaven, the Ṛbhus with skillful hands, Vāta and Parjanya of the mighty thundering bull—may the waters and the plants further our songs; may Bhaga, Rāti, and the prize-winning steeds come to my invocation.
May the ocean, the rivers, the dust, the intermediate region, Aja Ekapād, the thundering cloud, the serpent of the deep, and all the gods as well as my wise patrons, hear my words.
May we, as men, be yours for the feast of the gods; lead our sacrifice forward with success.
O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, you bounteous givers, quicken these prayers being recited.
I follow rightly the path of Truth, following the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first appointed.
We pray to the Lord of the Field, our neighbor, and to all the immortal gods who are ever-watchful.
The Vasiṣṭhas have uttered their speech like fathers, praising the gods like seers for our well-being. Like affectionate kinsmen coming to fulfill our desire, O gods, shake down wealth upon us.
Vasiṣṭha has praised the immortal gods who have extended themselves over all worlds. May they grant us wide-striding space today; and do you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings.
Our father discovered this seven-headed, lofty hymn, born of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*);
indeed, the one beneficial to all people, Ayāsya, generated its fourth part while reciting the praise-song for Indra.

Proclaiming the *ṛta*, meditating on the straight path, the sons of Heaven, the heroes of the Asura, the Aṅgirases, establishing the inspired singer as their station, conceived the first ordinance of the sacrifice.
Like swans, with his clamoring companions, Bṛhaspati cast aside the stone-made bonds; he bellowed toward the cows, and knowing the way, he sang aloud and praised them.
With two [verses] he helped [the cows], with one more he drove forth the cows that stood hidden in the cave at the bridge of falsehood;
Bṛhaspati, seeking light in the darkness, drove out the ruddy kine, for he disclosed the three worlds.
Having shattered the western stronghold, Bṛhaspati cut through the three [fortresses] together from the ocean; he found the dawn, the sun, the cow, and the light, thundering like the sky.
Indra shattered Vala, the guardian of the milch-cows, with his roar as if with a hand;
seeking the milk-mixture with sweat-anointed fingers, he made the Paṇi weep and stole away the cows.
With his true, radiant companions who seek wealth, he has shattered the enclosure of the cows;
Brahmaṇaspati, with his bull-like boars sweating from the heat, has won the treasure.
With a truthful mind, seeking the cows, they impelled the Lord of Cattle with their prayers.
Bṛhaspati, by means of those who shun mutual reproach and who are self-yoked, released the ruddy cows.
Exalting him with auspicious hymns as he roars like a lion in the assembly,
may we rejoice after the victorious Bṛhaspati, the bull, in every battle for the sake of heroes.
When he won the prize of every form and ascended to heaven and the higher dwellings,
they— though being many and bearing light in their mouths— strengthened Bṛhaspati, the bull.
Make our prayer true, O bestowers of vital strength; for you protect even the humble singer with your own inherent ways.
Let all adversaries fall behind; hear this, O Heaven and Earth, you who pervade all things!
By his greatness, Indra split asunder the head of the great ocean, of Arbuda;
he slew the serpent and set the seven rivers flowing. O Heaven and Earth, together with the gods, protect us!
Like water-fowls guarding their young, like the thundering sounds of a rain-cloud,
like waves breaking from the mountains, the hymns have roared toward Bṛhaspati in joyful exultation.
Reaching toward the cattle, the descendant of Aṅgiras led Aryaman away like Bhaga;
like Mitra among the people, he anoints the husband and wife, as Bṛhaspati anoints the swift steeds for the prize in battle.
Bṛhaspati, having overcome the mountains, drove out the cows— those which are helpful, hospitable, vigorous, desirable, golden-hued, and of blameless form— just as one winnows grain from the chaff.
Sprinkling the womb of the Truth with honey, Bṛhaspati cast down the rock like a meteor from the sky; drawing forth the cows from the stone, he split the skin of the earth as if with water.
With light, Bṛhaspati drove away the darkness from the mid-air, as the wind drives away the water-weed from the water; having seized Vala, he brought forth the cows, as the wind scatters a cloud.
When Bṛhaspati shattered the strength of the reviling Vala with fires and glowing hymns,
he seized what was enclosed as if with teeth and tongues, and made manifest the hidden treasures of the kine.
Bṛhaspati indeed discovered that secret name of these lowing cows which was hidden in the cave; like a bird breaking open its egg, he himself brought forth the ruddy kine from the mountain.
They beheld the honey fastened with a stone, like a fish dwelling in shallow water;
Bṛhaspati, having split it apart with a roar, drew it forth like a cup from a tree.

He found the dawn, he found the sun, he found Agni; with his song of praise, Bṛhaspati drove away the darkness. He tore out the marrow of Vala, who was embodied as cattle, as one might extract the pith from a joint.
Like frost that steals the leaves from the forests, Vala, through Bṛhaspati, caused the cattle to be lost;
he performed an act beyond imitation and without return, since the sun and moon rise from each other.
Like a dark horse with white spots, the Fathers adorned the sky with constellations;
they placed darkness in the night and light in the day; Bṛhaspati split the mountain and found the cows.
We have offered this homage to the Cloud-god, who roars repeatedly after many [days].
May that Bṛhaspati bestow vigor upon us with cattle, with horses, with heroes, and with men.
Auspicious is the aspect of Agni Vadhryaśva; his guidance is lovely, and his approaches are delightful.
When the clans, as good friends, kindle him at the forefront, he, offered with clarified butter, awakes and flashes forth.
Clarified butter is the strengthener of Agni Vadhryaśva; clarified butter is his food, and clarified butter is his delight.
Offered with clarified butter, he has spread himself far and wide; like the sun, he shines, having clarified butter for his libation.
O Agni, that face of yours which Manu and Sumitra kindled—let this be renewed for us.
Shine forth with wealth; enjoy our songs; disclose strength for us; bestow glory upon us here.
O Agni, whom Vadhryaśva, being implored of old, kindled for you—be pleased with this [offering].
Be the protector of our dwellings and the guardian of our bodies; protect this gift of yours which is among us.
Be glorious, O son of Vadhryaśva, and our protector; let not the hostility of men overcome you.
Like a bold hero, a shaker of things, yet a good friend—now I shall proclaim the name of the son of Vadhryaśva.
You have won together the treasures of the plains and the mountains; you have conquered the Dāsa and Ārya Vṛtras.
Like a bold hero who overthrows the people, O Agni, may you overcome those who attack us in battle.
Long-threaded, large-oxen-drawn, this Agni is a thousand-fold stallion and a hundred-leader, skillful and radiant;
being polished by men among the radiant ones, he shines brightly among the pious who possess good friends.
In thee, O Jātavedas, is the cow easy to milk, yielding abundance like one that never fails, always providing nourishment.
Thou, O Agni, art kindled by men who possess sacrificial gifts, by the well-disposed Sumitras, and by those seeking the gods.
Even the immortal gods, O Jātavedas, proclaimed your greatness, O son of Vadhryaśva, when the human tribes came to consult you; you, with those strengthened by you, won through the men.
Like a father bearing his son upon his lap, Vadhryaśva served you, O Agni; taking pleasure in his fuel, O youngest one, you protected him even from those who were previously powerful.

Evermore Agni has conquered the enemies of Vadhryaśva with men who have pressed the Soma; O you of brilliant luster, you have burned up even the common assembly and struck down even the powerful one who increased his strength.

This Agni of Vadhryaśva is the slayer of Vṛtra, kindled from of old, to be invoked with homage. As such, O son of Vadhryaśva, trample down our enemies, whether they be strangers or kinsmen, even those who are arrogant.
O Agni, enjoy this fuel of mine; welcome with delight the ladle dripping with ghee at the place of *iḷā*.
Stand upright upon the height of the earth during the auspiciousness of the days, O wise one, for the sacrifice to the gods.
May Narāśaṃsa, the most divine among gods, come here by the foremost path of the gods with his horses of every form;
may he, the most godlike, prepare the sacrificial food for the gods upon the path of Truth with reverence.
Men, bringing oblations, perpetually invoke Agni for the office of messenger.
With most-swift horses and on a well-rolling chariot, bring the gods here; sit down as the Hotṛ priest.
May the divine, beloved sacrificial grass spread out transversely, long in its length, becoming fragrant for us.
O divine *barhis*, with a mind free from malice, sacrifice to the longing gods, with Indra as their chief.

Touching the ridge of heaven or expanding further by the measure of the earth, O yearning Doors, with your greatness, hold fast the divine chariot, you who desire the chariot, along with the great [gods].
May the two goddesses, Dawn and Night, the daughters of heaven, skillfully fashioned, sit down upon their place; may the longing gods sit in your wide, auspicious lap, O you who desire them.
Upright is the pressing-stone, kindled is the great Agni; the dear abodes are in the lap of Aditi.
O two priests, the two household-priests, most wise in this sacrifice, do you two win wealth for us through the offering.
O three goddesses, sit upon this wide sacrificial grass; we have made it pleasant for you.
Like Manu, may they enjoy the well-placed sacrifice and the oblations—the goddess Iḷā, whose path is ghee.
O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, whatever beauty you have brought forth, and since you have been the companion of the Aṅgirases,
do you, the knowing one, desiring it, sacrifice at the path of the gods as a giver of wealth, rich in jewels.
O Lord of the Forest, having bound [the victim] with a cord, bring it to the path of the gods as one who knows;
may the god prepare and sweeten the oblations; may Heaven and Earth favor my invocation.
O Agni, bring Varuṇa for our sacrifice; bring Indra from heaven and the Maruts from the mid-air.
Let all the worshipful ones sit upon the sacred grass; let the immortal gods rejoice in the Svāhā-call!

O Bṛhaspati, that which was the first beginning of speech, when they sent it forth assuming names— that which was their most excellent and stainless part, hidden in the secret cave, has now been made manifest through their longing.
Where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind, purifying it like groats through a sieve—there friends recognize their friendships; auspicious is the mark placed upon their speech.

By means of sacrifice, they followed the track of Speech; they found her entered among the seers. Having brought her forth, they distributed her in many places; the seven singers celebrate her together.
One man, though seeing, has not perceived Speech; another, though hearing, does not hear her.
But to yet another she has revealed her body, as a longing wife, well-adorned, reveals herself to her husband.
Moreover, they say that in friendship he drinks deeply; they do not urge him on even in contests for prizes.
He wanders with the power of a barren cow; having heard the voice, it is fruitless and flowerless.
He who has abandoned his companion, the finder of wealth—that man has no share even in sacred speech.
Whatever he hears, he hears in vain; for he does not know the path of righteous action.
Friends possessed of eyes and ears have become unequal in their mental speed;
some appear like ponds reaching to the mouth or the armpits, while others look as if they have already bathed.

When Brahmins, as friends, perform the sacrifice together with the impulses of the mind fashioned by the heart, it is then that they distinguish themselves through their specialized knowledge; yet the knowers of the sacred word move about in various ways within this very rite.
Those who move neither hither nor thither, who are neither true Brahmins nor pourers of the Soma—
having seized upon speech with evil intent, these ignorant ones weave a web like a spider.
All friends rejoice in the glory that has arrived, in their comrade who is victorious in the assembly.
For he is the remover of their sin, the winner of nourishment for them; he is well-prepared for the prize-winning contest.
One sits nourishing the abundance of the *ṛc*s; another sings the *gāyatra* upon the *śakvarī* verses;
one speaks as a *brahmán* the knowledge of all that has been born; and another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice.
Let us now proclaim with inspired praise the generations of the gods,
so that one may behold them in a future age while the hymns are being recited.
Brahmaṇaspati forged these together like a smith; in the earliest age of the gods, existence was born from non-existence.
In the first age of the gods, existence was born from non-existence;
from that, the quarters were born, and from that, the one who stands upon his feet.
Earth was born from Uttānapad; from Earth the quarters were born.
Dakṣa was born from Aditi, and from Dakṣa, Aditi was born.
For Aditi was born as she who is your daughter, O Dakṣa;
after her were born the auspicious gods, the kinsmen of immortality.
O gods, when you stood there in the waters, firmly grasped together,
a thick cloud of dust rose up from that place as if from dancers.
When you gods, like ascetics, caused the worlds to swell,
you brought forth from there the sun that was hidden within the ocean.
Of the eight sons of Aditi who were born from her own body, she approached the gods with seven; she cast Mārtāṇḍa away.
With seven sons, Aditi went forth toward the ancient age;
for the sake of progeny, she brought back Mārtāṇḍa from death.
You were born fierce for victorious power, delightful, most mighty, and full of great pride;
even the Maruts strengthened Indra on that occasion when his mother brought forth the hero as the most excellent giver of wealth.
Even the predatory *pṛśanī*, seated in malice, was overcome by your many praises; thus they strengthened Indra.
Like embryos enveloped [in darkness], they emerged from the deep gloom of the night through his great stride.
Lofty are your feet as you go forth to sacrifice; the strengths (vāja) that were here have increased you.
O Indra, you held a thousand hyenas in your mouth; may you turn the two Aśvins hither.
Swiftly you go to the sacrifice from every side; O Nāsatyas, bring us for friendship.
O Indra, you held the Vasāvyā; the Aśvins, O hero, bestowed thousands of gifts.
Rejoicing according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*) for the sake of progeny, O Indra, with your vigorous friends you came to our purpose.
For with these wondrous powers (*māyā*) you approached the Dasyu; you cast down the dark mists and the glooms.
Even those of equal name, the destroyers, Indra struck down for him as he did the Dawns;
with your lofty and longing friends you went forth, and you struck down their heart-felt foundations.
You slew Namuci, the one eager for combat, making the Dāsa devoid of magic power for the sake of the seer;
you made pleasant paths for Manu, leading toward the gods like well-trodden tracks.
You have filled these names; as the sovereign, O Indra, you hold them in your hand.
The gods rejoice in your power; you have turned the trees upward from their roots.
That wheel of his which is set within the waters—may he indeed find sweetness for that.
That udder which is fixed upon the earth, you placed its milk within the cows and the plants.

When they say, "He has come from the horse," I consider him to have been born of vital power (*ojas*). He has come from fury (*manyu*) and has taken his stand in the dwellings; from whence he was born, Indra alone knows.
Like birds with beautiful wings, the Priyamedha seers have approached Indra with their supplications. Dispel the darkness, fill our eyes with light, and release us as if we were bound in a snare.
Whether seeking to win over the Vasus through prayer or through sacrifices to Heaven and Earth;
or those who are swift and wealthy in the contest for booty; or those who, being renowned, have granted fame to the one who prays well—hears them well.
The Asura of these [Maruts] reached toward heaven with a mind seeking glory; he kissed the earth.
Where the gods behold [the world] for the sake of prosperity, they act like the sky with their own precious gifts.
This is the song for these immortals who, in their fullness, yearn for treasure;
may they, perfecting both our prayer and our sacrifice, bestow upon us complete wealth.
Those seekers of Indra praise that deed of yours, they who desire to burst open the cow-filled enclosure—
those who wish to milk the great, lofty, thousand-streamed earth, the mother of many sons, all at once.
O Śacīs, bring Indra to our aid— he who is unbending, who subdues those who attack us,
the lord of the Ṛbhus, the bounteous one worthy of fair hymns, who bears the manly thunderbolt and abounds in food.
Whatever he has accomplished most abundantly as the ancient victor, Indra has filled himself with the name "Vṛtra-slayer.
The powerful Lord of Might has become manifest; whatever we desire him to do, may he perform that.
O Waters, the poet shall proclaim your supreme greatness at the dwelling-place of Vivasvat.
Indeed, the seven-by-seven have moved forth in three ways; the Sindhu has surpassed the flowing rivers by her might.
Varuṇa carved out the paths for you to travel, O Sindhu, when you rushed toward the prizes.
From the high ground you flow along the slope and over the ridges, as you rule over the foremost of these moving creatures.
His roar extends to heaven above the earth; he raises up infinite vigor with his radiance.
Like rains thundering forth from a cloud, the Sindhu flows on, bellowing like a bull.
Toward you, O Sindhu, the roaring rivers flow like mothers toward their young, like milch-cows with their milk;
like a warrior-king, you lead the two banks as you strive for the forefront of these rushing torrents.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, and Paruṣṇī, accept this hymn of mine;
O Asiknī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Suṣomā, hear it well!
First, you joined with the Tṛṣṭāmā to flow forth, together with the Susartu, the Rasā, and that Śvetyā;
O Sindhu, you travel on the same chariot with the Kubhā, the Gomatī, the Krumu, and the Mehatnu, by which [rivers] you proceed.
Straight-moving, dappled, and bright, she traverses the expanses and the regions by her greatness;
the Sindhu, unassailable, the most active of the active, is like a wonderful mare, beautiful and fair to behold.
The Sindhu has good horses, fine chariots, and beautiful garments; she is golden, well-fashioned, and rich in prize-winning steeds.
The youthful maiden is woolly and adorned with silk; the fortunate one wears a garment that increases sweetness.
Sindhu has yoked her easy-moving chariot drawn by horses; with it, may she win the prize in this contest.
For the greatness of this one is celebrated—the greatness of the unassailable, self-glorious, and overflowing one.

I draw you hither at the dawning of strengths; O Maruts, anoint Indra and the two worlds—heaven and earth—so that both day and night may be our companions and, as breakers-through, grant us wide space in every dwelling.
Therefore, press that most excellent libation; like a horse held by the hand, the pressing-stone is for the presser.
For it provides the noble one with conquering manly power, so that he may overcome even great wealth through his swift steed.
For this very libation of his has opened the waters, as he established a path for Manu in ancient times;
in the sacrifice to the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, who possesses a flood of cattle and is adorned with horses, they have established the sacrifices within the rites.
Strike away the treacherous Rākṣasas; hold fast Destruction and ward off malice.
Press out for us wealth consisting of all-heroic sons, worthy of the gods; O stones, bring forth the song of praise!
I sing even for you who are more powerful than heaven itself, who are more swift-handed than Vibhvan,
who are more eager for the Soma than Vāyu, and who perform better fatherly deeds than Agni.
May our glorious pressing-stones resound with our heavenly, celestial speech as they press the soma-juice;
where the men milk the desirable honey, making a noise all around, striving against one another.
The chariot-borne stones press out the Soma; they milk its juice for those seeking cattle.
Men milk the udder for the purpose of pouring it out; like men preparing oblations, they cleanse [the vessels] with their mouths.
O stones, you have become men of skillful hands who press the Soma for Indra.
May every excellence of yours go to the divine realm, and every treasure of yours to the earthly one who presses the juice.
Like rain-drops from the clouds, sprinkle wealth with your voice; like those possessing oblations, may the sacrifices of the wise be distinguished.
Like a priest for the excellent Maruts, I have praised this host of theirs, that it may be worthy and beautiful.
For the sake of glory, the youths have prepared their ornaments, as if for the ancient host of the Maruts through many nights.
The sons of Dyaus have moved forward like goats; those Ādityas have grown strong like steeds.
They who by their own greatness have surpassed heaven and earth, like the sun emerging from the clouds;
like powerful heroes worthy of praise, they are like youthful men who destroy the foe and look toward the heavens.
At your base, as if on the course of the waters, the earth trembles and is loosened.
This all-nourishing sacrifice is directed toward you; come hither together like those who bring offerings.

Like horses yoked to the poles by their reins, you are radiant with light at the break of dawn; like hawks, you possess your own glory and destroy the enemies; like travelers on a journey, you are far-reaching and sprinkle [the earth] with moisture.
When you, O Maruts, come forth from afar, you who are aware of the great treasure within the vast enclosure— O Vasus, knowing that which is to be won, drive away our enemies even from a distance.

The mortal man who, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, stands firm in the rites and offers gifts to the Maruts—he shall possess wealthy vigor and noble heroes; may he remain under the protection of the gods.

For they are the ones worthy of sacrifice at the rites, the helpers, most beneficent by their name "Ādityas. May they protect our inspired thought, speeding on their chariot, and may they, longing for the great journey at the sacrifice, favor us.
