Like inspired poets with their hymns, they are well-disposed; like gods who delight in sacrifice, they are seekers of sleep.
Like kings, they are brilliant and fair to behold; like blameless youths among the people, they are stainless.
Like Agni in brilliance, they have golden ornaments upon their breasts; like the winds, they are self-yoked and swift in providing aid.
Like the eldest among those who know the way, they are excellent leaders; like Soma-drinks, they provide good protection for one who walks the path of Truth.
Like winds, they are shakers and swift-moving; like the tongues of fires, they are radiant.
Like armored warriors, they are powerful; like the praises of the fathers, they are bounteous givers.
Like the spokes of chariots sharing a common hub, like victorious heroes gazing toward heaven,
like wooing youths sprinkling clarified butter, they are singers who chant hymns with perfect praise.
Like horses that are the swiftest, like chariot-steeds eager for the prize and bounteous in their gifts;
like waters flowing with downward streams, the Viśvarūpas move forward with their chants like the Aṅgirases.
Like pressing-stones are the wise ones, sons of Sindhu; like mountains, they are ever-shattering. Like playful children with good mothers, they are like a great host on its march in their brilliance.
Like the rays of the dawns, they have adorned the sacrifice; like those seeking beauty, they have shone forth with their ointments.
Like flowing rivers, they have moved with glittering spears; like those from afar, they have measured out the leagues.
O Maruts, growing strong, make us fortunate and well-endowed with jewels, we who are your praisers;
take heed of our hymn and of our friendship, for from of old your gifts of treasure have existed.
I have beheld the greatness of this great one, the immortality within the mortal clans.
His jaws, diverse and wide-apart, come together; insatiable, devouring, they consume much.
His head is placed in secret; his eyes look away; insatiable, he devours the woods with his tongue.
For him, they bring offerings together with their feet, stretching out their hands in reverence among the people.
Seeking his mother’s secret place further away, he glided over the broad plants like a child;
he found him glowing and licking the raw flesh within the lap of the earth.
O Heaven and Earth, I proclaim that truth to you both: as he is born, the embryo devours his two parents.
I, a mortal, do not understand the god; Agni alone is wise, for he is truly perceptive.
He who provides us with food greedily, who offers oblations of clarified butter and ghee, and nourishes us—for him you look out with a thousand eyes; O Agni, you face every direction.
"What sin among the gods have you committed, O Agni? I ask you now, for I do not know.
Playing and not playing, the tawny one has carved himself up for eating, joint by joint, like a knife carving a cow."
The forest-born one has yoked his horses that move in all directions, held fast by straight-tightening reins.
Well-born Mitra, together with the Vasus, has distributed [the offerings]; increasing, he has been strengthened by his joints.
Agni bestows a steed that brings booty; Agni [bestows] a hero, renowned and steadfast in his task.
Agni moves between the two worlds, anointing them; Agni [bestows] a woman, a wise one who bears heroes in her womb.
May the fuel for Agni the Benefactor be auspicious; Agni has entered the two great worlds.
Agni impels the solitary warrior in battles; Agni shatters many Vṛtras.
Agni indeed protected that Karṇa as he grew old; Agni burned Jarūtha out from the waters.
Agni rescued Atri within the heated vessel; Agni united Nṛmedha with progeny.
Agni has bestowed wealth adorned with heroes; Agni [bestows] the seer who wins thousands.
Agni has extended the oblation to heaven; the domains of Agni are distributed in many places.
The seers invoke Agni with hymns; men, oppressed on their journey, call upon Agni.
Birds flying in the mid-air call upon Agni; Agni goes around thousands of cattle.
The human tribes that have sprung from Manu and Nahusha invoke Agni;
Agni [follows] the Gandharva path of Cosmic Order; Agni’s pasture is established in the clarified butter.
The Ṛbhus fashioned a sacred prayer for Agni; we have uttered a great hymn of praise to Agni.
O Agni, youngest one, protect the singer; O Agni, win for us great wealth through sacrifice.
The Rishi who sat down as the Hotar-priest, offering up all these worlds— our Father— he,
seeking wealth through his prayer and providing protection for the first time, entered into the later generations.
What was the foundation, what was the starting point, and how was it? From what did Viśvakarman, the all-seeing, producing the earth and by his greatness unfolding the sky?
With eyes on every side and a face on every side, with arms on every side and feet on every side,
the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and with his wings.
What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth? O wise ones, ask yourselves with your mind this: upon what did he stand while supporting the worlds?

O Viśvakarman, those which are your supreme abodes, those which are lowest, and these which are intermediate—teach them to your friends at the oblation, O self-dependent one; worship yourself, increasing in your own body.
O Viśvakarman, growing strong through the oblation, sacrifice yourself to the earth and the sky!
Let other people around us be bewildered; here, let the bountiful Lord be our patron.
Let us invoke today for our aid Viśvakarman, the Lord of Speech, who is swift as thought in the struggle for booty;
may he, the benefactor of all and the performer of good deeds, take pleasure in all our invocations and grant us protection.
The Father of the eye, wise in his mind, generated these two [worlds] dripping with clarity as they bowed down;
when their former boundaries were made firm, then indeed Heaven and Earth spread themselves out.
Viśvakarman, the wise, the far-reaching, the Ordainer, the Disposer, and the supreme Seer—
whose sacrifices they enjoy with nourishment where they say there is one beyond the seven seers.
He who is our father and progenitor, who is the ordainer and knows all abodes and all beings—he alone is the sole name-giver of the gods; to him all other worlds go for instruction.
The ancient seers, like singers in great number, offered worship to him for wealth— those who,
when the unformed and formed realms were established, brought these beings into existence.
Beyond heaven, beyond this earth, beyond the gods and the Asuras—
what was that first embryo which the waters received, wherein all the gods beheld one another?
The waters first received that embryo, wherein all the gods came together; it was placed upon the navel of the Unborn, in which all worlds abide.
You do not know him who generated these [worlds], for something else has come between you.
Enveloped in mist and prattle, the reciters of hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, he who honors you nourishes all power and strength in succession.
With you as our ally—made of force, powerful, and full of might—may we overcome both the Dāsa and the Ārya.
Manyu is Indra; Manyu indeed was the god; Manyu is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas.
The human tribes that exist offer praise to Manyu; O Manyu, protect us, being in harmony with our fervor.
Come hither, O Manyu, you who are stronger than the strong; with fervor as your ally, strike down our enemies.
You are the slayer of foes, the slayer of Vṛtra, and the slayer of Dasyus; bring all treasures to us.
For you, O Manyu, are of surpassing might, self-existent, brilliant, and the subduer of adversaries;
you belong to all people, victorious and powerful. Bestow strength upon us in the battles!
Being without a share, O wise one, I have departed from you through the power of you, the mighty;
therefore, O Manyu, I have provoked you in my lack of resolve—come to me in your own form to grant me strength.
I am here for you; come toward me, O Victorious One, all-sustaining, facing me.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn toward me; let us two slay the Dasyus, and be mindful of your kinship.
Come forward and be on my right; then we two shall strike down many Vṛtras together.
I offer you the sustaining first portion of the honeyed soma; let us both drink the first draughts in silence.
O Manyu, with you as our companion on the same chariot, may the bold Maruts, exulting and shattering [the foe],—
men with sharp arrows, whetting their weapons, and having the form of fire— advance against us.
Like Agni, O Manyu, blaze forth with splendor; as our invincible army-leader, be present when called upon, O Conqueror!
Having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth; measuring out your power, drive away the adversaries.
Overpower the adversary against us, O Manyu! Breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the enemies!
Your fierce array has indeed never been held back; as the sole-born, you who are self-controlled, lead them into your power.
You alone, O Manyu, are invoked as the one among the many; sharpen every tribe for battle.
With you as our ally, we, whose splendor is unimpaired, shall raise a brilliant shout for victory.
O Manyu, like Indra, the unconquered maker of victory, be our protector here.
O Conqueror, we celebrate your beloved name; we know that source from which you have arisen.

O Vajra, O Sāyaka, you who are born together with power, you bear supreme conquering might as a subduer. O Manyu, invoked by many, through your wisdom be our companion in joy; bring us together in the clash for great wealth.
May both kinds of gathered wealth, brought together, be granted to us by Varuṇa and Manyu;
may the enemies, conceiving fear in their hearts, lie low, utterly defeated.
By truth is the earth upheld; by the sun is the sky upheld.
By cosmic order (*ṛta*) the Ādityas stand firm; Soma is established in heaven.
By Soma the Ādityas are strong; by Soma the earth is great;
moreover, Soma is placed in the lap of these constellations.
One thinks he has drunk Soma when they grind the plant;
but no one at all eats that Soma which the Brahmins know.
O Soma, you stand protected by various coverings and guarded by those belonging to the Bṛhatī meter;
hearing the pressing-stones, you remain there, for no earthly being eats of you.
O God, when they drink you up, from that you swell again;
Vāyu is the guardian of the Soma, the month is the form of the seasons.
Raibhī was her attendant, Nārāśaṃsī her companion; with the Gāthā, Sūryā’s auspicious garment, well-adorned, was brought forward.
Thought was her pillow, sight was her ointment;
heaven and earth were the bridal chest when Sūryā went to her husband.
The hymns were the cross-pieces, the *kurīra* was the head-band, and the meter was the crest-ornament;
the Aśvins were the suitors for Sūryā, and Agni was the leader of the procession.
Soma became the suitor for the bride; both Aśvins were the two wooers, when Savitṛ gave Sūryā to her husband as she was consenting in her mind.
The mind was her wagon-pole, and the sky was her canopy;
the two bright ones were the draft-oxen when Sūryā went to her husband's home.
Your two oxen, yoked by the Ṛg and Sāman, are the two Sāmans here;
your two wheels were the sense of hearing, and your path was in the sky, moving to and fro.
Pure are your two wheels as you go; the vital breath (*vyāna*) is the axle, firmly fixed.
Sūryā, ascending her mind-made chariot, went forth to her husband.
The bridal procession of Sūryā has set forth, which Savitṛ sent away;
on the Aghā days the cattle are slaughtered, and she is carried around the two Arjunī stars.
When you two, O Aśvins, came as suitors on a three-wheeled vehicle for Sūryā’s wedding, all the gods approved of that deed; Pūṣan, the son, chose you as his parents.
When you two, O Lords of Splendor, went to Sūryā for her choice, where was one of your wheels, and where did you stand for the sake of the assigner?
O Sūryā, two of your wheels the Brahmans know according to the seasons;
but that one wheel which is hidden, only those who possess true insight know it.
To Sūryā, to the gods, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa—
to those who are wise regarding all that has come into being— I have paid this homage.
These two move one after the other by means of their creative power; like two playing children, they go around the sacrifice.
One surveys all beings, while the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again.
Ever new he becomes as he is born; the banner of the days, he goes at the forefront of the dawns.
Arriving, he distributes his portion to the gods; the moon extends long life.

O Sūryā, ascend the *śalmali* tree, adorned with beautiful *kiṃśuka* blossoms, possessing every form, golden-hued, well-rolling, and with excellent wheels; ascend to the world of immortality and prepare a pleasant bridal procession for your husband.
Arise from here, for she has a husband; I worship Viśvāvasu with reverence and songs.
Seek another woman who dwells among the fathers and is manifest; that is your portion by birth—be aware of it.
Rise up from here, Viśvāvasu; we bow before you with praise.
Seek another woman who is in heat; unite her as a wife with her husband.
May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go to choose a bride.
May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may the lordship of the household be easy for us to govern.
I release you from the noose of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the kindly one, bound you.
In the womb of Cosmic Order, in the world of good deeds, I establish you unharmed together with your husband.
From here I release her, not from there; I make her well-bound from there. So that she, O bounteous Indra, may become possessed of good sons and good fortune.
May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking you by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot.
Go to the house so that you may be the mistress of the home; as one who has power, may you speak at the assembly.

May what is dear to you be fulfilled here through offspring; in this house, be watchful for the duties of the household. Unite your body with this husband; thus, may you two speak at the assembly until old age.
She becomes blue and red; the attachment of the *kṛtyā* is revealed.
Her kinsmen prosper, while her husband is bound in fetters.
Give away the woolen garment; distribute wealth among the Brahmins.
This sorcery has become footed; it enters the husband as a wife.
The body becomes unlovely and pale with this evil [state],
when the husband seeks to cover his own limb with the garment of the bride.
The wasting diseases that follow the bride from her people to her bright bridal procession—
may the worshipful gods lead them back again to the place from which they came.
May the highwaymen who lie in wait not find the husband and wife;
may they pass over the difficult path by easy ways, and may their enemies flee away.
Auspicious is this bride; come together and behold her.
Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart now and go back to your homes.
This is harsh, this is bitter; like a bone, it is not for eating, like poison.
Only that Brahmin who knows Sūryā deserves the bride’s garment.
The carving, the cutting up, and furthermore the slicing—behold these forms of Sūryā; but the Brahman purifies them.

I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the state of a householder.
O Pūṣan, send forth that most auspicious woman upon whom men sow their seed;
she who, longing for us, spreads her thighs apart, and upon whom we, longing, may cast our member.
For you, O Agni, they first drove Sūryā around with her bridal procession;
give the wife back to her husbands along with offspring.
Agni has given back the wife with life and with splendor;
may he who is her husband live for a hundred autumns, possessing long life.
Soma first obtained you; Gandharva obtained you next;
Agni was your third husband; your fourth is born of man.
Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni;
and Agni has given me both wealth and sons, as well as this woman.
Stay right here; do not be parted. May you both enjoy the full span of life, playing with your sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home.
May Prajāpati produce offspring for us; may Aryaman anoint us for long life.
Without ill fortune, enter the world of your husband; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds.
With eyes that are not terrible, be one who does not strike her husband; be auspicious to the cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster.
A mother of heroes, loving the gods, and pleasant—be a source of blessing to our bipeds and a source of blessing to our quadrupeds.
O bounteous Indra, make this woman rich in sons and fortunate;
bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh.
Be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your mother-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your husband’s sister; be a sovereign queen among your brothers-in-law.
May all the gods unite our hearts; may the waters unite them;
may Mātariśvan, Dhātṛ, and the Goddess of Direction unite us both.
For they have poured out from the presser, yet they did not regard Indra as a god—at that time when Vṛṣākapi, my friend, took his delight among the riches of the noble man. Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, you run away past the distress of Vṛṣākapi;
indeed, you find nothing elsewhere for the drinking of Soma. O Indra, you are superior to all.

What has this Vṛṣākapi done to you, this tawny beast, that you are now jealous of him? Or rather, he is merely the wealth of an enemy consisting of nourishing riches. O Indra, you are superior to all!
O Indra, may the dog that seeks out boars now bite this Vṛṣākapi whom you, O Indra, protect as a dear friend—even in his ear; for Indra is superior to all.
The monkey has defiled my beloved, well-fashioned, and clearly visible [garments].
Now I shall cause his head to cry out; may I not be an easy path for the evildoer. Indra is superior to all.
No woman has been more beautiful than I, nor more skilled in dalliance; no one has surpassed me in agility, nor can raise her thighs higher. Indra is superior to all.
"O Mother, O easy-to-find one, tell me truly how it will be:
my thighs, O Mother, my hips, and my head seem to tingle all over. Indra is superior to everything.
O fair-armed one, O lovely-fingered, broad-chested, broad-hipped one! Why do you, as the wife of a hero, threaten Vṛṣākapi? Indra is superior to everyone.
This cruel man regards me as if I were childless;
yet I am the mother of heroes, the wife of Indra, and have the Maruts as my friends. O Indra, I am superior to all.

In former times, the woman went to the common sacrificial feast or the assembly; now, as the ordainer of the Eternal Law, the mother of heroes, the consort of Indra, she is glorified. Indra is supreme over all.
Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate;
for her husband shall never die of old age, nor even later; Indra is superior to all.
O Indrāṇī, I have no delight without my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose dear oblation of water goes to the gods; Indra is supreme over all.
O Vṛṣākapi’s wife, O wealthy lady, you who have good sons and a good daughter-in-law—Indra shall eat your bulls, your dear oblation that brings all things to fulfillment; Indra is supreme over all.
"For fifteen bulls they cook for me all at once, even twenty;
and I eat fatness indeed; they fill both my sides. Indra is superior to everyone."
Like a sharp-horned bull bellowing amidst the herds, O Indra, this churning-drink is a joy to your heart, which the devoted one presses for you; O Indra, you are superior to all.
He does not master [the act] whose member hangs limp between his thighs;
he indeed masters it whose hairy member expands as he sits. Indra is superior to all.
He does not master [the world] whose hairy member expands as he sits;
he indeed masters it whose member dangles between his thighs. Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, this Vṛṣākapi has found a slain wild beast; he has found a sword, a new slaughter-basket, and a cauldron piled high with fuel upon the hearth. O Indra, you are superior to all!
Here I go, looking out and discerning between the Dāsa and the Ārya; I drink of the one who presses the soma with skillful hands, and I have gazed upon the wise sage. O Indra, I am superior to all.
The desert and the place of slaughter—how many *yojanas* apart are they?
O Vṛṣākapi, go home to your nearest dwelling; Indra is supreme over all.
Come back again, Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange for our well-being.
You who go to your home by way of sleep, O Indra, you are superior to all.
When you two, O Vṛṣākapi and Indra, went upward to the house—where was that much-harming beast, and to whom did you go, O you who bring joy to men? Indra is superior to all.
Parśu by name, the daughter of Manu, gave birth at once to twenty sons.
"Blessed indeed was her fortune," they said, "whose womb pained with labor. Indra is superior to all.
I sprinkle the demon-slaying, vigorous one; I approach the Friend for the broadest protection. Sharpening himself with our rites, Agni is kindled; may he protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Jātavedas, kindled with your flame, touch the sorcerers with your iron fangs;
seize the fools who worship false gods with your tongue, and having torn apart the flesh-eaters, cast them into your mouth.
O you who know both, set down your two rows of teeth; as a predator, sharpening them, [sharpen] both the lower and the upper.
And, O King, roam throughout the mid-air; seize the sorcerers with your jaws.

O Agni, fashioning arrows with sacrifices, sharpening their points with speech and coating them with thunderbolts—pierce the sorcerers in the heart with these; break their arms as they turn toward you.
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the destructive thunderbolt strike him down with its heat.
O Jātavedas, crush his joints apart; let the flesh-eating, flesh-craving fire tear asunder his mangled body.
O Jātavedas, wherever you now see him standing, O Agni, or moving about,
or flying through the paths in the mid-air— pierce him with your arrow, whetting it like an archer.
And, O Jātavedas, snatch away what has been seized from the sorcerer who grasps it with his spears.
O Agni, blazing forth, strike him down first; let the spotted vultures devour that raw-eater.
Speak here, O Agni, which one it is—the sorcerer who does this;
seize him with your fuel, O youngest one, and deliver him over to the eye of the one who beholds men.
O Agni, with your sharp eye protect the sacrifice; O wise one, lead it forward toward the Vasus.
Do not let the sorcerers deceive you, O watcher of men, as you burn fiercely against the injurious demons.
O watcher of men, survey the *rakṣas* among the people; crush his three foremost parts.
O Agni, burn his ribs with your heat; tear up the root of the sorcerer in three ways.
Let the sorcerer go three times into your snare, O Agni, he who strikes the Truth with falsehood.
O Jātavedas, flashing with your flame, strike him down before the very eyes of the singer.
O Agni, bestow that vision upon the singer by which you may see the hoof-smiting sorcerer; like Atharvan, with divine light, burn down the truth-despising, mindless one who does harm.
O Agni, whatever curse a pair utters today, or whatever harsh speech the singers produce, and whatever arrow is born from the wrath of the mind— with that, pierce the sorcerers in their hearts.
Crush the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, crush the demon with your flame.
Crush the worshippers of false gods with your radiance, burning fiercely against those who feed on life-breath.
May the gods strike down the wicked man today; may harsh curses return upon him.
May arrows reach his vital organs for his deceitful speech; may the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone.
O Agni, the sorcerer who anoints himself with human flesh, who [anoints himself] with the flesh of a horse or a beast, and who steals the milk of the cow— shatter their heads with your fiery heat!
The milk of the cow that belongs to the year—let no sorcerer, O watcher of men, consume it!
O Agni, whichever one should seek to satisfy himself with the first-milked cream, pierce him in his vitals from behind with your flame.
O sorcerers, drink the poison of the cattle! May those of evil intent be cut down for Aditi. May the god Savitar deliver them over; may they be deprived of their share of the plants. May they perish.
From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers; the *rakṣas* have never conquered you in battles.
Burn down the flesh-eaters together with their roots; let them not escape from your divine weapon.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front.
May those unaging, most fierce flames of yours, glowing against the one who intends evil, consume him.
From behind, from the front, from below, and from above, O King, as a seer protect us with your seer-power.
O friend, lead your friend to old age; O Agni, you who are immortal, protect us mortals.
O Agni, O victorious one, we place you around us as a fortress— you, the inspired sage,
of bold appearance, who day by day slays those who act with treachery.
With poison, burn up the treacherous ones and the Rākṣasas,
O Agni, with your sharp flame and with spears tipped with fire!
O Agni, burn up the pairs of *yātudhānas* and *kimīdins*;
I sharpen you, the undeceived one, O inspired sage, with my prayers; remain ever watchful.
O Agni, with your flame, crush the flame [of the enemy] on every side;
shatter the strength and the heroic power of the *yātudhāna* and the *rakṣas*.
The oblation-drinking, undecaying [Agni], who finds the light, is offered into the sky-touching fire as a welcome guest.
For his support and for the sake of the world, the gods have spread themselves out according to their own nature and their law.
The world was swallowed and hidden by darkness; when Agni was born, the sun became manifest.
At his birth, the gods, the earth, the sky, the waters, and the plants took delight in his friendship.
Impelled now by the gods worthy of sacrifice, I shall praise Agni, the undecaying and vast,
who with his radiance has stretched out this earth and heaven, and the two worlds and the mid-air.
He who was the first Hotṛ, beloved by the gods, whom they chose and anointed with clarified butter—
he, Agni Jātavedas, made the winged birds, the moving things, and whatever is stationary, and he created the dog.

O Jātavedas Agni, since you have taken your stand upon the summit of the world together with the realm of light, we impel you with our thoughts, songs, and hymns; thus you became worthy of sacrifice, filling both worlds.
Agni becomes the head of the earth at night; from him the sun is born as it rises in the morning.
Indeed, he moves swiftly, knowing this wondrous power of those worthy of sacrifice, even as he goes toward the waters.
He who, kindled by his greatness, was visible and shone forth from the womb of heaven,
the radiant one— in that Agni, all the gods who protect our bodies offered oblations with the hymn of praise (*sūktavāka*).
First the gods generated the Sūktavāka and then Agni, and then the oblation; he became their sacrifice that protects the body. Him Heaven knows, him Earth knows, and him the Waters know.
The Agni whom the gods brought forth, in whom they offered all the worlds—
by his flame, straightening himself, he heated this earth and heaven with his greatness.
For by means of praise, the gods generated Agni in heaven with their powers, he who fills both worlds. They made him threefold for the sake of existence; he ripens the plants of every form.
When the worshipful gods placed this Sūrya, the son of Aditi, in heaven;
when the two wandering ones became a pair, then indeed they beheld all living beings.
For the sake of the entire world, the gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner of the days—
he who has spread out the shining dawns and who, as he moves, unveils the darkness with his flame like a garment.
The wise, worshipful gods generated Vaiśvānara Agni, the ageless one—
the ancient, unaging, moving star, the powerful and lofty overseer of the spirit.
We address with hymns Agni Vaiśvānara, the seer who shines forever;
he who by his greatness has encompassed the two wide worlds, the god both from below and from above.
I have heard of two paths of the fathers: that of the gods and that of mortals.
Along these two, all this moving world comes together—that which lies between the father and the mother.
The two united ones bear him as he moves, born from the head, fashioned by the mind;
facing all beings, he stands unwavering, crossing over, radiant.
Where the lower and the higher speak together, which of us two, the leaders of the sacrifice, knows?
The friends have been able to reach the common feast; they have attained the sacrifice—who will declare this?
How many fires are there? How many suns? How many dawns? And how many waters? O Fathers, I do not speak to you out of idle curiosity; I ask you, O seers, for the sake of knowledge.
As much as the face of the Dawn, O Mātariśvan, when the fair-winged ones clothe themselves,
so much does the Brāhmaṇa bestow upon the sacrifice as he sits down below the Hotṛ-priest.
I shall praise Indra, the most heroic, who by his greatness has forced apart the luminous realms and the ends of the earth;
he who, upholding the people with his heroes, has filled [the world] and surpassed the rivers in his majesty.
May that Indra turn the sun around the wide expanses like the wheels of a chariot;
he struck down the black darkness with his brilliance, like a flood of water that does not stay still.

Sing forth for him a common, never-failing prayer—new and peerless, reaching from the earth to heaven—for Indra, who, like one surveying the ridges of the mountains, has discerned all births; he, the noble one, seeks no other friend.
For Indra, I send forth songs like waters released in an unceasing flow from the depths of the ocean—
he who, by his powers, has propped apart the earth and heaven on all sides as if with the axle of a wheel.

Soma, whose wrath is stirred, who possesses impetuous onset, the shaker, the vigorous, the wielder of the spear, the drinker of the dregs—he has overcome all plants and forests; no counter-measures have deceived Indra from his side.
Neither heaven and earth, nor the desert, nor the mid-air, nor the mountains have contained Soma when he flowed forth;
when his wrath is aroused, it shatters the firm and breaks even the solid things.
He struck down Vṛtra as an axe fells trees; he shattered the fortresses and dug out the rivers. He split the mountain like a new jar; Indra brought forth the cows with his own companions.

O Indra, wise one, you indeed cut through those crooked things like an axe through the joints of wood— you who destroy those men who violate the law of Mitra and Varuṇa, as if they were betraying a friend.
Those of evil intent who violate Mitra, Aryaman, the *saṃgir* (oaths), and Varuṇa— O bull Indra,
sharpen against those enemies your fierce, virile, and ruddy weapon of death.
Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth; Indra is lord of the waters, and Indra indeed of the mountains.
Indra is the lord of the prosperous, and Indra of the wise; Indra is to be invoked in times of peace and in times of exertion.
Indra has surpassed you, O Vṛtra, from the days that have passed, from the mid-air, and from the depth of the ocean;
he has surpassed the expanse of the wind, the ends of the earth, the rivers, and all inhabited lands.
Like the banner of the glowing dawn, let your insatiable weapon roll forth, O Indra.
Piercing like a stone released from heaven, strike down the deceitful enemies with your most scorching heat.
The months followed him, as did the forests, the plants, and the mountains;
both heaven and earth, yearning, followed Indra, and the waters followed him as he was being born.
When indeed, O Indra, will that manifestation of yours be known, when you shatter the demon who seeks [us],
so that those who betray their friends may lie scattered upon the earth like cattle at the slaughter?

O Indra, those who have extended themselves against us as enemies, swelling with great pride in their bands—let those foes be overtaken by blinding darkness; may the nights be filled with light for us, while they are shrouded in gloom.
For many indeed are the libations of men that have gladdened you, the prayers of the chanting seers.
Hearing this joint invocation with favor, come hitherward, passing beyond all who sing your praise.
O Indra, may we thus find your new and refreshing favors;
may we, the Viśvāmitras, now sing your praises and find your protection through the light of day.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty;
the fierce one who listens, for our protection in the conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras and is the conqueror of riches.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended it by the measure of ten fingers.
The Person alone is all this— whatever has been and whatever is to be—
and he is the lord of immortality, as well as of that which grows by means of food.
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this. All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
With three quarters the Puruṣa rose upward; one quarter of him was here again. From there he strode out in all directions toward that which eats and that which does not eat.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj, Puruṣa was born. Once born, he extended beyond the earth, both behind and before.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation,
spring was its clarified butter, summer the fuel, and autumn the offering.
They sprinkled that sacrifice, the Puruṣa born in the beginning, upon the sacred grass;
with him the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis performed the sacrifice.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) was gathered;
he made those into animals—those belonging to Vāyu, as well as those of the forest and those of the village.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born;
from it the meters were born, and from it the Yajus-formulas were produced.
From him were born the horses, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth;
from him indeed were born the cows, and from him were born goats and sheep.
When they divided Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what were his two arms, what were his thighs, and what are his feet called?
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his feet the Śūdra was born.
The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born;
from his mouth Indra and Agni were born; from his breath Vāyu was born.
From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved;
from his feet the earth, and from his hearing the quarters—thus they fashioned the worlds.
Seven were its enclosing sticks, and thrice seven were the fuel-sticks made,
when the gods, performing the sacrifice, bound Puruṣa as the victim.
With sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the firmament, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
He, the domestic lord, being awakened by those who keep watch, is kindled in the house at the place of *iḷā*, providing nourishment.
He is the desirable invoker of every oblation, all-pervading, radiant, and a good friend to him who seeks his friendship.
He of beautiful splendor, the guest in every house, has taken refuge in forest after forest like a swift hero.
Belonging to all people, he does not disdain any person; as one of the people, he dwells among every clan.
O Agni, you are most skillful with skill, most wise with wisdom; you are a seer, omniscient through your prophetic power.
As the Vasu among riches, you alone rule over all those treasures which Heaven and Earth nourish.

Knowing it well, O Agni, you have sat down upon your seasonal birthplace, rich in ghee, at the station of Iḷā. Your movements have become visible like those of the dawns; they are stainless like the rays of the sun.
Your splendors, like the lightning of the rain-cloud, have shone forth in various ways like the banners of the dawns—
when, released upon the plants and the forests, you yourself gather food into your mouth.

The plants received him as their timely embryo; the waters, the mothers, brought forth that Agni. Both the forest trees and the creeping plants, being pregnant, give birth to him alike and perpetually.
Fanned by the wind and impelled according to thy will, when thou spreadest abroad swiftly devouring the food,
thy undecaying hosts, O Agni, strive to burn it apart like chariot-horses.

Agni, the maker of wisdom, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, the invoker, the most pervasive thought—him indeed they choose as the one common to all for even a small oblation, and him alone for a great one; none other than you.
O Agni, here the wise ones, desiring you, choose you as the Hotṛ-priest at the assemblies,
when the god-seeking men, bringing oblations and having spread the sacrificial grass, present the offerings to you.
O Agni, yours is the office of the Hotṛ; yours is the seasonal office of the Potṛ; yours is the office of the Neṣṭṛ; you are the Agnīdh for the one who follows the Truth.
Yours is the office of the Praśāstṛ; you act as the Adhvaryu; you are both the Brahman and the master of the household in our home.

O Agni, for that mortal who offers to you, the immortal, with fuel or with the preparation of an oblation—you become his Hotar-priest; you go on your mission as messenger; you speak for him, you sacrifice, and you act as the Adhvaryu.
These thoughts, these words from us, these *ṛc*s, songs, and well-spoken hymns have come together for him—
seeking wealth for the wealthy Jātavedas, in which he, the increaser, finds delight even among those that have already grown great.
May I utter this newest hymn of praise for him, the ancient one who desires it; may he hear us.
May it dwell within his heart to touch it, like a longing, well-adorned wife for her husband.
In whom horses, bulls, oxen, barren cows, and rams are released and offered as oblations—
to that Agni, the drinker of sweet nectar, whose back is sprinkled with Soma, the ordainer— I generate a beautiful hymn from my heart.
The oblation has been poured into your mouth, O Agni, like ghee into the ladle, like Soma into the cups.
Bestow upon us wealth that wins booty, rich in heroes, highly praised, glorious, and vast.
I praise for you the charioteer of the sacrifice, the lord of the clans, the invoker, the guest of the night, the radiant one— blazing among the dry plants,
flickering among the green ones, the bull, the banner, the holy one who has reached the sky.
Both [gods and men] have made this Agni their clear-sighted upholder of the law, the accomplisher of the sacrifice;
like the young ray of light before the dawns, they kiss the son of Tanū, the red-hued one, who is placed in front.
We consider his paths to be strong, and those of the Paṇi; his branches were offered up for him to eat. When the terrible ones attained immortality, they then celebrated the divine race of men.
For the extension of *ṛta* is the sky, wide and spacious; homage to the great Aramati, the most praiseworthy.
Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa have come together in harmony, as well as Bhaga and Savitṛ of purified will.
The rivers flow forth with the rushing Rudra; they have sped across the great Aramati.
With them, the all-encompassing one, moving around his wide expanse, roars aloud and sprinkles everything within his belly.
The active Rudras, the Maruts who belong to all people, the falcons of heaven dwelling in the home of the Asura—
with them, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra, swift-moving with the swift-moving gods, look upon [the world].
Those who strive have attained enjoyment in Indra, in the sight of the Sun, and in the manly power of the Bull—
those singers who, at his assemblies, fashioned for him the companion Vajra according to his due honor.
Even the sun’s bay horses he has caused to halt; everyone fears Indra, the mightiest one. From the belly of the terrifying bull comes his roar, resounding day after day, unconquered and victorious.
Today, with reverence, offer a hymn of praise to your skillful Rudra, the lord of heroes;
he who, accompanied by his auspicious, self-moving, and eager steeds that travel swiftly from heaven, follows his own will and possesses his own glory.
For they have spread their fame among their offspring: Bṛhaspati the bull, and those born of Soma;
Atharvan first established [the rites] through sacrifices, and the Bhṛgus became renowned through their skillful deeds.
For they— Heaven and Earth of abundant seed, Narāśaṃsa, the four-limbed Yama,
Aditi, the divine Tvaṣṭṛ, Draviṇodas, the R̥bhukṣans, Rodasī, the Maruts, and Viṣṇu— are worthy of honor.
And may that sage Ahi Budhnya hear our call from afar at this invocation, he who belongs to the yearning ones.
O Sun and Moon, moving apart and dwelling in heaven, through your wisdom, O Śamī and Nahuṣī, take heed of him!
May Pūṣan, who belongs to all the gods, protect our journey; may the Son of the Waters and Vāyu aid us for our sacrifice.
Sing forth to Vāta, the breath of all, for greater prosperity! O Aśvins, you who are easily invoked, hear this on your path!
With songs we praise him who dwells over these fearless tribes, the self-glorious one;
with all the divine dames (gnās) we praise Aditi, the unassailable, and the youthful lord of the night, whose mind is set on manly deeds.

There Aṅgiras, the first by birth, sang forth; the pressing-stones, raised aloft, looked toward the sacrifice—those stones by which the far-reaching one became all-seeing, while the well-fashioned axe moved among the trees.
O Heaven and Earth, you have become great and wide; like two young women, the two worlds are our constant seat.
With these [powers], protect us in victory; with these, protect us in our strength.
At every sacrifice, that mortal honors the gods who, being most renowned for their fame, seeks to win them over with his prayers for favor.
O you who rule over all, the great treasure of the gods—
for all are of universal greatness, and all are worthy of sacrifice at the rituals.
These indeed are the joyful kings of immortality: Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Parijman;
and which of them is Rudra praised by men, the Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga?
And may Sūrya and Māsa, the rain-givers of the waters, who share a common dwelling, come to our seat by night,
when the Dragon of the Deep settles together with them upon their foundations.
And may the two gods, the Aśvins, lords of splendor, and Mitra and Varuṇa protect us with their powers.
He strives for great wealth and crosses over difficulties as if over a desert.
And may even the Rudras be gracious to us, the Aśvins, all the gods, Rathaspati, and Bhaga;
may Ṛbhu, Vāja, and the Ṛbhukṣans, the all-knowing ones who travel everywhere, [be gracious].

R̥bhu art thou, O R̥bhukṣan; R̥bhu art thou, the exhilaration of the worshipper. May thy two bay steeds, swift and vigorous, hasten hither—thou whose Sāman is difficult to overcome, like a human sacrifice performed with perfect success.
O God Savitṛ, make us free from shame; may he be praised among the wealthy patrons.
Like Indra with his steeds, he has drawn in the wheel and the reins of these people.
O Heaven and Earth, bestow upon these men, and upon us, great fame that extends over all people;
grant us nourishment for the winning of booty, and nourishment for the conquest of wealth.
O Indra, you who seek us, protect this singer for our aid, wherever he may be, O powerful one;
ever protect him for our aid. Let him be strengthened in his knowledge, O Vasu.
This hymn of mine, with its radiant course like the sun, has been strengthened for men; like a craftsman fashioning a horse-harness that does not fall apart, it is a means of unification.
They whose wealth has turned back toward them, whose golden [chariot] is yoked— like those who have won in the contest for manly deeds, they have reached their goal as if in sport.
I have proclaimed this before Duḥśīma, Pṛthavāna, Vena, Rāma, and the Asura Maghavans— those who,
having yoked five hundred [horses], made their path resound for me.
Indeed, here he has bestowed seventy-seven [cows] upon Adhi;
Tānva bestowed them at once, Pārthya bestowed them at once, and Māyava bestowed them at once.
Let these speak forth, let us also speak forth; utter the speech for the speaking pressing-stones!
O mountain-stones, swift ones, when you together bring the sound and the shout to Indra as you bear the Soma.
These speak out with hundreds and thousands; they roar aloud with their tawny voices.
Having performed their work well through their skillful action, the pressing-stones, even before the Hotṛ, have attained the right to eat the oblation.
These speak, having found the honey; they low repeatedly over the cooked meat. As they devour the branch of the ruddy tree, those well-fed bulls have bellowed forth.
They cry out loudly with the exhilarating, intoxicating draught; calling upon Indra, they have found the honeyed food.
Seizing hold together, the wise ones have danced with their sisters, making the earth resound with their rhythmic stamping.

The fair-winged ones have uttered their voice toward the sky; in the cave, the dark, impetuous ones have danced. They go downward to the appointed place of the lower region; bright as the sun, they have deposited abundant seed.

Like fierce [steeds] galloping forward, the bulls, harnessed together, have joined in bearing the yoke-poles; when they neighed, panting and swallowing [the fodder], one hears their snorting like that of racing horses.
Sing praise to those who have ten for their feet, ten girths, ten yokes, and ten harnesses; to those who have ten reins and are never-wearying, who carry ten poles and ten yoked teams.
Those stones, with their ten-fold mechanism, are swift; their desirable setting moves around. They have partaken of the first nectar of the stalk, the essence of the pressed Soma plant.
Those Soma-drinkers kiss the two bay horses of Indra; milking the stalk, they sit upon the cow.
Having drunk the Soma-mead milked by them, Indra grows strong, expands, and acts like a bull.
O bulls, your stalk has never failed you; you are always full of refreshment and well-fed.
Like great wealth, you are beautiful in your majesty, O stones, you who have delighted in his sacrifice.
The stones are piercing yet not pierced; they are untiring, unloosened, and free from death.
They are undiseased, ageless, steadfast, and powerful; they are well-fattened, without thirst, and free from craving.
O Fathers, firm indeed are you from age to age; desiring security, they do not leave their seat.
Undecaying, accompanied by the golden ones, with golden steeds, they have made themselves heard by their roar across the heavens and the earth.
At their release, the pressing-stones speak thus on their journey, as if with clear-sounding footsteps; like grain-gatherers sowing seed, they mix the Soma and do not diminish it as they devour it.

When the sacrifice was pressed, they raised their voices like playful children nudging their mother; release well the inspired thought of the one who has performed the pressing, and let the pressing-stones roll forth as they are being honored.
"Come, wife! Stay with me in spirit, O fierce one; let us now exchange words together.
These unspoken mantras of ours shall not bring us joy even on a later day."
"What shall I do with these words of yours? I have already set forth like the first of the dawns.
Purūravas, go back to your home; I am as difficult to capture as the wind."

Like an arrow from a quiver for the sake of glory, like a swift rush winning cattle and gaining hundreds; flashing forth when the will is not toward heroes, the roarers have made the lowing sound known, like kine.
Bestowing wealth upon her father-in-law and providing him with vigor, O Dawn, she departed from the nearby house when he desired her;
she reached his home, in which she took delight, piercing him day and night with her reed-like shaft.
Three times a day you struck me, O Vetasena, yet you continued to satisfy my longing.
Purūravas, I came according to your will; O hero, you were then the king of my body.
She who is well-purified, a row [of beauty], a friend of bliss, like an eye in the heart, moving and binding the knot;
those ointments have flowed like ruddy [dawns]; for the sake of glory, they have lowed like milch-cows.
When he was being born, the divine dames sat around him, and the self-praising rivers nourished him;
for when the gods, O Purūravas, strengthened you for the great battle, for the slaying of the Dasyus.
When I, a mortal, dwelt among these non-human women who cast off their garments, they rushed toward me like a trembling woman;
they were terrified, like horses that have touched a chariot.

When a mortal, seeking contact, unites with these immortal ones as if with the worlds through his sacred rites, they adorn their own bodies like birds; they are like playful horses, biting and snapping.
Like a falling flash of lightning she has flashed forth, bringing me desirable waters from the depths.
A manly son, well-born, has been begotten of the waters; may Urvaśī prolong her long life.

You were born indeed for the protection of the cow; you bestowed that strength upon me, O Purūravas. Knowing this, I instructed you on that very day, yet you did not listen to me; what do you say now, you who have failed?
When will the son, once born, seek his father; when, understanding, shall he shed tears like a turning wheel?
Who shall separate the husband and wife who are of one mind, while the fire shines among the parents-in-law?

I shall answer him who turns back his tears; let him not cry out like one distressed in his longing for welfare. I will send forth that which is yours among us; go home, O fool, for you have not attained [your goal].
May the good god fly away today, never to return, to go to the furthest distance.
Then let him lie in the lap of Destruction, and there let the impetuous wolves devour him.
O Purūravas, do not die; do not fall away; let not the malevolent wolves devour you.
There are no friendships with women; these are but the hearts of hyenas.
When, O Virūpā, I lived among mortals for four autumns through the nights, I ate a single drop of clarified butter once a day; even now, I move about satisfied by that very same thing.
Filling the intermediate space, the measurer of the region, I, Vasiṣṭha, entreat Urvaśī.
May the gift of my good deed attend you; turn back, for my heart is burning with grief.
Thus these gods say to you, O son of Iḍā: "Since you have thus become a kinsman of death, let your offspring worship the gods with oblations; and you yourself shall rejoice in heaven."

I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I prize your desirable exhilaration, you who, like beautiful clarified butter, pour it forth with your bay steeds. May my songs enter into you, whose form is golden-bay.
For those who have sung together toward the golden source, urging on the two bay steeds as if to the celestial seat;
for him whom they satisfy with bay steeds like milch-cows—sing a strengthening hymn to Indra, the lord of the bays.
That golden, iron thunderbolt of his is golden; golden is his desire, and golden it is in his two hands.
Splendid, with beautiful jaws, with golden wrath as his arrow—golden forms have been infused into Indra.
Like a beloved banner set upon the sky, the golden-hued thunderbolt has manifested itself with speed.
He of the golden crest struck the serpent; he who is of iron became one of a thousand flames, the bearer of the golden [lightning].
O Indra, golden-haired one, you have been delighted again and again by the ancient sacrificers who offered praise;
you take pleasure [in the sacrifice], and yours is all that is worthy of hymns—the perfect, desirable bounty born of the golden ones.
The two beloved bay steeds carry Indra—the wielder of the thunderbolt, the exhilarating one worthy of praise—to the intoxication in his chariot.
For him, for Indra, many libations are pleasing; the golden Soma drops have flowed forth.
The bay steeds have flowed readily for the desire of the steadfast one; the bay steeds have urged on the two swift bay horses.
He who goes according to his pleasure with his bay coursers—he has attained his desire for the bay steeds.
Tawny-bearded, tawny-haired, made of iron, he who grew strong at the swift draught as the drinker of the tawny juice;
he who, rich in prize-winning steeds, with his tawny coursers shall carry us across all difficulties.
Whose two golden jaws fly apart like two sacrificial ladles as he shakes them for the sake of strength;
when, having drunk of the exhilarating, desirable food, he cleansed his two bay steeds over the prepared chalice.
And indeed, the seat of the beloved one between the two worlds has roared like a prize-seeking steed;
for the great Dhiṣaṇā has been won by his might, and he, the beloved, has established lofty vital power within her.
Desiring the two worlds with your greatness, you take pleasure in every newest hymn that is dear to you.
O Asura, make the beloved dwelling of the cow manifest for the golden Sun.
O Indra, let the draft-horses of men carry you, the one who desires [the sacrifice], the one with bay horses, upon your chariot.
Drink of the offered mead as you please, delighting in the ten-fingered sacrifice at the communal feast.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, you have drunk the pressed juices of the ancestors; now this libation is yours alone.
Rejoice in the honeyed Soma, O Indra; O Bull, pour it all at once into your belly.
The herbs that were born first, three ages before the gods— of those brown ones, I now take heed of their hundred and seven powers.
A hundred, O mothers, are your abodes, and a thousand are your growths;
therefore, you who possess a hundred powers, make this man of mine free from disease.
Rejoice in response, O plants, you who bear flowers and produce fruit;
like victorious mares, may these healing herbs carry us across to safety.
"O Plants, you mothers; as such, O goddesses, I address you:
may I win back the horse, the cow, the garment, and your very self, O man!"
On the Aśvattha tree is your seat; on the Parna tree your dwelling has been prepared. You shall indeed be sharers of cattle, if you win back the man.
Where the plants have gathered together like kings in an assembly— that inspired sage is called a physician, the slayer of demons and the driver away of disease.
I have gathered all the plants— those rich in horses, rich in Soma, strengthening, and full of vigor—
for this man's safety.
The vital breaths of the plants rush forth like cattle from the cow-pen, O man, as they seek to win wealth for you.
Healing is your mother by name, and you yourselves are the healers; you are winged furrows, for whatever is diseased, you heal it away.
They have passed beyond all obstacles as a thief passes through a pen; the plants have shaken off whatever blemish was upon their bodies.
When I, seeking strength, take these plants in my hand,
the self of the wasting disease perishes, as if before the seizer of life.
O plants, you who creep limb by limb and joint by joint— drive the consumption away from there, like a fierce man who sits in the midst [of his enemies].
Fly away, O consumption, together with the blue jay, the woodpecker;
vanish together with the rush of the wind, together with the whirlwind.
May one among you protect another; may each of you assist the other.
All of you, being in full accord, further this speech of mine.
Those plants that bear fruit and those that are fruitless, those that are flowerless and those that are flowering—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from distress.
May they release me from the curse of the oath, and also from that of Varuṇa;
and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every sin against the gods.
As they descended from heaven, the plants spoke:
"The living man whom we shall reach, that person shall not come to harm."
Of those herbs whose king is Soma, many and hundred-eyed, you are the best; bring healing for my desire and peace to my heart.
The plants whose king is Soma, which are spread across the earth—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, bestow your power upon this woman.
May the one who digs you up not be harmed, nor he for whom I dig you;
may all our bipeds and quadrupeds be free from disease.
Those plants which hear this and those which have gone far away— let all the creepers come together and bestow their power upon her.
The plants hold a consultation together with Soma, their king:
"O King, we shall carry across that man for whom the Brahmin performs [this rite]."
O herb, you are the highest; the trees are your subordinates. May he who assails us be our subordinate.
O Bṛhaspati, come toward my divinity, whether you are Mitra, Varuṇa, or Pūṣan;
or if you are with the Ādityas, the Vasus, or accompanied by the Maruts—send down Parjanya for Śantanu, O Bull.
The divine messenger, swift and wise, Devāpi, has come to me from you. Turn toward me; I place this radiant speech within your mouth.
Bestow upon us, O Bṛhaspati, speech that is radiant from the mouth, free from disease, and vigorous—that by which we two may win rain for Śantanu; the honeyed drop from heaven has entered [us].
May our honeyed drops enter [thee]; O Indra, bestow upon us a thousand chariots.
Sit down to the office of the Hotṛ; sacrifice at the proper time; O Devāpi, honor the gods with the oblation.
The seer Devāpi, son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, sitting down to the office of the Hotṛ-priest and being skilled in the favor of the gods,
released from the upper ocean the celestial waters of rain toward the lower ocean.
In this upper ocean, the waters stood encompassed by the gods;
they flowed forth, released by the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, sent by Devāpi among the Mṛkṣiṇīs.
When Devāpi, the domestic priest for Śantanu, was chosen for the office of *hotṛ* and meditated with compassion,
Bṛhaspati, bestowing it, granted him speech that is heard by the gods and wins the rain.
O Agni, whom Devāpi, the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, the mortal man, kindled while glowing with fervor—
being celebrated by all the gods, impel Parjanya, the bringer of rain.
The ancient seers approached you with their songs; all [the gods] approached you at the sacrifices, O much-invoked one.
Bring to us thousands of chariots; come to our sacrifice, O you whose horses are ruddy.
O Agni, these ninety-nine thousand offerings have been bestowed upon you;
with them, O Hero, increase your many bodies. Impelled by us, grant us rain from heaven.
O Agni, deliver these ninety thousand as a portion to the bull Indra;
knowing the paths that lead to the gods according to the seasons, place Aulāna also among the gods in heaven.
O Agni, drive away the adversaries; drive away the difficulties, the disease, and the demons.
From this vast ocean of heaven, release for us here an abundance of waters.
Whom among us do you, the wise one, impel—the wide-striding, bellowing [bull]—to grow strong?
What gift shall he give at the breaking forth of his power? He fashioned the Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt and caused it to swell.
For he, with his flashing lightning, seeks the *sāman*; through his lordship (*asuratva*), he has settled in the wide womb.
Overpowering with those who share his dwelling, he [subdues] the magic powers of his brother, not without the seventh.
He, seeking booty, went on foot where it was difficult to tread, intending to win the light;
he sat around the hundredfold wealth of the one with the evil heart, unassailable, striking down the phallus-worshippers by his wondrous form.
He, the youthful steed, hastens through the streams for the sake of cattle, rushing toward the prizes of war;
where the footless ones, joined together though without chariots, with horses born of wooden troughs, speed forth like clarified butter and water.
He, the skillful one whose boons cannot be obstructed by the Rudras, having left his home behind, came here free from blame.
I think he has come to expose the pair of Vamra, seeking food and making them weep as he plunders them.
He, the lord of the house, subdued the Dāsa Tuvīrava, the six-eyed and three-headed;
indeed, Trita, strengthened by his power, struck the boar with a spear-pointed of iron.
Standing erect against the treacherous man, he has hurled his arrow at the one who attacks;
he, the most heroic among men, well-born for us, shattered the fortresses as the worthy slayer of Dasyus.
Like a cloud raining upon the pasture, may he find for us a path to our dwelling;
when the falcon, with iron claws, settles upon the soma-drop, he slays the Dasyus with his limbs.
With his powerful and mighty deeds, he delivered the arrogant Śuṣṇa to Kutsa for his wretched destruction. He guided the praised sage Atka, who won for him both [booty] and heroes.
Bestowing gifts with his manly deeds, this wondrous one is like Varuṇa, the possessor of magic power;
this youthful guardian of the seasons has been recognized—he who measured out Araru, the four-footed beast.
Through his hymns of praise, Auśija Ṛjiśvan burst open the cow-stall of Pipru with his bull-like power;
when the worshipper had pressed the Soma, the song shone forth, and he, advancing toward the fortresses, overcame them with his wondrous form.
Thus, O great Asura, for the sake of your growth, Vamraka crept toward Indra on his feet;
approaching him, may he grant us well-being—he has bestowed upon us food, strength, a secure dwelling, and everything.
O Indra, be steadfast; O Maghavan, one such as you is indeed our enjoyment here. Praised and drinking the pressed soma, be for our prosperity.
May Savitṛ together with the gods protect us; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
Bring forth well the seasonal portion for the sake of bearing; offer it to Vāyu, the pure one, who roars at the sacrifice.
He who has attained the drinking of the bull’s milk—we choose Aditi for our complete well-being.
May the divine Savitṛ impel strength toward us—toward the upright sacrificer who presses the soma—so that we may honor the gods with simple devotion. We choose Aditi for our complete well-being.
May Indra be well-disposed toward us at all times; may King Soma look upon our prosperity.
Just as they have established the bonds of friendship, we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
O Indra, by means of the hymn and through his power, he has joined the joint; O Bṛhaspati, you are the one who prolongs our life.
The sacrifice is Manu, for he is our father and our providence; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
Now, Indra’s divine power is well-performed; Agni, the wise seer and singer, is in the house.
May the sacrifice be dear and most intimate in the assembly. We choose Aditi for complete well-being.

We have not committed many evil deeds against you in secret, nor, O Vasus, have we openly provoked the gods. O gods, let none of us be clothed in falsehood; we choose Aditi for our complete well-being.
May Savitar drive away disease; may the mountains push it far down.
Where the pressing-stone, the honey-squeezer, is raised loudly, we choose Aditi for universal well-being.
May the pressing-stone stand upright for the presser, O Vasus; drive all enmities far away.
May that god Savitṛ be our praiseworthy protector; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
O cows, eat nourishment and fatness upon the pasture, you who are anointed at the seat of Order in the reservoir.
Let body be the medicine for body; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
The singer who fulfills the rite is the protector of all; Indra indeed is the auspicious providence for those who press the soma.
He whose milk-stream fills the heavenly udder—for his sake we choose Aditi and complete well-being.
Wondrous is your radiance; your aid fulfills our intentions. There are rivals who are unassailable and reach old age.
With the straightest line, the one seeking your favor strives to win the foremost prize of cattle.
Awake, O friends, with one mind; kindle Agni together, you many who dwell in the same nest.
I invoke for your protection Dadhikrā, Agni, and the goddess Uṣas, along with Indra.
Make it pleasant; extend your prayers; fashion a ship that can be steered with oars.
Prepare the weapons; make them ready. O friends, lead the sacrifice forward toward the east.
Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the yokes; sow the seed here in the prepared womb.
May our song and our prompt obedience bring us abundant harvest; may the sickle come closer to the ripened grain.
The seers yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately, the wise ones, seeking favor among the gods.
Prepare the buckets; set the straps in place. Let us pour from the water-skin that is full of water, well-dispensing and inexhaustible.
I pour out the water-bearing, inexhaustible well, which has a well-fashioned mouth, excellent buckets, and is easy to draw from.
Satisfy the horses; may you be victorious for our welfare. Prepare the chariot that brings well-being.
Pour forth the drink for the heroes from the well with wooden buckets, stone wheels, and leather arm-cases.
Make a pen for him, for he is your protector; sew on many broad shields.
Make iron forts, unassailable; let not your chalice leak, but make it firm.
I turn toward you your worshipful prayer for aid—O Gods, the divine, worthy of sacrifice, and holy—here;
may that great Cow, like one who has gone to pasture, yield for us a thousand streams of milk.
Pour forth the golden one into the lap of the wood; fashion him with stone-made axes.
Embrace him with ten girths; yoke the steed to both poles.
The draft-animal, bearing both poles and firmly grasping them, moves between them like a bird within its nest.
Set the lord of the forest in the wood; establish him there, digging out the well without labor.
O men, bring forth the filler, the filler; urge him on and stir him for the winning of booty.
Bring hither the son of Niṣṭigri, Indra, with pressing haste, that he may drink the Soma here.
May Indra boldly protect your overturned chariot;
O much-invoked one, favor us in this glorious contest for the winning of wealth.
The wind blew her garment upward when she won a thousand [cows] at the chariot-race;
Mudgalānī became the charioteer in the quest for cattle, and Indrasenā distributed the prize in the contest.
O Indra, ward off the thunderbolt of the one who seeks to strike us down or who assails us;
O Maghavan, keep far away the weapon of the Dāsa or the Ārya.
Exulting, he drank from the pool of water; his horn shattered the enemy as he advanced.
Bearing his testicles like a burden, seeking renown, he swiftly extended his forelegs, desiring to win.
They made him bellow as they approached him; they made the bull urinate in the midst of the contest. By means of him, Mudgala won in the prize-fight a well-bred horse and a hundred thousand cattle.
The bull was yoked for the sake of the Kakarda; his long-maned charioteer shouted aloud. As the well-yoked horse rushed forward with its chariot, the footprints reached even unto Mudgalānī.
And the wise one struck out its felly; he harnessed the bull here, seeking to master it.
Indra aided the lord of the cows; the humped beast sped forth with his feet.
Favorably the shaven-headed one moved about with his goad, being harnessed to the wooden yoke by the leather thong.
Performing manly deeds for the sake of many people, he beheld the cattle and put forth his powers.
Behold this yoke-mate of the bull, the mallet lying in the middle of the race-course,
by which Mudgala won hundreds and thousands of cattle in the contests for booty.
Far away are the evils; who indeed has seen such a thing? They unyoke him whom they had yoked.
They bring him neither grass nor water; he bears the burden beyond the yoke-pole, pointing out the way.

Like a woman cast aside, she has attained the knowledge of her husband; like one who swells with milk, pouring from a leather bag, may we conquer even with a chariot that is just starting its course; may our gain be auspicious and full of wealth.
O Indra, you are the eye of the entire world, the eye of the eye itself;
for as a bull you seek to win the race with your bull-like companion, urging on even the eunuch as your ally.
Swift, sharpening his weapons like a terrifying bull, the striker, the agitator of the peoples;
the roaring, unblinking, sole hero, Indra has conquered a hundred armies at once.
With him who is thundering, unblinking, victorious, eager for battle, immovable, and bold—
with that Indra, O men, conquer and prevail in combat, with the bull who holds arrows in his hand.

He, the controller, with his host of arrow-handed men and those bearing quivers, is the one who joins in battle; Indra is the conqueror of the joined forces, the drinker of Soma, strong of arm, wielding a fierce bow, and shooting with well-aimed arrows.
O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot, slayer of demons, driving away our enemies;
shattering the armies, crushing them in battle, and conquering, be the protector of our chariots.
O Indra, discoverer of strength, ancient one, preeminent hero, powerful, vigorous, victorious, and fierce;
O conqueror of men, master of warriors, born of might, winner of cattle—ascend your victorious chariot!

O kinsmen, follow this Indra; O friends, exert yourselves together after him—he who pierces the enclosures, the winner of cattle, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, who conquers the battlefield and crushes the foe with his might.
Follow this Indra; O friends, exert yourselves together after him.
Piercing the cow-pens with his might, the pitiless hero Indra, of a hundredfold wrath,
the unshakable subduer of armies and the invincible— may he protect our hosts in the battles.
May Indra be their leader; may Bṛhaspati, the sacrificial fee, the sacrifice, and Soma go before them.
May the Maruts march at the head of the divine armies as they shatter and conquer.

The fierce roar of the gods has arisen—the host of Indra the bull, of King Varuṇa, of the Ādityas, and of the Maruts; the cry of those high-minded ones who cause the worlds to tremble as they conquer.
O Maghavan, brandish our weapons aloft; rouse the spirits of my warriors.
O slayer of Vṛtra, let the vigor of the swift steeds be stirred up, and let the shouts of the victorious chariots go forth on high.
May Indra be on our side when the banners meet; may those arrows which are ours be victorious.
May our heroes be superior; O gods, protect us in our invocations.
Bewildering the minds of these men, seize their limbs, O Apvā;
go away! Advance against them, burn them up with sorrows in their hearts; let the enemies be possessed by blinding darkness.
Advance, O heroes, and conquer! May Indra grant you protection.
May your arms be mighty so that you shall be invincible.
Soma has been pressed for you, O much-invoked one; come quickly to the sacrifice with your two bay horses.
To you these songs, offered by the inspired hero, have flowed; O Indra, drink of the pressed juice!
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, drink here of the juice pressed by men from the water-washed soma; fill your belly with it.
O Indra, you for whom the stones have poured out this [juice], increase your exhilaration with them, for you are borne by hymns.
I offer a true, forward-flowing draught for the bull, for thee, O Lord of Bay Steeds, of the pressed juice, as thou hast come hither.
O Indra, rejoice here with our songs, being praised by all our prayers and with power.

Through your aid, O Lord of Might, and by your heroic power, the *uśij* who know the cosmic order (*ṛta*) have assumed vital strength; O Indra, praising you in the dwelling of man, they stand as your companions at the feast, blessed with progeny.
O Lord of the bay horses, through the well-uttered praises of thee, the most bountiful and far-shining one, the people have extended their most liberal aid,
O Indra, as thy worshippers through thy gracious gifts.
Come near, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, with your two bay horses, to drink of the pressed soma.
Indra, the sacrifice has reached you who are patient; you are the mindful observer of this worshiper’s rite.

They attend upon him who wins a thousand spoils, who overcomes the assailant, the bounteous lord of the pressed juice, the well-praised; they honor with songs the peerless Indra, and the adorations of the singer celebrate him.
The seven divine waters, joyous and uninjured, by which you, O Indra, breaker of forts, crossed the Sindhu—
those ninety-nine flowing streams— you found a path for the gods and for man.
You released the great waters from the curse; you alone, O God, were watchful over them.
O Indra, with those [waters] which you won in the conquest of Vṛtra, may you nourish your body for all life.
Indra is the heroic power, worthy of fair praise; even the voice of prayer invokes him who is invoked by many.
Śakra, the one who comes to our aid, struck down Vṛtra, made wide space, and conquered the hostile armies.
We invoke for our good fortune the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the fierce one who listens, who comes to our aid in conflicts, who slays the Vṛtras, and who wins riches.
O Vasu, when will you desire our hymn? Let the waters flow for the one who has prepared the long-pressed juice for Vātāpya.
He whose two bay steeds, well-yoked and moving in different directions, follow the tail-feathers; he, the lord of the house, like two long-maned ones, traverses both realms.
Indra, the doer of evil, fled from the waters like a weary mortal who is afraid,
when the powerful one harnessed [his steeds] for glory.
Indra took pleasure in these two together, honoring them as they were yoked to the chariot;
Indra, the hero, [prevailed] over the two rivers that flow in different directions.
He who has mounted upon the two long-maned [horses] that are wide-expanding as if for nourishment— he,
the possessor of beautiful jaws, wins with his two jaws.
He of lofty power has praised with the lofty ones; the hero has fashioned [all things] by his might, like R̥bhu and Mātariśvan through their mental powers.
He who, golden-hued and majestic, fashioned the thunderbolt for the easy slaughter of the Dasyu—
his jaw unhurt, like the wondrous firmament.
Sharpen us against our adversaries; with our hymns may we conquer those who offer none.
A sacrifice without prayer does not please you at all.
When your triple flame stood upright at the yokes of the sacrifice in its dwelling, you,
in harmony with the two [priests], mounted the self-glorious ship together with the active one.
For your glory, the speckled cow became the vessel for pouring; for your glory, the flawless ladle, with which you pour into your own cup.
Whether it was Śatamvāja who thus praised you, O Asura, or Sumitra who thus praised you,
or Durmitra who thus praised you— you helped the son of Kutsa in the slaying of the Dasyus, and you protected the protégé of Kutsa in the slaying of the Dasyus.

Now indeed you both seek that very same thing; you spread out your thoughts like two weavers weaving garments. You have awakened him to come together; like two fair days, you bestow nourishing food upon us.
Like two camels at the watering-places, you rest upon the heights; like two vigorous draft-horses, you hasten to the command.
For you two stand like glorious messengers among the people; do not stay away like two buffaloes from the drinking-place.

Like the two wings of a bird joined together, like two variegated beasts, come to the sacrifice with the *yajus*. Shining like the fire of the god-loving man, you two worship in many places like those who travel all around.

May you come to our call like kinsmen, like a son to his father, like two fierce ones with splendor, like two lords of men for the sake of victory, like two leaders for prosperity, like two rays of light for enjoyment, and like two who are prompt to hear.
Like two young bulls with swelling testicles, like Mitra and Varuṇa, the upholders of *ṛta*, bestowers of a hundred boons;
standing high in the dwelling-place with strength and vigor, they are like two rams, worthy of worship, full of moisture.
Like two ploughshares, you are bearers of strength, swift destroyers; like two hunters, you are swift destroyers, far-reaching.
Like two water-born conquerors, you are exhilarating; as such, O two aged ones, grant me agelessness and freedom from death.
Like a Pajra woman, you move about your lover; like a needle in its tasks, O fierce ones, you carry us across.
Like the Rbhus, you possess swift horses; like Vāyu, you scatter [the clouds], bestowing dwellings and riches.
Like two cauldrons filled with honey in their bellies, eager for fortune, they are destroyers of enemies and shatterers of foes;
like two birds flying through the air, bright-shining, they move with the speed of thought, following the mind as if on a journey.
Like two great ones, find a firm footing in the depths; like two feet, provide a ford for one who crosses.
Like two ears, remember the instruction we give; like two shares, grant us wondrous wealth.
Like two *āraṅgara* bees you stir the honey; like two honey-bees in a cow-horn with the opening downward;
like two poor laborers sweating from toil, you two accompany strength and vigor as if from a well-watered pasture.
May we succeed in our hymn; may we win the prize. Come hither to our prayer, O you who ride in one chariot!
Like fame, like ripe honey within the cows, Ābhūtāṃśa has fulfilled the desire of the Aśvins.
The great bounty of these [donors] has become manifest; every living being has been released from darkness.
The great light given by the Fathers has arrived; the broad path of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has appeared.
High in heaven stand those who give sacrificial gifts; those who give horses dwell with the sun. Those who give gold partake in immortality; O Soma, those who give clothing prolong their lives.
Divine is the fulfillment, the sacrificial fee, and the worship of the gods; for [the gifts] do not come from the stingy, for they do not give.
But now, many men, offering their sacrificial fees, give out of fear of reproach.
They who behold with human eyes the hundred-streamed Vāyu, the light-finding sun;
they who satisfy and bestow gifts at the assembly, they milk the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that has seven mothers.
The giver of sacrificial fees comes first when summoned; the giver of sacrificial fees goes at the head as the leader of the village.
Him indeed I consider the lord of men who was the first to bring forth the sacrificial fee.

They call him indeed the seer, him the Brahman, the director of the sacrifice, the chanter of Sāmans, and the reciter of hymns; he knows the three bodies of the Bright One, he who first prospered through the sacrificial fee.
The sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) gives the horse; the sacrificial gift gives the cow; the sacrificial gift gives the moon as well as the gold.
The sacrificial gift wins the food which is our very self; the wise man makes the sacrificial gift his armor.
