The liberal patrons do not die; they do not go to ruin; the liberal patrons are never harmed and they never falter.
This entire world, this very heaven, and all that exists—all this he gives away as sacrificial fees to them.
The liberal givers have first won the fragrant womb; the liberal givers have won the bride who is well-robed.
The liberal givers have won the draught of wine from within; the liberal givers have won those who go forth uninvited.
For the liberal patron they groom the swift horse; for the liberal patron this maiden adorns herself.
This dwelling of the liberal patron is like a lotus-pool, like a celestial palace, beautifully adorned and brilliant.
Well-yoked horses carry the liberal giver; the well-rolling chariot of the Dakṣiṇā moves forward.
O gods, protect the liberal giver in battles; the liberal giver is the conqueror of enemies in the encounters.
Desiring what has Saramā come here? For the path is far, leading away to distant realms. What was our mission? What was the night’s duration? How did you cross the waters of the Rasā?
Sent as Indra’s messenger, I wander about, seeking your great treasures, O Paṇis. Out of fear of the one who leaps across, he protected us; thus I crossed the waters of the Rasā.
"What is Indra like, O Saramā, what is his appearance, he for whom you have come as a messenger from afar?
Let him come here; we shall make him our friend, and then he shall be the lord of our cattle."
I do not know that one who can deceive; he indeed deceives him for whom I have run as a messenger from afar.
They do not hide him in deep-flowing rivers; O Paṇis, you shall lie slain by Indra.
These are the cows, O Saramā, which you sought as you flew around the ends of heaven, O fortunate one.
Who would release them to you without a fight? Moreover, our weapons are sharp.
O Paṇis, may your words be beyond the reach of an army; may your wretched bodies be proof against arrows. May the path you must travel be unassailable; Bṛhaspati will show no mercy to either of you.
This treasure, O Saramā, rooted in the rock, is filled with cattle, horses, and riches.
The Paṇis, who are excellent guardians, protect it. You have come in vain to a track that is empty.
May the seers come hither, sharpened by Soma—the Ayāsyas, the Aṅgirases, and the Navagvas.
May they divide this stall of cattle; then let the Paṇis vomit up these words.
Thus have you come, O Saramā, driven by the sudden power of the gods.
I shall make you my sister; do not go back. O fortunate one, we shall grant you a share of the cattle.
I know not brotherhood nor sisterhood; Indra and the terrible Aṅgirases know them.
They, desiring my cattle, looked on when I went away. Depart, O Paṇis, to a far distance!
Go far away, O Paṇis, to a distant place; let the cows come forth, lowing according to the *ṛta*.
Bṛhaspati, Soma, the pressing-stones, and the inspired seers have found those that were hidden.
They spoke first regarding the sin against Brahman: the boundless ocean, Mātariśvan, Vīḷuhara, Tapas, Ugra, Mayobhū, and the divine waters, the first-born by *ṛta*.
King Soma, the first, without malice restored the Brahmin’s wife;
Varuṇa and Mitra were the attendants, and Agni, the Hotṛ, led her away by the hand.

"If they have said, 'This is the wife of a Brahmin; she is to be seized by the hand as a pledge,' she must not stand as a prize for a messenger to be sent away; thus is the kingdom of a Kṣatriya protected."
The gods spoke concerning her in the past, as did the seven seers who sat down for austerity:
"A terrible wife brought home by a Brahmin brings instability even to the highest heaven."
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) moves about, performing his various duties; he becomes a single limb of the gods.
Through him, Bṛhaspati recovered his wife, who had been led away by Soma, just as the gods [recovered] the *juhū* ladle.
The gods indeed gave her back, and men as well;
the kings, making their word true, gave back the wife of the Brahmin.
Having restored the wife of the Brahmin and having been freed from sin by the gods,
they partook of the nourishment of the earth and worship the wide-striding Viṣṇu.
Kindled today in the dwelling of man, O Jātavedas, you, a god, sacrifice to the gods.
Bring them hither, O you who are great as Mitra; you are the wise messenger, the seer, and the one of keen insight.
O Tanūnapāt, fair-tongued one, anointing the paths that lead along the way of Truth with honey, make them sweet;
fulfilling our prayers through our meditations and the sacrifice, bring our ritual to the gods.
Being invoked, worthy of praise and adoration, come, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus!
You are the youthful Hotṛ of the gods; as such, being impelled, sacrifice for them as the most skilled sacrificer.
The sacred grass is strewn toward the east upon the earth’s surface at the beginning of days for her dwelling;
it spreads itself out further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi.
Let the spacious doors open wide, like women adorning themselves for their husbands; O divine, lofty, all-impelling doors, be easy of access for the gods.
Pressing the juice, the worshipful Dawn and Night, close at hand, have sat down in their place;
two celestial maidens, lofty and richly adorned, assuming a splendor of bright hues.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, measuring out the sacrifice for man to worship;
the two poets who impel [the rite] in the assemblies, pointing toward the eastern light with their direction.
May Bhāratī come quickly to our sacrifice; may Iḷā, manifesting here like Manu, and Sarasvatī—may these three goddesses, skillful in their work, sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass.

O Hotṛ, most skilled in sacrifice, being impelled today, do thou, the wise one, worship here the god Tvaṣṭṛ— he who fashioned these two parents, Heaven and Earth, and adorned all beings with their forms.
Release [the victim] by thyself, anointing the offerings for the gods in due season;
let Vanaspati, the immolator, and the god Agni sweeten the oblation with honey and ghee.
As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods.
At the command of this Hotṛ, in the speech of the Eternal Order (ṛta), let the gods eat the oblation consecrated with the cry of Svāhā!
O wise ones, bring forth your inspired hymn according as the thoughts of men arise;
let us impel Indra with truthful deeds, for he is the hero, the lover of songs, who is well-known.

For the inspired thought from the seat of Cosmic Order has shone forth; the bull, son of the Earth, has reached the kine with his rays. He has arisen with a mighty roar and has encompassed even the vast regions.
Indra, indeed, knows this by report, for he is the victorious maker of paths for Sūrya.
Making the cow his mate, the unshakable one became the lord of heaven; born of old, he is irresistible.
Indra, being praised by the Aṅgirases, shattered with his might the ordinances of the great ocean;
he who, through his truthfulness, established the support and spread out even the many regions.
Indra is the counterpart of heaven and earth; he knows all libations and slays Śuṣṇa.
He has spread out even the great sky with the sun, and as the most steadfast one, he has propped it up with a pillar that is itself unshakable.
For with his thunderbolt the slayer of Vṛtra struck down Vṛtra; he shattered the magical powers of the godless one who was waxing strong.
O bold one, you struck him down here with boldness, and then, O Maghavan, you became mighty-armed.
When the dawns unite with the sun, his rays find the wondrous light;
when the star of heaven is seen, no one truly knows from whence it comes again.
Far indeed have those waters gone, the first of them that flowed forth at the impulse of Indra. Where is their beginning, where is their base? Where now is your middle, and where is your end?
You released the rivers that had been swallowed by the serpent; then indeed they burst forth with speed.
Those seeking release and those already released—now, once set free, they do not rest.
Like longing women, they have gone toward the river together; from of old, the breaker of forts has been sought as their lover.
O Indra, may your earthly treasures come to our home, and may your many bounties reach us.
O Indra, drink of the pressed juice according to your desire; for the morning pressing is indeed your first draught.
Rejoice, O Hero, to slay the enemies! We shall proclaim your heroic deeds through our hymns.
O Indra, come with that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought, for the drinking of the Soma.
Let your bay horses hasten quickly hither—the stallions with whom you come, rejoicing.
With the golden-hued splendor of the sun, clothe your body in the most excellent forms.
O Indra, being invoked by us, your friends, sit down and rejoice in unison.

O Indra, since these two great worlds, heaven and earth, could not encompass that majesty of yours in your states of exhilaration, come now to that dwelling with your beloved, harnessed bay horses, toward the food you hold dear.
O Indra, for whom you have perpetually performed deeds of joy against the enemies that cannot be imitated—this Soma has been pressed for your exhilaration;
it stirs your abundance and your power. O Indra, this Soma is yours for your rapture.
This is your vessel, O Indra, won through ancient wealth; drink the Soma from it, O Śatakratu!
The trough is full of the intoxicating mead, which all the gods indeed desire.
For from many sides, O Indra, bull-like hero, people who have set forth their offerings call upon you.
May these libations of ours be the sweetest for you; take pleasure in them.
I shall proclaim your ancient deeds, O Indra, and those first exploits performed even now:
you, whose wrath was true, loosened the mountain and made the cow easy to find for the sake of the sacred word.
Sit down here among the hosts, O Lord of Hosts; they call you the wisest of poets among sages.
Nothing whatsoever is done without you in this world; O Maghavan, sing the great, wondrous hymn!
O Maghavan, look upon us as we implore you; O Friend, Lord of Wealth, be mindful of your friends.
O maker of joy, grant us delight; O you of true strength, give us our share even in wealth that has not yet been distributed.
Heaven and Earth, acting in concert with all the gods, have aided his impetuous strength.
When he came, performing his great Indra-power, having drunk of the Soma, he grew strong, possessed of wisdom.
Viṣṇu proclaims that greatness of his, having drunk with might from the stream of honeyed juice.
Having slain Vṛtra with the gods who accompany him, Indra, the bounteous one, became preeminent.
When you, bearing weapons, stood together with Vṛtra the serpent for battle to win the praise,
all the Maruts, along with your very self, O fierce one, increased your mighty Indra-power.
As soon as he was born, he drove away his rivals; the hero looked toward manly power and the field of battle.
He split the mountain and released the flowing waters; through his skillful work, he propped up the broad firmament.
Then Indra indeed surpassed all powers; he pushed heaven and earth far apart.
Boldly he brought down the iron thunderbolt, a blessing for Mitra and Varuṇa who offer oblations.
Here, before the powers of Indra, the exuberant one, the fierce ones fled in terror from his wrath;
when the mighty one, with his might, shattered Vṛtra who bore the waters and was enveloped in darkness.

When the two, striving together with their greatness, met for the first heroic deeds to be performed, the thick darkness was cast down; Indra, struck by his own power, prevailed in the first invocation.
Then all the gods magnified your manly powers with eloquence accompanied by Soma;
Vṛtra the serpent, subdued by the blow of Indra’s hand, devoured his food greedily like Agni with its jaws.
Proclaim his many friendships with skillful words, with hymns, and with companionship.
Indra, subduing both Dhuni and Cumuri, listens to Dabhīti because of his faithful devotion.
Bring us many riches in good horses, with which I may be mindful while reciting my prayers.
May we cross over all difficulties by easy paths; find for us today a wide and secure ford.
The two heats have pervaded the threefold world on all sides; Mātariśvan has come to their delight.
Desiring to obtain the milk of heaven, they have sought it; the gods have known the hymn of equal power.
Three Nirṛtis wait upon the Ordainer; for the far-famed bearers of the oblation know them well. The seers have discerned their foundation—that which lies within the highest secret ordinances.
The young woman with four braided locks, well-adorned, wearing clarity as her garment, has a face of clarified butter;
upon her two strong-winged males have settled, where the gods received their allotted portion.
The single Suparṇa has entered the ocean; he gazes upon this entire world. With a simple mind, I beheld him from nearby; the Mother licks him, and he licks the Mother.
The wise poets, with their sacred words, fashion into many forms that which is but one—the fair-winged bird. Establishing the meters at the sacrifices, they measure out twelve cups of Soma.
Arranging thirty-six and four, and establishing the meters up to twelve, the seers,
having measured out the sacrifice with their wisdom, set the chariot in motion by means of the *ṛc* and *sāman*.
Fourteen other powers belong to him; seven wise ones lead him forth with speech.
Who here can declare the ford that reaches [him], the path by which they drink of the pressed juice?
In a thousand ways are the fifteenfold hymns; as vast as heaven and earth are, so great is that.
In a thousand ways are the thousands of greatnesses; as far as the Brahman extends, so far extends speech.
What wise man knows the application of the meters? Who has attained the inspired speech that belongs to the sacrificial hearths?
Whom do they call the eighth hero among the officiating priests? And who indeed has discerned Indra’s two bay steeds?

Some wander around the edge of the earth; they have stood yoked to the poles of the chariot. When Yama is established in his palace, they distribute the portion of their weariness among these [beings].
Wondrous indeed is the growth of the young child, who does not go to his two mothers to suckle;
though she who has no udder gave birth to him, he has now grown great, immediately setting out on his mighty mission as a messenger.
Agni has indeed been established by name as the most effective in his work, he who gathers the forests together with his tooth of ash;
crushing them forward with his sacrificial ladle at the well-performed rite, like a bull snorting in the pasture.
Like a bird perched upon a tree, that divine Indu of yours—spraying, scattering, and surging like a flood;
like a bearer of oblations with his flame, exuberant and of mighty vows—he traverses the paths.
O undecaying one, as you spread forth, the unshakable winds cannot encompass you who are burning like fire;
like joyful warriors seeking a hero, they have reached Trita, urging him on toward his goal.
He indeed is Agni, the best of the Kaṇvas, the friend of Kaṇva; he overcomes the enemy, whether far or near.
May Agni protect those who praise him, may Agni protect the patrons; may Agni grant us their favor.
O Supitrya, for Jātavedas, the most powerful and victorious one, Tṛṣucyavana has hastened forth;
he who, with boldness, grants a boon even in the waterless desert to the one who desires the greatest wealth.
Thus is Agni praised for wealth by mortals together with patrons, the noble son of strength, along with men— those who,
like well-established friends, are devoted to the *ṛta*, and who, like the heavens, surpass all humans in splendor.
"O Son of Strength, O Victorious One!"—thus does the bull-like voice of Upastuta praise you.
We shall praise you, possessing excellent heroes through you, as we extend our lifespan further and further.

Thus, O Agni, have the seers, the Upastutas, the sons of Vṛṣṭihavya, spoken to you. Protect them and the praising patrons; "Vaṣaṭ! Vaṣaṭ!"—thus they have reached upward; "Homage! Homage!"—thus they have reached upward.
Drink the Soma for great Indra-power; drink, O most mighty one, to slay Vṛtra!
Drink, being invoked, for wealth and strength; drink your fill of the sweet mead, O Indra, and be filled with vigor.
Drink of this pressed Soma, O Indra, which is rich in nourishment and has been set forth—the best of what is poured.
Bestowing well-being, rejoice in your heart; turn toward us for the sake of wealth and good fortune.
May the divine Soma exhilarate you, O Indra; may that which is pressed among mortals exhilarate you.
May it exhilarate you with that by which you have created wide space, and may it exhilarate you with that by which you utterly destroy your enemies.
May Indra, the doubly mighty, the unassailable bull, come with his two bay horses to the poured-out soma-juice.
O slayer of Aruṣa, drink your fill of the pressed honey-sweetness brought forth in the vessel; satisfy yourself completely.
Make the sharp weapons of the sorcerers blaze out; unstring the firm bows of those driven by evil spirits.
To you, the fierce one, I grant power and strength; having overcome the enemies, strike them down in their battles.
O Indra, stretch out your glories against the enemy; like the firm bowstring, ward off our assailants. Increasing toward us with your powers, O unassailable one, cause your body to grow strong.
O Maghavan, this oblation is offered for you; O Sovereign, accept it without resentment.
For you, O Maghavan, is the pressed juice; for you is the cooked offering. Eat, O Indra, and drink of what has been set forth.

Come, O Indra, to these offered oblations that have been set forth; accept them with favor, both the cooked food and the Soma. Bearing refreshments, we welcome you; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.
I send forth this eloquent speech for Indra and Agni with hymns, as one drives a boat upon the river.
Like spokes of a wheel, the gods revolve around us—those who are givers of wealth to us and who break through obstacles.
O gods, you have not indeed made hunger a weapon of death; even for one who has eaten, deaths approach.
Moreover, the wealth of the liberal giver does not fail him, while the one who does not give finds no one to show him mercy.

He who, though possessing food, hardens his heart toward the needy man who longs for nourishment and has come to him in distress— he serves only those who are before him, and even then, he finds no one to comfort him.
He indeed is the liberal giver who bestows wealth upon the suppliant who wanders about, emaciated and desiring food.
He is ready for him when called upon on a journey, and he makes him a friend for future times.
He is no friend who does not give food to a friend who stays with him and seeks his company. Let him depart from such a man; that is no home. One should seek another giver, even if he be a stranger.
The stronger man should indeed give to the one who implores him; he should look toward the longer path.
For riches revolve like the wheels of a chariot, passing from one person to another.
The thoughtless man gains food in vain; I speak the truth: that is his own destruction.
He nourishes neither Aryaman nor his friend; he who eats alone becomes the possessor of all sin alone.
The ploughshare, while ploughing, produces food; he who clears the path with his feet surpasses him.
Speaking the sacred word, the priest is a better winner than the one who does not speak; the liberal kinsman shall overcome the one who gives nothing.
The one-footed has stepped out beyond the two-footed; the two-footed follows after the three-footed.
The four-footed comes at the call of the two-footed, standing by while beholding the fivefold rows.
Even two hands that are alike do not perform the same work; even two mother-cows do not yield the same amount of milk;
even twins do not have equal strengths; and even two who are kinsmen do not give gifts in equal measure.
O Agni, shining among mortals in your own dwelling, you of pure vows, you strike down the devouring demon.
You rise up, well-invoked; you rejoice in the clarified butters when the ladles have been brought together toward you.
Offered with the song of praise, that Agni shines forth, worthy of invocation;
his face is anointed with the ladle.
Agni, whose face is honeyed, is anointed with clarified butter when offered oblations; he shines forth, the possessor of radiant wealth.
Being praised, you are kindled for the gods, O bearer of oblations;
as such, mortals invoke you.
O mortals, worship that immortal Agni with clarified butter—
the invincible lord of the household.
O Agni, burn away the demon with your invincible flame; shine as the guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
O Agni, with your face do you burn up the sorceresses,
shining brightly among the wide dwellings.
Thee, the bearer of oblations, the best of sacrificers among the human race, those dwelling in wide realms have kindled with their songs of praise.
"Thus," "thus," so my mind thinks: "May I win cattle and horses; have I not drunk of Soma?"
Like violent winds, the draughts have raised me up; "Have I not drunk of Soma? [he asks.]
The draughts drunk have borne me up, like swift horses a chariot; "Have I not drunk of Soma? [he asks].
The thought has come near to me, like a lowing cow to her dear calf;
"Have I drunk of the Soma? [he asks].
Like a carpenter fashioning a chariot-seat, I turn my thought around within my heart: "Have I drunk of the Soma?"—so I ask.
"Indeed, not even the five tribes have come within the range of my sight;
have I drunk of the Soma? he asked.
"Neither both heaven and earth together are equal to even one of my wings; have I not drunk of the Soma? so he says.
By my greatness I have surpassed the sky and this great earth;
have I not drunk of the Soma?
"Come, I shall set this earth down here or there; have I not drunk of Soma? (RV 10.119.9)
"Swiftly indeed shall I strike the earth here or there;
have I not drunk of Soma?"—thus [he thought].
"One wing of mine is in heaven; the other I have drawn down below.
Have I not drunk of Soma? so he asked.
I am of great majesty, risen up to the very clouds; have I not drunk of the Soma?
I go to the house, well-prepared, the carrier of oblations to the gods; have I not drunk of the Soma?
That indeed was the eldest in all the worlds, from which was born the fierce one of brilliant valor;
as soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies—he in whom all his helpers rejoice.
Increasing in power and possessing abundant vigor, you, as an enemy, instill fear in the Dāsa.
Winning both the unbreathing and the breathing, they cry out to you at the offerings during the exhilarations of the soma.
All turn their will toward you when these helpers become twice or thrice as many.
Mix that which is sweeter than the sweet with sweetness; fight well for us with honey against honey.
For thus indeed do the sages rejoice after you as you win the riches at every exhilaration.
O bold one, extend your more powerful and firm strength; let not the evil-doing sorcerers harm you.
Through you we prevail in battles, beholding many things worthy of war. I urge on your weapons with my words; I sharpen your vital powers with my prayer.
I would praise the one of many forms, the skillful, the most powerful Āptya among the Āptyas.
He pierces the seven Dānus with his might and overcomes many adversaries.
You have bestowed that lower and higher [gift] in the dwelling where you protected us with your aid;
you cause the two wandering parents to stand firm, and from there you send forth many heroic deeds.
Bṛhaddiva, the foremost winner of light, proclaims these holy words as strength for Indra;
he rules over the great stall of cattle, the self-ruling lord, and has thrown open all his own doors.
Thus has the great Atharvan Bṛhaddiva spoken to Indra as his own body;
the stainless sisters dwelling in the mother [Earth] impel him and strengthen him with power.
In the beginning, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) arose; once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists.
He supported this earth and yonder heaven. To which god shall we offer our worship with an oblation?
He who is the giver of self, the giver of strength, whose command all the gods revere—
he whose shadow is immortality and whose [other side] is death— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
He who by his greatness became the sole king of all that breathes and blinks,
the lord of this biped and quadruped world— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
To him whose greatness these snow-capped mountains proclaim, whose they say is the ocean together with the Rasā river;
to him whose arms are these quarters of space—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

By whom the formidable heaven and the earth were made firm, by whom the sky was propped up and the firmament established; he who is the measurer of the mid-air and of space—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
To whom the two shouting worlds, supported by his aid and trembling in their minds, looked up;
he upon whom the risen sun shines forth—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

When the great waters went forth, containing the universe within them as a germ and generating Agni, from that there arose the one life-force (asus) of the gods; to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
He who by his greatness surveyed the waters as they held creative power and generated the sacrifice—
he who was the one God above all gods— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

May he who is the progenitor of the earth, or he of true law who begot the heavens, or he who begot the great, shining waters—him may he not harm! To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
I praise him who is like a treasure of wondrous luster—the lovely, gracious guest who is free from hostility.
May he, Agni, the invoker and lord of the household, bestow upon us all-sustaining riches and heroic strength.

O Agni, graciously accepting and delighting in my word, you who know all ways and are most skillful, you whose garment is clarified butter, prepare the path for our prayer; the gods have brought you forth according to your sacred law.
Immortal one, circling the seven stations, grant your favor to the pious donor who serves you;
O Agni, delight in him who has approached you with fuel, and bestow upon him wealth consisting of heroic sons and self-sustaining prosperity.
The seven [priests], bringing oblations, invoke the banner of sacrifice, the first domestic priest,
the vigorous one— the Agni who hears us, whose back is anointed with ghee, the bull, the god who bestows heroic strength upon the giver.
You are the first messenger, most excellent; being invoked for the sake of immortality, take your delight.
The Maruts have cleansed you in the house of the donor; the Bhr̥gus have caused you to shine forth with their hymns of praise.
O Agni of noble will, milking the well-yielding cow that provides all sustenance for the sacrificer who loves the sacrifice—
you, whose back is dripping with ghee, shining thrice over the cosmic orders (*ṛta*), and moving as the path around the sacrifice, you manifest your supreme wisdom.
At the break of this very dawn, men have sacrificed, making you their messenger;
the gods have magnified you for your greatness, O Agni, as they purified the clarified butter at the sacrifice.
The Vasiṣṭhas, the wise ones, have invoked you, the powerful one, chanting your praises at the sacrifices, O Agni.
Bestow upon the sacrificers an abundance of wealth; and do you all protect us always with your blessings.
This Vena, enveloped in light, impels the daughters of Pṛśni within the expanse of the mid-world;
at the meeting of the waters and the sun, the sages lick him with their hymns as if he were an infant.
Vena, born of the clouds, raises the wave from the ocean; the back of the beloved one has been seen.
Upon the ridge, on the summit of *ṛta*, he shines; the throngs have sung together toward their common womb.
Many mothers of the calf, dwelling in the same nest, lowing toward their common goal, have mounted upon the ridge of Truth;
there the voices lick the honeyed nectar of immortality.
Knowing his form, the sages yearned; they indeed went to the cry of the wild buffalo.
Moving according to the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), they stood over the river; Gandharva found the immortal names.
The Apsaras, smiling at her lover, the woman, bears him in the highest heaven.
Moving among the wombs of his beloved, being beloved himself, that Vena sits upon the golden wing.
When they beheld you with longing hearts as you flew upon the vault of heaven—
the golden-winged messenger of Varuṇa, the restless bird in the womb of Yama— then they saw you.
The Gandharva has stood erect upon the vault of heaven, facing us, bearing his brilliant weapons;
clothing himself in a fragrant robe fair to behold, he has generated his own dear names like the light of heaven.
When the drop goes toward the ocean, beholding with the eye of a vulture in the wide expanse,
the ray, longing with its bright luster, has made dear things manifest in the third realm.
O Agni, come to this sacrifice of ours—the fivefold path, the threefold, with seven threads.
Be the bearer of our oblations and our leader; for you have lain for a very long time in deep darkness.
From the godless I go forth as a god, moving secretly while perceiving the hidden depths; I attain immortality.
Since I, being auspicious, abandon that which is inauspicious, I depart from my own kinship toward a stranger as my kinsman.

Beholding the guest of another, of a different lineage, I measure out many abodes for the Law (Ṛta). I proclaim what is auspicious to the Father, the Asura; from that which is unworthy of sacrifice, I go toward the portion worthy of sacrifice.
I have spent many years within him; choosing Indra, I leave my father behind.
Agni, Soma, and Varuṇa—they pass away; the kingdom has turned back, and I am returning to it.
Those Asuras have indeed become devoid of magic; and you, O Varuṇa, do not desire me.
O King, distinguishing the untruth by means of truth, come to the sovereignty over my kingdom!
This is the light; this indeed was the desirable; this is the manifestation, the wide mid-air.
Let us two slay Vṛtra; come forth, O Soma! Being the oblation, let us worship thee with the oblation.
The Seer, by his poetic power, fixed his form in heaven; Varuṇa, through his might, released the waters.
Like women seeking security, the rivers carry his bright color; they bear it aloft, pure and radiant.
These [waters] attend upon his supreme power; he dwells within them, rejoicing in their own inherent nature.
Like subjects choosing a king, they, shrinking away from Vṛtra, have stood apart from him.
They call him the swan, the companion of those who loathe [evil], moving in friendship with the celestial waters;
the sages, through their inspired thought, have discerned Indra as he moves about according to the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I am with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
I support both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [support] Indra and Agni, and I [support] both Aśvins.
I sustain the crushing Soma; I sustain Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and Bhaga.
I bestow wealth upon the one who offers oblations, the well-protecting sacrificer who presses the juice.
I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of treasures, the conscious one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice.
The gods have distributed me in many places, me who have many abodes and who cause many to enter.
Through me he eats food who perceives, who breathes, and who hears what is spoken. Those who lack understanding dwell near me; hear, O famous one, for I speak to you with faith.
I myself alone declare this, which is pleasing to both gods and men:
whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahmin, him a seer, him a man of great wisdom.
I bend the bow for Rudra so that his arrow may strike the hater of sacred knowledge;
I stir up strife among the people; I have entered heaven and earth.
I bring forth the Father upon its summit; my source is within the waters, in the ocean.
From there I spread out through all the worlds, and with my highest point I touch that very heaven.
I alone blow forth like the wind, setting all worlds in motion; beyond the sky and beyond this earth, I have become so great in my majesty.
Neither distress nor misfortune, O gods, reaches that mortal whom Aryaman,
Mitra, and Varuṇa lead together in harmony across his enemies.
For that indeed we choose from you, O Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—
by which you deliver the mortal from distress and lead him beyond his enemies.
May they—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—surely come now for our protection;
may they, the best leaders, lead us, and as the best deliverers, carry us across our enemies.
You—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—protect the universe on every side.
May we abide in your dear protection, O excellent leaders, beyond our enemies.
May the Ādityas—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—overcome our adversaries;
may we invoke the mighty Rudra with the Maruts, Indra, and Agni for our well-being, passing beyond our enemies.
May Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman, the leaders of us all,
lead us safely across all difficulties and beyond our enemies— the kings of all people.
May Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us prosperity for our aid;
may the Ādityas, far-extending, grant us wide protection when we pray for it, beyond our enemies.
Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, released even the Gaurī cow that was stuck by the foot, so do you release us from this distress; O Agni, prolong our life further.
The goddess Night, approaching, has looked out in many places with her eyes; she has put on all her splendors.
The immortal goddess has filled the wide space, the depths, and the heights;
with her light, she drives away the darkness.
The goddess Dawn, approaching, has driven away her sister, Night;
indeed, the darkness departs.
May she come to us today, at whose approach we have settled as birds do in their dwelling upon a tree.
The villages have settled down; those with feet and those with wings have settled down;
even the hawks seeking their prey have settled down.
Drive away the she-wolf and the wolf; ward off the thief, O Night. And then, become easy for us to cross.
The dark, manifest darkness has approached me, shimmering intensely;
O Uṣas, drive it away like a debt.
I have brought these [songs] to you like cattle; O Night, daughter of Heaven, accept this hymn as one who has won the prize.
O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations; kindling you, may we nourish our bodies.
May the four quarters bow down to me; with you as our overseer, may we conquer the hostile armies.
May all the gods be with me in my invocation—the Maruts accompanied by Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
May the wide world of the intermediate space be mine; may the wind blow for me in this desire.
May the gods bestow wealth upon me through sacrifice; may the blessing be with me, and with me the invocation of the gods.
May the divine Hotṛ-priests, the foremost, grant us their favor; may we remain unharmed in body and possessed of heroic sons.
Let them offer for me those oblations which are mine; let the intention of my mind be fulfilled. May I not fall into any sin whatsoever; O All-Gods, speak in our favor!
O six divine expanses, make wide room for us; O all you gods, display your heroism here!
May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies; may we not fall into the power of the enemy, O King Soma.
O Agni, repelling the wrath of our enemies, do you, an undeceived guardian, protect us on every side. Let those who pursue us turn back again; let the minds of these who have awakened perish.
Dhātṛ, the ordainer of ordainers, who is the lord of the world— the god who is our protector and overcomes the assailant—
may both Aśvins and Bṛhaspati protect this sacrifice and the sacrificer from misfortune.
May the wide-ranging bull, invoked by many, grant us protection in this call, he who is rich in food;
O Indra, Lord of the bay horses, be gracious to our progeny—do not harm us, do not abandon us.
May those who are our rivals fall away from us; with Indra and Agni we drive them off.
The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas have made me a high-reaching, fierce, perceiving, and sovereign overlord.
Neither non-being nor being existed then; there was not the atmosphere, nor the sky beyond it.
What was concealed? Where? In whose protection? Was there water, unfathomable and deep?
There was neither death nor immortality then; there was no sign of night or day.
That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhayā*); other than that, nothing else existed beyond it.
In the beginning, there was darkness hidden by darkness; all this was an indistinguishable ocean.
That which was, enveloped by the void, that One came into being through the power of heat.
In the beginning, Desire arose within that, becoming the first seed of mind.
Sages, searching in their hearts with inspired thought, discovered the bond of Being in Non-being.
Transversely stretched is their cord; was there below, or was there above? There were seed-bearers, there were powers; self-sustenance was beneath, impulse was beyond.
Who truly knows? Who here can declare it? Whence was it born, whence came this creation?
The gods are subsequent to the emergence of this world; then who indeed knows from whence it first came into being?
From whence this creation has arisen— whether he fashioned it or whether he did not—
he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he indeed knows, or perhaps even he does not know.

The sacrifice which is stretched out on all sides with threads, extended by a hundred and one divine acts—these fathers who have come weave it; they sit at the outspread [loom], saying, "Weave forward! Weave back!"
A man stretches it out and a man weaves it; a man has spread it across this firmament.
These pegs have settled near their seat; they have made the Sāman-hymns into the warp-threads for weaving.

What was the measure, what the model, what the foundation? What was the clarified butter, what was the enclosing-stick? What was the metre, what the prelude, what the hymn, when all the gods sacrificed to the God?
The Gāyatrī became the companion of Agni; Savitṛ was united with the Uṣṇih;
Soma, great through his hymns, was joined with the Anuṣṭubh; and the Bṛhatī aided the speech of Bṛhaspati.
The Virāj is the glory of Mitra and Varuṇa; the Triṣṭubh is Indra’s portion here of the day.
The Jagatī has entered all the gods; by means of it the seers and men have fashioned [the world].
By that [sacrifice], when the ancient sacrifice was born, the seers and our human ancestors performed their rites;
I believe with my mind’s eye that I behold those who first offered this sacrifice.
Accompanied by hymns, accompanied by meters, and accompanied by measures, the seven divine seers,
beholding the path of the ancients, the wise ones took hold [of it], like charioteers taking hold of their reins.
O Indra, O subduer, drive away all our enemies to the east, drive them away to the west,
and drive them away to the north and to the south, O hero, so that we may rejoice in your wide protection.
Just as those who possess barley reap the grain in due order, separating it out,
so do thou bring here the food of those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.
For there is no chariot-pole for you to travel by season, nor has fame been found in the assemblies;
yet the inspired poets, desiring cattle, horses, and strength, seek Indra, the bull, for friendship.
O Aśvins, lords of splendor, drinking deeply the surā-liquor together with the Asura Namuci, you two aided Indra in his deeds.
Like parents for their son, both Aśvins protected you, O Indra, with their poetic wisdom and wondrous powers;
when you drank the exhilarating Soma with your might, Sarasvatī refreshed you, O Maghavan.
May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, through his aids, be gracious; may he, the all-knowing, drive away our enemies and grant us fearlessness. May we be masters of heroic vigor.

May we abide in the good-will of that one worthy of sacrifice, and also in his auspicious benevolence. May that Indra, the excellent protector and possessor of riches, drive our enemies far away from us.
May the heaven, whose wealth is praised, and the earth, assist the sacrificer;
may the two divine Aśvins increase the sacrificer with their favors.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, upholders of the people, we worship you two who are well-disposed through your inspired will. Through your friendship and your active power, may we overcome the Rākṣasas.
And now, when we desire to win from you that which is dear—
possessing our own share of wealth— or when the giver prospers with his own wealth, let no one withhold his riches.
Yonder other sky was born, O Asura; you, Varuṇa, are the king of all.
The head of the chariot has taken pleasure [in this]; let not one who harms the ender be guilty of such sin.
In this very man, O Śakapūta, the enemy slays the heroes who have fled even when their friend is well-disposed;
or when the steed bestows protection upon his own dear and worshipful bodies.
For your mother is Aditi, O wise ones; like the sky, let the earth be purified with milk.
Bestow what is dear upon us, and cleanse yourselves with the rays of the sun.

For you two, O lords of the work, have sat down like one who stands upon a chariot, like one who sits upon the pole, like one who dwells in the forest. As such, Nṛmedhas protected us when we were lamenting from distress; Sumedhas protected us from distress.
Sing forth this strengthening hymn for this Indra, whose chariot is foremost;
the maker of space even in close combat, the slayer of Vṛtra in the clash of battles, be our inspirer. May the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows!
You released the rivers to flow downward; you slew the serpent.
O Indra, you were born without a rival; you nourish every desirable thing. We embrace you—let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.
May all hostilities be utterly dispersed; may the prayers of our noble patron reach us.
O Indra, you are the hurler of the weapon at the enemy who seeks to slay us. That gift of yours which bestows wealth—let the bowstrings of our adversaries snap upon their bows.
O Indra, whatever person who seeks to harm us like a wolf assails us from any side, cast him beneath our feet;
for you are the subduer and the conqueror. Let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.
Whoever assails us, O Indra—whether he be a kinsman or a stranger—diminish his strength, even as the great heaven [overshadows the earth]. May the bowstrings of our adversaries snap upon their bows.
O Indra, we who long for you grasp at your friendship.
Lead us along the path of Truth past all difficulties. May the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows!
O Indra, bestow upon us that boon which yields according to the singer's desire;
may the great cow, with her flawless udder, swell for us with milk in a thousand streams.

Since you, O Indra, have filled both worlds as the Dawn fills them, you, the great sovereign of the great ones and of all people—the goddess Mother has brought you forth; the auspicious Mother has brought you forth.
Relax the firm strength of the mortal who seeks to strike us down;
cast him beneath our feet, he who points at us. The divine Mother has brought him forth; the auspicious Mother has brought him forth.

O slayer of enemies, O Śakra, shake down those great, all-glittering refreshments with your powers, O Indra, with all your aids. The divine mother brought him forth; the auspicious mother brought him forth.
When you, O Indra of a hundred powers, shake all things down like wealth for the one who presses the soma,
with your thousandfold aids— then the divine Mother gave birth [to you], the auspicious Mother gave birth.
Let the missiles fall away on all sides like drops of sweat;
let ill-will depart from us like the threads of dūrvā grass. The divine mother has brought [the child] forth; the auspicious mother has brought him forth.

For you, O wise one, bear a spear like a long hook; with your eastern foot, O Maghavan, you strike down the branches as Yama does. The divine mother gave birth to you; the auspicious mother gave birth to you.
O gods, we do not diminish you; we do not neglect you; we act in accordance with what is heard in the sacred hymns.
With our wings and with our armpits, we clasp you closely here.
On that tree with beautiful foliage where Yama drinks together with the gods—
there our father, the lord of the people, looks back upon the ancients.
I gazed upon him with resentment as he wandered in that evil way, following after the ancients; therefore, I yearned for him once again.
O boy, the new, wheelless chariot which you fashioned with your mind—
single-seated and facing in every direction— you mount it even though you do not see it.
O Child, the chariot which you caused to roll forth from among the inspired poets—that very chariot followed after the Sāman; thus was it set upon the boat from here.
Who gave birth to the boy? Who fashioned the chariot?
Who indeed might tell us today how it was that he became the one to be followed as a bride-price?
Just as she became the one to be followed, from that the summit was born;
the foundation was stretched out in front, and the exit was made behind.
This is the seat of Yama, which is called the dwelling place of the gods;
this is his flute that is blown, and he is adorned with songs.
The one with long hair bears Agni; the one with long hair bears the poison; the one with long hair sustains the two worlds, heaven and earth.
The one with long hair makes the entire sun visible; the one with long hair is called this light.
The sages, girdled by the wind, wear soiled garments of reddish-brown;
they follow the blast of the wind when the gods have entered [into them].
Intoxicated by the state of the sage’s silence, we have ascended to the winds;
you mortals behold only our bodies.
He flies through the intermediate space, beholding all forms;
the sage is the well-disposed friend of every god, for the sake of their good deeds.
The horse of Vāta, the friend of Vāyu, and the sage impelled by the gods—
he dwells in both oceans, the eastern and the western.
Moving in the path of Apsarases, Gandharvas, and wild beasts, Keśin, the knower of the intention, is a sweet and most exhilarating friend.
Vāyu churned for him; Kunannamā pounded it, as Keśin drank from the vessel of poison together with Rudra.
O gods, you raise up again that which has been cast down; O gods, you restore again even the one who has committed sin.
O gods, O gods, you bring back to life once more.
These two winds blow from the ocean and from afar:
may one breathe strength upon you, and may the other blow away whatever is harmful.
O Vāta, blow hither healing; O Vāta, blow away whatever is disease. For you, possessing all remedies, go as the messenger of the gods.
I have come to you with healing remedies and with means for your safety. I have brought you auspicious strength; I drive away your consumption.
May the gods protect him here; may the host of Maruts protect him;
may all beings protect him, so that he may be free from harm.
The waters indeed are healers; the waters drive away disease.
The waters are the healers of everything; may they provide healing for you.
With these two hands of ten fingers, with the tongue as the forerunner of speech—
those two which are free from disease— with them we touch you.
In your friendship, O Indra, those priests, mindful of the *ṛta*, rent Vala asunder;
there, honoring the dawns, you released the waters and performed wondrous deeds for Kutsa against the dragon.
You released the plants; you split the mountains apart; you drove out the cattle and drank the beloved honey.
By your wondrous power you made the trees grow; the sun blazed forth through the song born of the Eternal Order (*ṛta*).
In the midst of heaven, Sūrya unyoked his chariot; the Ārya established a counter-measure against the Dāsa.
Indra, acting with Ṛjiśvan, shattered the firm fortresses of the wily Asura Pipru.
Boldly opening the unassailable treasures, the tireless Ayāsya crushed the godless ones.
Like the sun in the month, he took away the wealth of the citadels; being praised, he shattered his enemies with his radiant weapon.
With an army that does not fight, the all-pervading Vṛtra-slayer, cleaving through with his power, sharpens his impetuous blows.
He was terrified by Indra’s thunderbolt as it struck; the radiant one fled, and Uṣas abandoned her wagon.
These are indeed your famous deeds, yours alone: that you made one [of the two] devoid of sacrifice;
you established the ordering of the months in the sky, and by you the father bears the rim that was split apart.
Savitar, with sunbeams and golden hair, has raised his eternal light in the east.
At his instigation, the wise Pūṣan goes forth, the guardian who beholds all beings.
Beholding men, he sits in the midst of heaven, having filled the two worlds and the intermediate space.
He looks upon all the oil-laden ones; he stands between the eastern and the western sign.
The foundation of wealth, the gatherer of treasures, he gazes upon all forms with his powers;
like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true, he stands like Indra in the contest for riches.
O Soma, when the waters beheld Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva, they flowed apart according to the Eternal Law (ṛta).
Indra, hastening after them, perceived that; he saw the enclosures of the sun.
May Viśvāvasu, the celestial Gandharva who measures the mid-region, sing this for us:
whatever is true and whatever we do not know—may he, impelling our thoughts, protect our prayers.
He found the winner at the foot of the rivers; he threw open the doors of those confined within the rocky enclosures.
Gandharva proclaimed their nectarous secrets; Indra fully understood the skill of the serpents.
O Agni, yours is glory and vital power; your rays shine brightly, O Lord of Light. O Sage of great luster, through your might you bestow upon the donor praiseworthy strength.
With purifying luster, with bright luster, with undiminished luster, you rise up with your radiance.
Moving between your two mothers as their son, you protect them; you fill both heaven and earth.
O Son of Strength, Jātavedas, rejoice in our excellent praises and our prayers, for you have been well-disposed toward us.
In you they have gathered many-formed refreshments, which possess wondrous aids and are born of noble power.
O Agni, ruling over us, spread yourself abroad with living beings; bestow wealth upon us, O Immortal One. You shine forth with a form worthy of being beheld; you fulfill our victorious will.
The wise ordainer of the sacrifice, who rules over great bounty—
unto him you grant the auspicious gift of beauty, great nourishment, and winning wealth.
Men have placed before them for their welfare Agni, the observer of Truth, the mighty one visible to all;
you, the god with ears that hear, most far-reaching, the divine one, through song throughout the ages of mankind.
O Agni, speak here to us; turn toward us and be well-disposed.
Bestow upon us, O Lord of the People, for you are the giver of wealth to us.
May Aryaman grant us [wealth], may Bhaga grant it, and may Bṛhaspati grant it.
May the gods grant it, and may the goddess Sūnṛtā grant us riches.
We invoke King Soma for protection, Agni with our songs of praise,
the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the priest.
We invoke Indra, Vāyu, and Bṛhaspati, who are easy to call, here,
so that every person in our assembly may be well-disposed toward us.
Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to bestow gifts;
[urge] Vāta, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and the prize-winning Savitṛ.
O Agni, with your fires, increase our prayer and our sacrifice;
impel us toward the gift of wealth for the sake of the gods.
O Agni, son of strength, this singer has found refuge in you alone; for there is no other kinship than yours.
For your protection is auspicious and provides triple shelter; keep the weapon of those who would harm us far away.
O Agni, your births are like a downward slope for one who seeks nourishment; like a companion, you reach down toward all beings.
May our steeds and our prayers win the prize; they move forward of their own accord like a herdsman leading his cattle.
Or indeed, O self-dependent Agni, you spare much brushwood as you devour it; even the fallow lands become mere mounds. Let us not provoke your fierce weapon with our might.
When you go devouring over the heights and down into the depths, you spread out like an eager army;
when the wind blows after your flame, you shave the earth as a barber shaves a beard.
His lines of chariots were seen returning; there was but one path, yet many were the chariots, when you, O Agni, stroking your arms, reached down from above toward the earth spread out below.
Let your strength rise up, let your flame rise up, and let your powers rise up, O Agni, as you exert yourself.
Expand upward, bow down as you grow; may all the Vasus sit upon you today.
This is the gathering place of the waters, the dwelling of the ocean; prepare another path than this one, and go along it according to your desire.
In your coming and in your going, let flowering durvā grass grow;
let there be lakes and lotuses—these are the dwellings of the ocean.
Even that Atri, who had grown old in the *ṛta*, you made fit for his purpose like a horse for its journey;
when you restored Kakṣīvat, you made him new again like a chariot.
Like that very horse, the prize-winner whom the dustless ones have stretched out,
you two have unfastened Atri, the youngest, like a firm knot, from the mid-air.
O Heroes, most wondrous in deed, O radiant ones, bestow your favors upon Atri;
for then, O Heroes of heaven, our hymn of praise shall never cease for you.
O Aśvins, rich in bounty, let that gift and your favor come to us,
so that you two heroes may carry us across in the battle at our broad dwelling.
O Nāsatyas, you two went with winged birds to Bhujyu, who was tossing about in the ocean at the far shore of the firmament; you brought him back for his rescue.
Come to us with your favors, O most bountiful ones, like two bringers of peace, you who possess all knowledge;
O heroes, provide for us nourishments that swell like a spring.
For this immortal drop of yours, O Indu, hastens like a steed—
the skillful one, the life of all— for the Ordainer.
This poetic power, this *Ṛbhu*-like thunderbolt, is with us for the liberal giver;
it bears aloft the sharp-edged intoxication, like the effective, creative exhilaration of the *Ṛbhus*.
The impetuous bull has looked down upon these his own wives for the sake of the active falcon,
O Ahīśuva.
That which the fair-winged one, the son of the falcon, brought from afar— that which has a hundred wheels and whose path is the sky.

That lovely, ruddy form of the soma-juice, free from predators, which the falcon brought for you with his foot—that very thing has extended our vitality and the span of our life; through it, kinship has remained awake.
Thus, O Indra, by means of the Soma-drop, you have restrained even among the gods that great hostility.
Through wisdom, O wise one, you have extended our strength and our lifespan; through wisdom, this pressed juice has been offered from us.
I dig up this herb, this plant most powerful,
by which one repels a rival wife and by which one wins a husband.
O you with upturned leaves, auspicious one, impelled by the gods, victorious one:
blow away my rival; make my husband mine alone.
I am the superior one; may I be superior to those who are superior. And let her who is my rival be inferior to those who are inferior.
I do not even utter her name; she finds no delight in this man.
We send the rival wife away to the furthest distance.
I am the conqueror, and you are the victorious one. Having both become powerful, let us together overcome my rival wife.
I have brought to you the subduing one; I have overcome you with greater power.
May your mind run toward me like a cow toward her calf; may it run along the path like water toward the furrow.
O Forest, O Forest, you there who seem to vanish away—why do you not ask the way to the village? Does fear not seize you?
When the cicada chirps in response to the screeching of the cricket,
the forest goddess exults as if she were being driven by clashing cymbals.
And it is as if cattle are grazing; it appears like a dwelling house. And the forest-path at evening lets out its sounds like carts.
"He calls the cow by his limbs; he has felled the wood with his limbs.
Living in the forest, one thinks at evening, "He has bellowed."
The forest does not kill unless another approaches it;
having eaten sweet fruit, it lies down at its pleasure.
I have praised Araṇyānī, the mother of wild beasts, who has the scent of ointment, who is fragrant, who provides much food, and who requires no plowing.
I place my trust in your first wrath, when you slew Vṛtra, the manly one, and set the waters free;
when both world-halves submit to you, even the earth trembles at your might, O wielder of the stone.
O blameless one, with a mind seeking glory, you crushed Vṛtra—the master of magic—with your own magical powers.
Men choose you alone in their quests for cattle; they choose you at all sacrifices where oblations are offered.
O much-invoked one, take pleasure in these patrons who, O Maghavan, have increased as they have attained wealth.
They sing praises for their offspring and descendants in times of distress, seeking the prize-winner at the winning of wisdom and in the contest for undiminished riches.
He indeed shall take pleasure in well-sustained wealth, he who understands his exhilarating and impetuous joy.
O Maghavan, the one who increases you and performs the sacrifice with offerings quickly brings forth booty and riches through his men.
O Maghavan, being praised, by your greatness grant wide space to our host; bestow wealth upon us.
You are Mitra and Varuṇa, the master of wondrous power; like a dispenser of food, O wonder-worker, you distribute it to us.
Having pressed the soma, O Indra, we praise you, and having won the prize, O you of many heroic deeds;
bring us prosperity for which we long, so that, protected by you, we may win it ourselves, for ourselves, and for our offspring.
Lofty indeed art thou, O heroic Indra, born to overcome the Dāsa tribes with the Sun.
Like Soma at its source, we bear within us that which was placed in secret, hidden, and concealed in the waters.

Or let the wise singer, longing for the favor of the seers, chant his songs toward the noble one. May we be those who take delight in the Soma offerings, and may they likewise rejoice in the food portions borne by your chariot.
O Indra, hero, I have recited these prayers for you; grant strength to men from among men.
Be of one mind with those in whom you take pleasure; protect both the singers and their families.
Hear the call, O hero Indra, from the broad earth; you are praised by the hymns of Venya.
As the wave flows to the depths through the channels, so let your swift-moving songs flow toward your ghee-filled womb.
With his guiding powers, Savitṛ has set the earth in motion; in a supportless space, Savitṛ has fixed the sky.
Like a horse, he has milked the roaring atmosphere; Savitṛ has bound the ocean fast within the unswerving realm.
Where the ocean was fixed and roared, Savitṛ, the Son of the Waters, knows that;
from there the earth arose, from there the mid-air emerged, and from there heaven and earth were spread out.
Then this other, worshipful thing came into being through the abundance of the immortal world:
the fair-winged Garuḍa, indeed, was born first from Savitṛ; he follows his law.

Like cattle toward the village, like a warrior toward his horses, like a lowing cow, well-disposed, yielding milk to her calf— like a husband to his wife, may Savitṛ, the upholder of heaven, possessor of all boons, come down to us.
O Savitṛ, just as Hiraṇyastūpa, the Aṅgiras, invoked you for this prize of victory, so do I,
praising and adoring you for protection, remain watchful for you as for a stalk of Soma.
Though already kindled, you are kindled again, O bearer of oblations to the gods.
Come to us with the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus; come to us for our mercy.
Enjoying this sacrifice and these words, come hither; O kindled one, we mortals invoke you, we invoke you for mercy.
I praise you, Jātavedas, the possessor of all boons, with my inspired thought;
O Agni, bring hither to us the gods who are true to their vows, for the sake of mercy, those who are true to their vows.
Agni the god became the domestic priest of the gods; men and seers have kindled Agni.
I invoke Agni for the winning of great wealth—him who is gracious—for the winning of wealth.
Agni protected Atri, Bharadvāja, and Gaviṣṭhira; he protected Kaṇva and Trasadasyu in battle.
Vasiṣṭha, the domestic priest, invokes Agni for mercy—the domestic priest for mercy.
By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered.
We proclaim faith with our speech upon the summit of fortune.
O Śraddhā, make this which I have uttered dear for one who gives, dear for one who desires to give, and dear among those who enjoy and sacrifice.
Just as the gods established faith among the fierce Asuras,
even so, establish this our proclamation among the liberal patrons who perform sacrifice.
The gods and those performing sacrifice wait upon Faith, with Vāyu as their guardian;
through Faith and with a purpose of the heart, one finds wealth by means of Faith.
We invoke Faith in the morning, Faith at midday; we invoke Faith at the setting of the sun. O Faith, inspire us with faith here!
Truly, you are a great ruler, a wondrous devourer of enemies;
he whose friend is never slain nor ever overcome.
Bestower of well-being, Lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of the foe, the sovereign;
may Indra, the bull, the drinker of Soma, who grants us fearlessness, go before us.
Drive away the Rakṣas, drive away the adversaries; shatter the jaws of Vṛtra.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, crush the fury of the enemy who assails us.
O Indra, strike down our adversaries; cast those who attack us low. Whoever seeks to harm us, send him down into the deepest darkness.
O Indra, turn away the mind of the hater, turn away the weapon of him who seeks to conquer us.
Grant us protection from his wrath; drive far away his deadly blow.
Moving to and fro, the active ones wait upon Indra at his birth,
having obtained excellent heroic power.
O Indra, you are born from strength, from power, and from might;
O bull, you are indeed a bull.
O Indra, you are the slayer of Vṛtra; you have extended across the mid-air, and you have propped up the sky with your might.
O Indra, you bear in your arms the hymn that is in harmony with you,
whetting the thunderbolt with your might.
O Indra, you are the conqueror of all beings by your might;
as such, you have pervaded all the worlds.
For some the Soma is purified; others attend to the clarified butter;
may he go even to those for whom the honey flows forth.
Those who are unassailable through austerity, those who have gone to heaven through austerity,
and those who have performed great austerity— may he go even to them.
Those who fight in the great battles, the heroes who sacrifice their bodies,
or those who give away a thousandfold dakṣiṇā— may he go even to them.
O Yama, may he go even to those ancestors who were formerly observers of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), upholders of the order, and increasers of the order, who practiced ascetic heat (*tapas*).
O Yama, go also to the seers who are rich in austerity, born of austerity, those poets with a thousand paths who protect the sun.
O one-eyed, misshapen Arāyī, you who are ever-seeking, go to the mountain!
With the warriors of Śirimbiṭha, with them we drive you away.
Driven away from here, driven away from there—let her who has harmed all embryos be driven off!
O Brahmanaspati, go forth, O sharp-horned bull, against the Arayi!
That wood which floats there on the far shore of the river, devoid of men—
seize it, O you of evil intent, and by means of it go to the furthermost distance!
When you went forward, O frogs, with your bellies like copper,
all the enemies of Indra were slain, their lives as fleeting as bubbles.
These have led the cow around; they have carried Agni around.
They have established glory among the gods—who shall dare to attack them?
May our prayers impel Agni like a swift horse in races;
through him may we win prize after prize.
O Agni, with that army of yours through which we win back the cattle,
send that forth for us to gain wealth.
O Agni, bring us solid wealth, vast and rich in cattle and horses; anoint the hole, turn back the miser.
O Agni, you have caused the sun, the ageless star, to ascend to heaven;
bestowing light upon all people.
O Agni, you are the banner of the people, the most beloved and the best, seated upon the sacrificial altar; be mindful of the singer, bestowing vital strength upon him.
May we now bring these worlds to fulfillment, O Indra and all the gods.
May Indra, together with the Ādityas, fashion for us the sacrifice, our own bodies, and progeny.
May Indra, together with the Ādityas and the host of Maruts, be the protector of our bodies.
When the gods, having slain the Asuras, went forth, guarding their divine status.
They brought the sun hitherward with their skillful works; then indeed they beheld his vigorous self-power all around.
May Sūrya protect us from heaven, Vāta from the intermediate space, and Agni from earthly beings.
Be pleased, O Savitṛ; your flame deserves a hundred libations.
Protect us from the falling lightning bolt.
May the god Savitṛ grant us sight, and may Parvata also grant us sight;
may Dhātṛ bestow sight upon us.
Bestow sight upon our eye, sight for us to see clearly with our bodies;
may we behold this world both together and apart.
O Sūrya, may we behold you who are so beautiful to look upon; may we, with eyes that watch over men, see clearly.
Yonder sun has risen; here has my good fortune arisen. Knowing this, I, the victorious one, have won over my husband.
I am the banner, I am the head; I am the fierce one who pronounces the verdict.
Let my husband attend to the will of me, the victorious woman.
My sons are slayers of enemies, and my daughter is a sovereign queen; moreover, I am victorious, and my fame among my husband is supreme.
By means of that oblation with which Indra, having performed the rite, became preeminent in glory—O gods, I have now performed this very act; indeed, I have become free from rivals.
Free from rivals, slayer of rivals, victorious, and all-conquering— may she take away the splendor of the others, just as one takes the wealth of those who are weaker.
I have completely conquered these co-wives, I who am the overcomer, so that I may rule supreme over this hero and over the people.
Drink of this potent, overflowing draught; unyoke your two bay steeds here along with all your chariot.
O Indra, let not other sacrificers detain you; these juices have been pressed for you alone.
For you the juices have been pressed, and for you they shall be pressed; the strengthening songs call upon you.
O Indra, enjoying this libation today, you who know all things, drink the Soma here.
Whosoever, desiring the gods, presses Soma for him with a yearning mind and with his whole heart—for him Indra does not give up his cattle; he makes that [Soma] for him both praiseworthy and lovely.
He remains unnoticed by this one who, though wealthy, does not press Soma for him; Maghavan casts that man down into the pit and slays his haters of the sacred word without being commanded.
Desiring horses, desiring cattle, and desiring strength, we call upon you to come to us. Serving in your new favor, O Indra, may we invoke you for our good fortune.
I release you with this oblation so that you may live, from unknown consumption and from royal consumption;
if the *grāhi* has seized him, O Indra and Agni, release him from her grasp.
Whether his life-span is exhausted, or he has passed away, or has already been led into the presence of Death—I bring him back from the lap of Destruction; I have rescued him for a hundred autumns.
With an oblation that has a thousand eyes, a hundred autumns, and a hundredfold life-span, I have brought him hither;
so that Indra may lead him for a hundred autumns to the further shore of all misfortune.
Live for a hundred autumns, increasing in strength; live for a hundred winters and a hundred springs.
May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati restore this man to a life of a hundred years through this oblation.
I have brought you back; I have found you. You have returned, renewed. O you who are whole in every limb, I have found for you your entire sight and your entire lifespan.
May Agni, in accord with the sacred word (*brahman*), acting as the slayer of demons, drive away from here the disease that,
having an evil name, has settled upon your womb and your embryo.
Whatever disease of evil name has settled upon your fetus or your womb—
Agni, together with the sacred word (*brahman*), has driven that flesh-eater away.
He who kills your embryo as it falls, or one that is stationary, or one that crawls;
he who seeks to destroy you once you are born—him we cause to perish from here.
He who spreads apart your thighs so that he lies between the husband and wife,
he who licks the interior of the womb— him we cause to perish from here.
Him who approaches you as a brother, having become your husband, or as a lover,
and him who seeks to destroy your offspring— him we cause to perish from here.
Him who lies down with you after having deluded you with sleep and darkness,
and him who seeks to destroy your offspring— him we cause to perish from here.
From your eyes, from your nostrils, from your ears, and from your chin— Yakṣman of the head, I tear it away from your brain and from your tongue.
From your neck, from your *uṣṇihā* joints, from your vertebrae, and from your spine;
from your shoulders and from your arms, I pull away the consumption that affects your forearms.
From your entrails, from your intestines, from the rectum, and from the heart;
from the kidneys, from the liver, and from the spleen, I pull the disease away from you.
From your thighs, from your kneecaps, from your heels, and from your forefeet—
from your hips and from your buttocks— I tear away the disease for you.
From your urethra, from your anus, from your body hairs, and from your nails—
from your entire self— I now tear away this consumption.
Born from every limb, from every hair, and from every joint— this consumption (yakṣma) from your entire self, I now tear away from you.
Go away, O Lord of the Mind; depart and move far off. Look toward Nirṛti, for the mind of the living is manifold.
They choose indeed what is auspicious as their boon; they harness what is auspicious on the right.
Auspicious is the eye in the realm of Vaivasvata; the mind of one who lives is directed toward many places.
Whatever we have committed through a curse, an execration, or an imprecation, whether waking or sleeping— may Agni place all those evil deeds and unpleasant things far away from us.
O Indra, O Brahmaṇaspati, whatever offense we commit against you,
may the wise Aṅgiras protect us from the enmity of our foes and from distress.
We have conquered today; we have prevailed; we have become sinless. May that evil intention, whether waking or sleeping, which we hate, strike him; may it strike him who hates us.

O gods, since the dove has come here as a messenger sent by Nirṛti, seeking what she desires, let us offer praise to him and perform an atonement; may it be well with our bipeds and well with our quadrupeds.
May the dove sent to us be auspicious; O gods, may this bird be sinless within our homes.
May Agni, the sage, accept our oblation, and may the winged missile spare us.
The winged missile shall not harm us; it makes its footprint upon the hearth, in the place where the fire is kindled.
May it be well with our cattle and our men; O gods, let the dove not injure us here.
What the owl cries out is in vain, and what the pigeon makes its footprint in the fire;
to him whose messenger this has been sent—homage be to that Yama, to Death!
Drive away the dove with a *ṛc*-verse; driving it out, rejoicing in the food, lead the cow around.
Causing all misfortunes to vanish, let it fly away most swiftly, leaving us strength behind.
Make me a bull among my equals, one who overcomes rivals;
make me the slayer of enemies, a sovereign ruler, and a lord of cattle.
I am here, like Indra, unharmed and uninjured, having conquered my rivals.
All these enemies of mine are now stationed beneath my feet.
Right here I bind you fast, like two ends of a bowstring with a cord. O Lord of Speech, restrain these [words] so that they shall speak only what is beneath me.
I have come as the conqueror, with the power of Viśvakarman.
I have won your mind, I have won your resolve, and I have won your assembly.
Having taken your security and well-being, may I become preeminent among you; I have stepped upon your heads.
Speak up from beneath my feet like frogs from the water—like frogs emerging from the water!
For you, O Indra, this honey is poured out; you are the sovereign of the pressed vessel.
Do you bestow upon us wealth with many heroes; you, having heated yourself with fervor, have won the light of heaven.
We invoke Śakra, the winner of light, who rejoices greatly in the soma-juice, toward the pressed draughts.
Take note of this our sacrifice here; come hither! We pray to Maghavan, the conqueror of rivals.
Under the law of King Soma and Varuṇa, and under the protection of Bṛhaspati and Anumati— O Maghavan, O Dhātṛ, O Vidhātṛ, today, being praised by me, I have drunk from your jars.
Impelled, I have made my portion even in the course of the rite; as the first patron, I have polished this hymn.
O Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, when I came to you with what I had gained at the pressing, it was in your house.
Now, the greatness of Vāta’s chariot: it goes breaking [the trees], its roar thundering;
touching the sky, it moves, making the regions ruddy, and it goes scattering the dust of the earth.
They hasten forth following the various movements of the wind; they go toward him as women to a common gathering.
With them, the god, the king of this entire world, travels in a chariot yoked with them.
Traveling by paths through the intermediate space, he does not rest for even a single day.
The first-born friend of the waters, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*), where indeed was he born, and from whence did he come into being?
The self of the gods, the embryo of the world—this god moves according to his will. His sounds alone are heard, not his form; to that Vāta we pay worship with an oblation.
May the wind blow pleasantly toward the cows; may they graze upon the nourishing plants.
May they drink from the fat, life-bestowing waters. O Rudra, be gracious to the footed creature that seeks your protection.
Those who are alike, those who are diverse, those who are of one form, whose names Agni knows through sacrifice—
those whom the Aṅgirases produced here through austerity— to them, O Parjanya, grant great protection.
Those who extended their bodies among the gods, whose every form Soma knows—
grant us, O Indra, those cows that swell with milk, rich in offspring, within our stall.
Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods and the ancestors, has brought them—the auspicious and true ones—into our cow-pen; may we abide together with their offspring.
May the radiant, lofty one drink the Soma-mead, bestowing unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice;
he who, impelled by the wind, protects by his own self, has nourished all creatures and shines forth in many ways.
Radiant, vast, well-sustained, the best winner of booty, the truth established upon the support of heaven according to the law—
this light has been born, the slayer of enemies, the slayer of Vṛtra, the greatest destroyer of Dasyus, the slayer of Asuras and rivals.
This is the best, the highest light among lights; it is called the all-conquering, the wealth-winning, the great.
All-shining, the mighty splendor of Sūrya has spread wide for us to see, along with unfailing, steadfast power.
Shining with light, you went to the sun, to the luminous realm of heaven—
by you, the All-maker, who is favored by all the gods, were all these worlds brought together.
O Indra, you protected that chariot of the one who presses the juice and desires the sacrifice;
you heard the call of the Soma-offerer.
You struck off the head of the wildly reeling Makha from his skin;
you went to the house of the Soma-presser.
O Indra, you repeatedly loosened for the longing Āstrabudhna that mortal Venya for the sake of the mindful one.
O Indra, bring that sun, which is behind, to the front,
even against the will of the gods.
Come hither with thy wood; the cows follow thy path with their full udders.
Come hither with a wealth-bestowing thought, O most liberal one, enkindling the sacrifice along with the bounteous givers.
Like those who bear the weight of their fathers, we, the bounteous givers, take up the thread once more and perform our sacrifice.
Dawn rolls away the darkness of her sister by her noble birth, following her accustomed path.
I have brought you here; be within, stand firm and unshakable.
Let all the people desire you; let not the kingdom fall away from you.
Be right here; do not waver, like a mountain immovable. Stand firm here like Indra, and maintain sovereignty here.
Indra has established this man as firm with a firm oblation;
may Soma speak in his favor, and may Brahmaṇaspati likewise.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, and firm are these mountains;
firm is this entire moving world, and firm is this king of the people.
Firm is your King Varuṇa; firm is the god Bṛhaspati.
May Indra and Agni both maintain your kingdom firmly.
With the firm oblation we touch upon Soma as something firm;
and so may Indra make the clans bring tribute to you alone.
With the *abhīvarta* oblation by which Indra was turned toward victory—
with that, O Brahmanaspati, turn us toward sovereignty.
Overpowering our rivals, overpower those who are hostile to us; stand over him who attacks us and him who bears malice toward us.
May the god Savitṛ turn toward you;
may Soma turn toward you; may all beings turn toward you, so that you may be victorious.
O gods, with that oblation by which Indra, having performed the rite, became preeminent in glory—that very thing I have now performed; indeed, I have become free from rivals.
Free from rivals, a slayer of rivals, a sovereign ruler, and all-conquering— may I be the supreme lord over these beings and over this people.
O pressing-stones, may the god Savitṛ impel you according to the sacred law. Be harnessed to the poles; press out the juice!
O pressing-stones, drive away misfortune and evil intent;
make the rays of light our medicine.
The pressing-stones, in unison, exult upon the lower stones,
bestowing manly vigor upon the Bull.
O pressing-stones, may the god Savitṛ now impel you according to the sacred law for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the soma.
The sons of the Ṛbhus have loudly proclaimed their lofty dwellings;
